GERMAN (Welland) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 181) to amend the General Railway Act of 1888.
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. German) please state briefly the purport of the Bill ?

The object of the Bill is to put the law in such a condition that persons owning property adjoining a line of railway, which property is injured or destroyed by fire resulting from the operation of the railway, will be able to secure compensation for damages more readily than under the law as it now stands. The present law makes it incumbent on owners of property injured or destroyed by fire from a railway to prove negligence on the part of the railway company. Practical experience has demonstrated that this is always difficult, and very frequently impossible. The evidence to prove negligence must he secured from the railway itself. It is quite evident that most of the locomotive engines at present on our Canadian lines of railway are equipped with screens of sufficient fineness to prevent the discharge of sparks and cinders that would be likely to set fire to the property adjoining the line of railway. But the difficulty is that the engine driver with a heavy train, coming to a piece of track on which is anything like a heavy grade, will immediately throw open the screen, the result being that large cinders, as large as an ordinary sized bird's egg will be discharged from the locomotive and carried upon property adjoining the railway. As the law stands at present, if the fire ori-Mr. SHERRITT.
ginates on the right of way and extends to property adjoining, the railway company have been held by the courts to be prima facie guilty of negligence. But if the fire originates on the adjoining property it is incumbent on the owner to prove negligence on the part of the railway company before he can recover damages. This, in many cases is impossible. For instance, a farmer has a large part of a crop of grain or hay destroyed by fire from a locomotive and sustains a loss of forty or fifty dollars. In order to prove negligence on the part of the railway company he has to ascertain in the first place, the number of the engine. That is a difficulty in itself. Then he lias to go himself or send experts to examine the engine to see whether it is equipped with a proper screen. Let ns suppose that on examination the engine is found to be properly equipped in this respect. Then, in order to prove negligence on the part of the railway company the farmer must call the engine driver to prove, if possible, that that engine driver had opened the screen allowing the free exit of sparks and cinders, which otherwise would not have escaped from the engine. We all know that when you have to prove your case with adverse witnesses you have great difficulty. The proposed amendment will absolutely overcome that. It will put the onus of proof on the railway company ; they will be compelled to prove that there was no negligence on their part. The Bill provides that if it is shown that the fire originated from sparks, cinders, or other burning substance which has escaped or has been discharged from a locomotive engine operated or being run on the line of railway, that is sufficient to fix upon the company the liability for the loss which has been sustained, unless they can show on.their part some good reason why it should not be fixed upon them. I think that the amendment is certainly in the interest of the people who own property adjoining a line of railway, and it is an amendment which fills a long-felt want throughout the country districts. I most sincerely trust it will be allowed to carry.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) please explain the object of the Bill.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY.
speechtext:
In 1893 parliament authorized the printing for the Intercolonial Railway and Prince Edward Island Rail-

way to be done in the maritime provinces as it was found to be more convenient to do it there than in Ottawa. There is a provision in the Bill to the following effect:
That the cost is not to exceed what would be charged at the bureau in Ottawa.
Now the King's Printer always certifies bills for printing as fair and reasonable ; ever since 1893 that has been the certificate put upon these bills. However, the Auditor General has decided that the certificate is not sufficient, that the terms of the statute must be carried out. Now the Order in Council is to change the law so as to authorize bills to be paid on condition that the cost does not exceed customary and fair commercial rates for similar work and for supplies of similar quantities. That is the intention of the statute, that is to , say it is to give effect to what has been done since 1893 ; but I must admit that what has been done since 1893 is to some extent a departure from the terms of the statute.

The MINISTER OP JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick) moved for leave to introduce a Bill (No. 183) respecting the Des-.iardins canal. He said : The object of the Bill is to confirm a discharge given by the governement to certain landowners within the limits of the city of Hamilton of a mortgage which was on their property. Those who are from that part of the country will remember that in 1832, Sir Allan McNab, who was then president of the Desjardins Canal Company, borrowed money from the then government, acting through the receiver general, to the extent of £5,000 to aid in the construction of that canal. To secure this money, Mr. Peter Hamilton gave a mortgage on some property which he then owned and which is now within the limits of the city of Hamilton. That property has since been subdivided and is now vested in a certain number of private individuals. The original mortgage has been lost. After having examined the question, a year ago or thereabouts, we came to the conclusion that it was possible that prescription might be invoked against the government if we endeavoured to enforce the claim when a case was brought against the different property holders, and it was then alleged that no money had ever passed in connection with this original transaction. As no money bad ever been paid over to Mr. Hamilton, and considering that during all these years we have not sought to enforce that mortgage against any one of the holders who had improved the property and who now were in possession of it, we decided not to enforce our claim. The discharge of the old mortgage was given to the persons interest-107
ed. I have personally some doubts as to the rights of the government to give a discharge of a claim of that sort. In order to set that doubt at rest we think proper now to come to parliament and get the sanction of parliament for what we did.

I desire to say a word or two in support of the Bill. As a resident of Hamilton, I am aware of the circumstances which the Minister of Justice referred to. The land covered by this mortgage is owned by hundreds of people, poor people and wealthy people ; and it would be exceedingly difficult, even supposing that it was possible, to maintain at the present day that anything was due on this mortgage from each of these people who may have been primarily liable. The amount of costs that would follow any attempt to enforce this mortgage would be something enormous. There is a grave doubt indeed whether there ever was any liability under it. Members of the legal profession fifty and sixty years ago, who were familiar with all the facts at the time regarding this mortgage, treated it as an unexisting security, as something that had no claim behind it ; and for sixty years at least this document which was again brought into existence apparently about a year ago, was treated as an absolute nullity. So that it would be a most unfortunate thing for many unfortunate poor people who own small portions of the property in the city of Hamilton, if any attempt were now made to enforce it.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Mr. LaRIVIERE asked :
1. Has the following report been communicated to the honourable the Minister of Customs :-

Winnipeg, May 12, 1903.
To the President and Members of the
, Council of the Winnipeg Board of Trade. Gentlemen,-Your committee, appointed on the 11th May to report upon -the German surtax, beg to submit the following :-
1.	That the date fixed by the government, viz., July 1, 1903, before which German goods, to escape the surtax, must be entered for consumption, and duty paid, will not allow sufficient time for Canadian importers to receive goods for which bona fide orders were placed before April 16th last. A large quantity of such purchases are for fall and winter delivery ; and in some cases importers have sold these goods on the old tariff. And we would, therefore, suggest that the board should strongly urge upon the government the necessity for an extension of the time to September 30, 1903, in which bona fide purchases may be entered for consumption in this country at the old rate of duty.
2.	That as Winnipeg and other western points are situated at long distances from the seaboard (transportation talcing from two to six weeks from Montreal and other eastern Canadian ports), legislation providing for a uniform date of entry would greatly discriminate against the larger portion of Canada. And it would, in our opinion, be only a matter of justice to all parties concerned that the arrival of goods at any seaport in Canada in the vessel in which they are shipped should be considered evidence by the government of their arrival ; and additional time allowed to pass entry and pay the duties on such goods reaching their final port of destination.
Respectfully submitted,
Chairman Committee. 2. Is it the intention to so extend the date fixed by the government, viz., July 1, 1903, bo as to give ample time to western importers to enter at the old rate of duty ?

1.	Yes. .
2.	As this is a subject that has not only engaged the attention of the Winnipeg board of trade, but of traders throughout the Dominion, I will say a few words in reference to it so that business men may be apprised of the action which the department, sanctioned by the Governor in Council, are about to take. The resolution before the committee defined that goods ordered prior to tile 16tli of April should be admitted without tlie surtax being charged, provided the goods were for immediate transportation. The time had to be defined by the department, and we thought that by giving ten weeks we would allow time either to cancel the orders that had been given or to make arrangements to transfer the goods via some other country. That notice reached the business men of the community, but very soon afterwards communications from all parts of the country reached the department pointing out that there were exceptional circumstances connected with the German trade, particularly that some kinds of goods were ordered and had to be made after the order went in, such as goods for the holiday trade, and it was impossible for the merchants to cancel the order, and even
Mr. LaRIVIERE.
if they did cancel it they would be in this position, that travellers had already been on the road with samples selling them. The department after considering the matter and finding that a greater portion of the orders would be covered by the 30th of September, instead of the 30th of June, it is my intention to recommed to my colleagues an extension of time, maintaining firmly that the order must have been actually placed before the 16th of April, but that the time for the importation under the term ' immediate transportation ' shall be extended to the 30tli of September. With reference to the second suggestion of the Winnipeg board of trade, that inasmuch as goods landed in Canada might require some weeks before they reached the port of destination and make entry, to require not only that goods should be landed in Canada, but entered in Canada, would be manifestly unfair. The department has no desire to deal inequitably with any merchants living in any part of the country, and it is the intention to have that rectified by providing that the arrival of the goods at any port in Canada shall be sufficient notice to the depaitment.

speechtext: I just wish on this item to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) to the point I raised some time ago. It is that prisoners of all grades are carried in the North-west Territories as first-class passengers and they sit in the coaches with those who have purchased first-class tickets. I drew the attention of the House some time ago to the fact that last fall there was a murderer and two or three other condemned criminals of the lowest type travelling from Edmonton to Regina in a car, and sitting in a seat adjoining a number of students who were going to attend the Normal School at the latter place. In Ontario and other parts our volunteers have to travel second class, and they have frequently been known to travel in box cars and cattle cars. I think it is a very improper thing that criminals should be allowed to travel in coaches with ordinary passengers.

I think this is a matter which ought to be dealt with by the mounted police. The mounted police have charge of the conveyance of prisoners in the North-west Territories, and I apprehend that because officers connected with the police like to travel first-class they take these prisoners with them. However, now that our attention is drawn to it, I think that practice should be avoided if possible.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: We want something more than to be left at the mercy of the mounted police, although I always stand up for the mounted police. I am perfectly willing that the mounted police should be able to have every possible comfort, but I object to these prisoners riding in that way. Do I understand that the Hon. Minister of Justice will give the subject his attention ?
I will have the attention of the officers of the mounted police drawn to this remark.
What is covered by this item ?

I think this is practically all expended in the Northwest Territories. Judging from the way in which it is drafted you would imagine that it was intended to cover expenditures other than those in the North-west Territories, but as a matter of fact, it is almost entirely expended there. It covers for instance the maintenance of prisoners at police barracks; transport of prisoners by North-west mounted police; Crown prosecutors; legal services and expenses; jury and witness fees; coroners inquests; sheriffs' fees; clerk of courts, &c. Last year these services cost; Maintenance of prisoners, $11,224; jury and witness fees, $11,673; transport of prisoners, $3,847; sheriffs' fees and expenses, $761 ; extradition fees, $2,091; and so on.

Yes.
Travelling allowances and expenses of judges In Manitoba, $3,000.
Is this the usual sum for this purpose.
Yes. This amount has been paid under authority of Order in Council since 1882, and there has been no variation.
There are travelling allowances for all the judges in all the provinces.

Yes, but they are dealt with differently. In Ontario a round sum is paid each year to each judge, and in Quebec there is an allowance of $6 per diem while judges are attending court in other districts.
In Nova Scotia it is a lump sum per circuit.
Yes.
In Manitoba it is a per diem allowance.

It is fixed by Order in Council passed in 1882. The judge is allowed his actual moving expenses from his residence to the place where the court is held and return, and $5 per day during the time he is absent.
Travelling allowances of judges in British Columbia, $13,000.
This seems to be a large amount compared with the other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: The distances are very great in that province. The payment is based on an Order in Council passed in 1887, which says that the travelling allowances of the Supreme Court judges shall be fixed and determined by their actual and reasonable disbursements for travelling and hotel accommodation to be certified by themselves according to a stipulated form. In the case of county court judges an Order in Council of 1879 provides that each judge shall be paid his actual moving expenses from his residence to where the court is held and return, and $5 per diem for the time he is absent attending to the duties of his court.

I may say that when I was in British Columbia last fall I had quite a conversation with one of the judges, and from my experience of travelling through that province I am quite sure that they are not overpaid.
They are not.
In fact I believe they are underpaid.
Yes.

It did seem to me that the cost of living and especially the cost of travelling is much greater in British Columbia than it is in any other part of Canada. One can hardly appreciate it until he has travelled in that country, and I think the government would be justified in making an even more liberal allowance for this purpose. It is not as liberal an allowance as in the older provinces, taking into consideration the increased expenses in British Columbia.
The judges in British Columbia are paid less than is received by the judges in Quebec and Ontario.
On what basis are the judges paid for the weekly high court sittings in Ottawa and in London ?
When the judge sits at Ottawa he is allowed $25 for moving expenses and $10 for London, besides a per diem allowance of $5 during the time he is absent from his residence attending to this court.
What do you mean by ' moving expenses ' ?

I should think that would mean the ordinary transportation expenses and the per diem allowance would go to pay his board bill.
Salary of divorce and matrimonial court, New Brunswick, $500.
Is that under the statute ?
That amount is voted each year. If it were omitted from the estimates one year the judge would not have it, as there is no statute which sanctions the payment of this sum.

Is there any difference in this regard between the judge of the Matrimonial Court of New Brunswick and the judge of the corresponding court in Nova Scotia ? The Minister of Justice knows that at the time Nova Scotia entered confederation the judge holding the position of Judge in Equity was, by statute, authorized to dispose of divorce cases and matrimonial cases generally. The title of Judge in Equity has been, I think, continued in Nova Scotia for that reason; but apart from that the title of Judge in Equity has no significance in Nova Scotia, as all the judges in that province have the same general jurisdiction. Last year the hon. gentleman brought this matter up in the course of the discussion of my estimates. speechtext: There are increases of $50 each in the case of five or six officials.

For the purchase of law books and works of reference for the Supreme Court library, $4,500.

The condition of the library of the Supreme Court at the present time is not, I think, very creditable to the country or to the court or to my hon. friend's department, although I have no doubt that no blame is to be attributed to him in that regard. The books are increasing to such an extent that it is almost impossible to do any work there. The room which is now used as a library was never very suitable for the purpose, and now that the number of books has increased so very greatly, there is really no room at all for counsel. It is impossible for the officers of the court, the librarian and the assistant librarian, to do their work properly. It is impossible for counsel to prepare their briefs. The whole library is to some extent in a jumble for lack of space. Besides I believe a large number of books are stored in the attic and another large number in the cellar. I think some steps should be taken to provide the library with better accommodation. To do that may involve a larger proposition than anything we can discuss very fully this afternoon. Still, I think it is right that the attention of the government should be brought to this condition of affairs, and I am sure that my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, who has some practical acquaintance with it, will realize it just as much as I do. If my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works would go down there and look at it, his inspection would convince him that some remedy should be sought at a very early date. It is the highest court in the country, and counsel from all over Canada come there, and they have no place in which to get ready for the argument of their cases, except the library of the Supreme Court. The space formerly used as

a means of communication between the two ends of the court-house is at the present time crowded with shelving, and one can barely edge his way through it. The condition of affairs is such that I am sure my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works should consult the hon. Minister of Justice and see whether something cannot be done to improve it.

The matter has been brought to my attention by the hon. Minister of Justice, as well as by a delegation which I met some two weeks ago. Personally, I believe the best policy would be to erect a new building, especially for the court, but whether that would meet the views of my colleagues I do not know. I doubt whether any improvements could be made in the present building. The matter, however, will receive the consideration of the department as early as possible, and I hope to be able to make some recommendations at an early date.

I would like to add to what my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has said that not only is the present court building very inconvenient, but it is exceeding dangerous to have the valuable library there in the condition in which it is at present. Some of the books could never be replaced, and it would cost from $50,000 to $60,000 to replace the whole library.
There are the records of the court besides.

Yes. I visited the building with my hon. colleague the Minister of Public Works, and we agree that no improvements of any value could be made and that the whole building would have to be reconstructed.

I think that the building has been patched up as much as it possibly can be. When suggestions were made with regard to acquiring more land, I have always thought that there was no need whatever of our acquiring any more ground, as we have all we require in order to construct all the public buildings this country needs. The ground on which this building is erected, together with such additional land as could be taken in, would suffice to provide ample accommodation for the records of the court and the library and probably the Department of Justice.

I fear very much that we have not ground enough, judging by recent requirements, for the public buildings we require. I agree with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition that the site of the Supreme Court may suffice for one building, but if we are to have the public buildings required in Ottawa, I fear that it will be necessary to spread out and acquire more ground. When one looks to the great increase of business Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
during the past few years, one can form some idea of what may be the increase during the next twenty years, and we will have to face the necessity of acquiring more land for public buildings. No doubt a good building could be erected on the site of the Supreme Court. But whether it will be better to build on the open grounds is a matter for serious consideration. Opinions differ very much, but it will be most desirable to maintain the open spaces we have now and not crowd the buildings so close together.

It seems to me that if we would build a high level bridge across the canal, we have there unoccupied land belonging to the government which we might use. A portion of this is taken up by the park, but if necessary for a public building, I do not see why we should not encroach on the park. We have, however, a lot of ground unoccupied, not used for park purposes, which we might use to build on. Then there are some departments which might be further away. At Washington many of the buildings are some three miles apart, no doubt owing to the great scarcity of ground. In this city there are departments which might be transferred to another portion of the city, and which could be easily reached by the electric cars. And it would not be difficult to get ground not very expensive, but which would be a little remote from the grounds here, and which would suit the purposes of the departments which the public do not often require to visit.

The suggestion of the hon. Minister of Public Works is, in my opinion, a very good one. There is no doubt that we shall have to acquire more land to meet the requirements of the public service. I would throw out the suggestion that the government look out for some other site on which to erect a new parliament building and devote the present building to departmental purposes. In this we would be following the examples set in London and Paris and other capitals, and it seems to me that we could devise a plan for a building in which the representatives of the people could meet which would be a credit to the country at large.
