That is an amount which has been voted for several years past for the purchase of law books for the Supreme Court library. I do not think that my hon. friends who visit the library will find there is any objection to the expenditure, because we are obliged to expend a large sum for reports, for we receive the Canadian reports, also the British and the American reports that are of value. In addition, we must buy text books. Those who are obliged to maintain a working law library find it an exceedingly expensive undertaking.
One of the objections is that after you get the books you will have no place to put them.
No place to use them.
And not even much of a place to put them.

That is the great difficulty.
Exchequer Court of Canada-junior second-class clerks, $1,000.
How many junior seQpnd-class clerks are there ?
There are two in the department-one has reached the maximum of his class, and I am making special provision for the other.
Then, this covers the salary of only one clerk ?

Yes, it should read ' second-class clerk.'
Junior second-class clerk, Duncan Clark, notwithstanding any thing in the Civil Service Act, $900.
The hon. minister seems to be giving this officer three statutory increases at once.

I wish to explain the circumstances. I can fairly say with regard to the Civil Service Act that I heartily approve of the conditions it imposes on the executive with regard to the treatment meted out to civil servants. This is one of the departments controlled by the Act, and so we could not give this officer more than $50 increase in one year. But there are special circumstances in this case which lead me to come to parliament and ask its approval of what I have done in increasing his salary to the extent of $150. The registrar of the Exchequer Court, under whose immediate direction this young clerk is, wrote to the deputy minister of Justice that this young gentleman has been in the department for nine years. He says :
He has proved himself a faithful, reliable and able officer, and the work he has to do is one of responsibility and requiring skill. Mr. Clark keeps all the documents and books in this office and takes down in shorthand and transcribes on the typewriter all my correspondence. He sells law stamps and generally does all the work at the counter, and in the discharge of such duties has proved himself most faithful. I may also add that he has not yet got one annual statutory increase. I believe he is most deserving of the increase which I now recommend.
I concur in the recommendation of the Deputy Minister of Justice, and I think it my duty to come to the House and get the statutory increase which has been recommended.
Has he been getting the regular or statutory increase from year to year ?

With one exception, in 1897. From the information which was furnished to me about this young gentleman by the registrar of the exchequer court, if they were deprived of his services now they would find it very difficult to replace him with the salary they are now paying, $900.

I wish to draw attention to this feature of the ease, that there are many deserving clerks in the civil service who have had no statutory increase for a good many years, some of them owing to the fact that they were in the maximum of their class and could not be transferred to another class. This clerk has been receiving the regular statutory increase, it appears, with the exception of one year; hut there are many others who have remained for several years without it, and it seems to me an injustice to them.

This is a case of special merit. This young man went into the department many years ago, and has risen to the position he now occupies. He is vigilant and active in his duties, and under these circumstances we ought to show our approbation of what he has done.

I think I can point out instances where men have been in the service over twenty years and have received no statutory increase for the last eight or ten years.
Contingencies-judge's and registrar's travelling expenses, salaries of sheriffs, &c., printing and stationery, &c., and $50 for judge's books, $1,000.

In regard to travelling expenses this is a very expensive court. The Exchequer Court sits at various places throughout the Dominion as occasion requires. If there is a case at Halifax or Vancouver originating in the Exchequer Court, and where it is necessary for witnesses to be heard, the judge goes to such place. As a result of that arrangement four-fifths of the time of the judge and registrar of the Exchequer Courtis spent in travelling about from place to place. At the present moment the judge of the Exchequer Court is at Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, trying a case. To-morrow lie may have to go. to British Columbia. I think he is careful in his expenses. I understand the expenditure stands now at the amount at which it stood in 1890. I think that is fair evidence of the fact that the judge has not been extravagant.
Additional to registrar as editor and publisher of exchequer reports, $300.

The registrar of the Exchequer Court has taken the responsibility of editing and publishing reports of the judgments rendered in that;' court, and for these services he has been receiving for many years the sum of $300. The registrar of the Supreme Court performs a like duty with respect to the judgments of that court and he also receives an additional salary.
Charles Morse, for furnishing reports of Exchequer Court decisions to legal periodicals, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $50.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: These reports are extracts of the judgments which are rendered, and are furnished to the legal papers for the information of the general public.
I do not see that the government should pay for that service. The papers who are publishing that legal information should pay for It themselves.

My hon. friend, who like myself belongs to the profession, knows that the unfortunate publishers of legal periodicals are not as a rule overburdened with this world's wealth. These periodicals, though they are exceedingly useful to the profession, are not a source of great remuneration to the publishers. As the expenditure has been going on for a number of years, it is hardly worth while to object to it now.
Salary of registrar in Admiralty, Quebec, $666.06.
With reference to this item and the next one for salary of marshall, in what way dre these officers distinct from the registrars at St. John and Halifax ? Are they paid on a different basis ?

These gentlemen who are connected with the Admiralty Court at Quebec were appointed at the time that court was a branch of the Imperial Admiralty Court, and their appointments were made subject to the approval of the home authorities. At the time of the change in our admiralty system when the A dmiralty Court ceased to be a branch of the Imperial Court and became a branch of the Exchequer Court of Canada, these officers who were then in the receipt of a salary were taken over, it was understood their salary was to continue on as long as they remained in the office at the same rates that they were then paid.

I think in the admiralty courts df other provinces the marshall and the registrar are paid by fees, which are a burden upon the litigants. I suppose the intention is, after the present incumbents cease to hold office, to place the court in that respect on the same footing as tlie courts in the other provinces.

The Act provides that when these incumbents cease to hold office their successors should come within the operation of our Exchequer Court Act, which provides that they should be paid by fees. In addition to this salary they receive fees also.
To provide accommodation when necessary for Exchequer Court in Admiralty, $300.

Is this vote usually drawn upon ? Do not the judges in the Exchequer Court and the Admiralty

Court make use of the court-house buildings Why should a stenographer travel to Ot-provided in each of the provinces ?	tawa ?

Sometimes a claim is made upon us, but this vote is not usually drawn upon. Take, for instance, the case of the Halifax court-house which, as far as my limited knowledge enables nie to speak, is under the joint control of the province and the county.
The city and county.

Yes, the city and county. A claim has been made on us by the county in respect to the occupation of the court-house by the judge of the Exchequer Court. The point is still in dispute, but it is to meet such cases that we have this vote. It has not been drawn upon to any extent.
Yukon Territory-travelling allowances of judges, $1,500.
Do the judges in the Yukon go on circuit at all ?

Very little, but they sometimes sit at White Horse and occasionally they have to move away from Dawson. I have made inquiry as to the amount spent under this vote and 1 find it is very small'as a rule.
How much was expended last year ?

I have been referred to page M-17 of the Auditor General's Report and I have looked the matter through, but I cannot find that there appears to have been any amount paid. I cannot speak with any degree of accuracy. But I asked what amount had been paid under that item, and I was told that the judges sometimes went to White Horse and that a certain expenditure was made, but that last year a very small amount was paid.
The difficulty I find about page M-17 is that there is no item at the top to show out of which vote these things have been paid.

That is the page given to me in the brief that was prepared for me in connection with my estimates, but, upon looking at the page, I find that it does not give me any information whatever. There is an item for travelling expenses of $791.75 made up as follows :
George Craig, stenographer, travel, Dawson to Ottawa and return, $322.45 ; George D. Taylor, police magistrate, travel, Bothwell, Ontario to Ottawa, and removal expenses to White Horse, $49.30.
I do not find any item showing the travelling expenses of judges.
Would the hou. gentleman explain what is the meaning of this item of $791.75 for travelling expenses ?

In respect to Mr. Taylor, I know that this expenditure was connected with his removal when he went into the country, but in respect to Mr. Craig, why we should pay his travelling expenses from Dawson to Ottawa and return, I am not in a position to say. I am quite willing to allow that item to remain over for the purpose of making inquiry as to these expenses.
Item allowed to stand.
Salaries of sheriff and clerk of Territorial Court at $4,000 each, $8,000.
In the Auditor General's Report at page M-54, there is some correspondence in reference to sheriff's fees. Would the hon. minister give us any explanation about that ?

That was a difficulty that occurred with the sheriff previous to the estimates of last year. The sheriff was in the habit of receiving in addition to the salary voted to him a portion of the fees, but last year it was decided by the government that in future he should not have the right to receive any fees.
What are we to understand by that ? Are the fees paid into the consolidated revenue fund, or are they abolished 1

They come into the consolidated revenue fund. The arrangement with the sheriff formerly was that he received a certain amount by way of salary, then he had a living allowance and lie retained one-half or one-tliird of the fees of his office. The Auditor General argued that it was doubtful whether the government had the right to make any such arrangement as that with the sheriff and after considerable discussion and some correspondence, it was decided that we would take statutory authority to pay the sheriff eacli year a fixed salary of $4,000, and take away his right to sheriff's fees. So that, the fees now go into the consolidated revenue fund.
Was that put into the form of a statute last year ?
Yes. and the salary was fixed at $4,000 a year.
Do you make an allowance to the sheriff besides that for his travelling expenses ?
We give the sheriff a living allowance in the dis-; trict.
How much ?
One thousand eight hundred a year.
And no travelling expenses ?

No.
Salaries of deputy sheriff and two assistant Clerks of Territorial Court at $1,800 each, $5,400.

Is that necessary ? We have a sheriff and a chief clerk of the Territorial Court, as well as a deputy sheriff and two assistant clerks, I would like to ask the hon. minister if he lias looked into this matter at all. I do not know whether it is necessary, but I would not think it necessary.

I have been recently pressed for the appointment of two additional clerks of the Territorial Court, and I have withstood the pressure up to the present time because I could not believe it was absolutely necessary. I was under the impression that a chief clerk and two assistants ought to do the work of the court. But, in respect to the sheriff my information is that a sheriff and an assistant are required. The courts have had a good deal of work to do during the last two or three years, and I do not think any complaints have been made that the officials have not had plenty to do. There is considerable litigation going on in the Yukon.
Salaries for two stenographers of Territorial Court at $2,000 each, $4,000.
Are these salaries in any way provided for by charges made against litigants ?

The litigants are charged an amount which is more than sufficient to provide for that expense.
Yukon-living allowance of judges at $5,000 each, $15,000.

Three or four years ago we had as an explanation of this item, that living expenses were very high in the Yukon, but notwithstanding that the cost of living Is decreasing, the allowance is kept as high as ever. What is the explanation of that ?

My hon. friend will remember the trouble we had last year with respect to the living allowance paid to the judges in the Yukon. That trouble arose out of the fact that a certain sum was allowed by the Department of Justice, and in addition to that the judges were allowed residence, and fuel and light, by the Department of Public Works. We thought It better to take the position that we should pay these gentlemen in addition to their salaries of $5,000 a year each, a fixed sum of $5,000, in view of all claims for living allowance. They now receive no per-quisities or allowances of any description that we know of, except this sum. This was done last year after the difficulty had arisen in connection with Judge Dugas. I may say that it became necessary for us to 'take action against Judge Dugas to make him account for certain perquisites he received outside of his living allowance paid

by the Department of Justice. We came to the conclusion that he should have to account for anything he was paid by any other department than the Department of Justice, and we are having that issue settled in the courts now. To avoid all possible difficulty in the future, we have decided that the judges shall each receive $5,000 a year as salary, and $5,000 as living allowance, and no more. That amount was fixed after the discussion last year in the House.
Are the judges given residences besides that amount ?

No, we do not give them anything whatever except the $5,000. We take the position that we give a judge in the Yukon $5,000 over and above what would be paid to a judge in a similar position in one of the older provinces, in order to compensate him for any additional expense he may be put to in connection with his residence in that country.

That is a good deal better system than the former system which was growing to be a scandal, because no one could tell what we were paying these judges every year or from what source it was coming. This system has the merit of showing us how much we are actually paying. I am not prepared to say whether the amount is too high or not, but it is claimed that the cost of living in the Yukon has much decreased, and if that be so, it would seem that the compensation is very ample. I see that in addition to that we are paying the sheriffs and other officials as well. I do not see why we should do that now. We are giving them good salaries, and in other portions of the country they would have to provide for their own living.

This amount for living expenses is put in the estimates every year, so that we may be in a position to reduce the amounts at any time we may think proper. It was originally suggested that the judges should receive $10,000 a year all told, and that that should be put in the statutes, but we thought it wiser to give the Yukon judges the usual salary paid to other judges in a similar position, and to vote the living allowance each year, so that we could decrease it at any time we thought we would be justified in doing so. I think, however, that the conditions have not yet reached that position where we should decrease the amount, but at all events, under the present system we can consider it each year.

The explanation af the minister appears to be satisfactory, provided that the decrease be made at as early a period as possible. I am not in a position to judge as to whether the $10,000 a year all told is too high or not, but it appears to me that it is quite questionable whether the additional $5,000 for living allowance is not

decidedly too high at the present time. We pay a judge in the province of Ontario $5,000 a year, apd out of that he has to furnish his own living. Suppose we estimate that at $3,500, and allowing, as we do, the Yukon judges $5,000 a year for living allowance, that would place their living expenses at $8,500 a year. As the result of the agitation from this side of the House last year, what has been referred to as an improper method of remunerating these judges has been done away with, and I have faith that the Minister of Justice will see to it that next session these living allowances will be revised. I do not want to put the judges in the Yukon on any unfair basis, but we should put them as nearly as possible upon an equal basis with the judges in the other parts of the country.
Did I understand the minister to say that there was a suit in progress against one of the Yukon judges to compel him to restore some moneys he has retained ?

I did not say that. Last year we had a considerable discussion here with respect to the living allowances that were paid to the judges in the Yukon. I said that they received a certain amount by way of living allowance under the authority of parliament voted in the estimates, and it was discovered that in addition to the amount paid to them by the Department of Justice, they received divers other amounts from the Department of Public Works. I did not say they received money, but they received benefits such as being allowed to reside in houses that were the property of the government, or, that the rent of their houses had been paid by the Department of Public Works, or, that fire-wood or light had been supplied to them. When the matter was discussed in the House it was my opinion that it was more or less irregular that they should receive these allowances outside of the Department of Justice, and in order to have that opinion properly tested, I drew the attention of the judge to the fact, and asked him to refund the money. He replied that he was under no obligation to do so, because that was one of the conditions under which he went into the Yukon, and as the matter was in issue between us, I thought the proper way to have it tested was by a suit, and a suit was begun.
Who is trying the suit ?
That is an insinuation which I think I must repel. It will be tried in the Exchequer Court.

Do I understand the minister to say that the suit that is being brought is to recover, amongst other things, the money which represents rental and the expenditures for fuel and lighting which were in controversy a year ago ?

Yes.
Living allowances of sheriff, deputy sheriff, clerk of the court, assistant clerks, police magistrate and stenographers of Yukon Territorial Court, at $1,800 each, $14,400.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will the minister tell us how much money Sheriff Eilbeck draws for salary, living allowances and incidentals, not only in his department, but in the other departments of the government ?	.

The hon. gentleman is rather unfair in expecting me to answer for all the other departments of the government. So far as the Department of Justice is concerned, he receives $4,000 as salary and $1,800 as living allowance.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I see he was paid also expenses in connection with the execution of O'Brien, erecting scaffold, executioner's fee, &c., $586.80.

These are expenses which are paid in the other provinces by the provincial governments. When persons like O'Brien have to be disposed of, the Sheriff cannot be expected to pay the expenses out of his own pocket.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: They cost a good deal, however. I also find that Sheriff Eilbeck is paid large sums by the Department of the Interior for selling town lots. He must be a valuable officer. I think his salary as sheriff should cover his services in selling government property at auction ; yet he is paid auctioneer's fees. I would like to know how much he draws altogether.

I cannot say how much he drew in connection with the hanging of O'Brien ; but judging from the Auditor General's report, O'Brien proved to be an expensive luxury to the Dominion of Canada. It cost a good deal to catch him and a good deal to try him, but I think the way in which he was captured and disposed of reflected great credit on the administration of justice in the Yukon, especially on the North-west Mounted Police.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I see that Mr. F. C. Wade, Crown prosecutor, got $3,000 for his services in connection with the prosecution of O'Brien. It appears to me that these officials are drawing pretty large sums.

I notice that all these officials are paid about as much for living allowances as they are for salaries. If their salaries are fairly adequate for the work done, I do not see why we should pay their board also. In no other part of Canada is it done. I could see some reason why it should have been done in the early history of that country, when living was exceptionally high ; but to-day living in Dawson is as luxurious as in most other parts of Canada, and the cost of living is not so great as it was. We pay two deputy sheriffs a salary of $1,800 each, which would be con-

sidered a fairly good salary in other parts of Canada ; and why we should add to that $1,800 more for living allowance I cannot understand. It practically means that we are paying $3,600 for a deputy sheriff in the Yukon, whereas in other parts of Canada such an official would not be paid half that amount. We are paying all these officials good salaries, and I do not see why we should pay them living allowances also.
The' MINISTER OF JUSTICE. I agree with the hon. gentleman that the officials in the Yukon are being paid reasonably good salaries, and I think the question of living allowances is one that must be considered in the immediate future ; and in view of the discussion which has taken place to-day, I will look into it very carefully. When these estimates were prepared in December last, I was told that the cost of living in the Yukon was still very high, and was fairly represented by the amount we allowed. Of course, I cannot speak from my own experience, as I have not been there ; but one of the gentlemen whom I consulted on the subject was connected with the North-west Mounted Police.

With reference to this increased cost of living in the Yukon, may I ask the minister if he knows the cause of it ? I understand that in the Yukon they are now producing grains and vegetables of the very best quality, and I fail to discover how it is that our officials there require so much compensation on account of the cost of living. I rather fear it is because of the extravagant habits they have got into, and I am not sure that this parliament is justified in cultivating those habits. Perhaps it would be wise to put a little check upon these officials, and ask them to live more as other people do.

Of course, if grain and vegetables were grown in the Yukon to a sufficient extent to meet the local needs. I would agree with my hon. friend. But if he supposes that to be the case, his knowledge of the Yukon is about as imperfect as mine. That is not my information. For instance, I have been informed that $75 a month has to be paid for a maid servant ; and if everything else costs on the same scale, one can understand what living in the Yukon means.

I understand that the hon. minister's source of information is the government officials. Of course, that does not explain why domestic help is so expensive. When there is so much immigration coming to the country, perhaps the government can do something in the way of providing increased help there.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I notice that there does not appear to be any regular scale of living allowance. The sheriff is allowed $1,800, and the police magistrate, who bears a good name-George L. Taylor-receives a salary Mr. SPROULE.
of $2,400 and a living allowance, from September 9 to June 30, of $2,433.
The police magistrate receives $1,800 living allowance.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Auditor General's Report says he receives $2,400.
That was before last year.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Besides that, he is paid $469 for a trip from Bothwell to Ottawa, nnd from Ottawa to White Horse.
When he went into the country, the expenses of getting into White Horse were allowed him.

Take the stenographer there. He gets $2,000 per year, which is the same price as a stenographer gets here, and the work is not so heavy. But in addition he gets $34 per week for living expenses. Take the deputy sheriffs, they get $34 per week for living expenses, over and above their salary of $150 per month. If you were adding ten or twenty per cent to the salaries for the increased cost of living, that would perhaps not be unreasonable, but when you double the salaries, I think you are paying too much. It cannot cost a man $34 more per week to live there than here.
I do not say that there is not a great deal in what my hon. friend has said.
If that be the case, then the hon. minister had better look into it.
Certainly.

But we have the same thing every year. Although there is partial admission of the soundness of our criticism, still from procrastination or from some other cause, the government puts off applying any remedy and there is no improvement.

There is an improvement. Formerly the sheriffs were paid salaries by way of fees, but a remedy has been applied. The question is whether $1,800 per year for living allowance is too much. My information is that it is a reasonable amount, but in view of what my hon. friend has said, I shall make further inquiries, and if I conclude that that is too much, I am not compelled to pay it. The vote simply puts a certain amount at the disposal of the government, but the government is under no obligation to pay it out. It is not a contract.
The vote is for a specific purpose, and I do not see how the hon. minister can get out of paying it. If we vote an amount for salary, we have to pay that out.

If a man is voted a certain salary then a bargain is entered into with him; but with respect to

living allowance, that is an amount which is to be paid him in addition to his salary unless we come to the conclusion that it is too high and notify him that we will not pay it. He then has the option of taking what we offer or giving up his place.

As regards the cost of living in the Yukon, let me quote a few items from the ' Dawson Times ' of April the 3rd, 1903. Butter, 50 cents per pound; fresh eggs, $1.50 per dozen; cream cheese, 50 cents per pound; lard, 35 cents per pound; potatoes, 21 cents per pound; onions, 20 cents per pound; carrots, 20 cents per pound; beets, 20 cents per pound; apples, 9 to 10 cents; oranges, 25 cents; lemons, $1.50; flour, $4 per hundred pounds; rolled oats, 20 cents per pound; sugar, 15 cents per pound. Fresh meats : sausages, 50 cents per pound; beef, 30 to 75 cents per pound; pork, 43 to 50 cents; mutton, 35 to 60; veal, 35 to 75; poultry, 45 cents; turkeys, 40 to 50 cents; ducks, 40 cents; white fish, 50 cents; oysters, $1.50- 1 do not know per pound or not. Canned fruits and vegetables, canned tomatoes, which are retailed here at 10 cents, sell in Dawson at 50 cents; beans, 25 cents; canned peas, 25 cents. These are the retail prices in Dawson. Everything seems to sell at extraordinary prices compared with the prices in Ontario. Dried apples which we can buy in Ontario at three cents, are sold at Dawson at thirty cents; peaches, apricots and pears are sold at thirty cents. Pearl coal oil sells at $7, but 1 do not know whether it is $7 per gallon or not; oats, seven cents; hay 15 cents; bran, seven and a half cents.
This will give some idea of the cost of living in the Yukon. Of course this is in the month of April when things perhaps are higher than at any other season, but according to these quotations, it would cost a man twice, if not three times as much, to actually live in the Yukon as it would in Ontario.

No doubt it would cost him a good deal more, but the hon. gentleman has partially answered himself by referring to the fact that he has quoted the market when it is at its highest. But compare some of the items with Ontario prices. Butter sells at 50 cents in Dawson and at 25 cents here, which would indicate that in the staple articles of life, the cost is twice as high as it is here. But when we give these employees $34 per week for increased cost of living, it seems to me we are giving an extravagant sum. You can get your board here at $6 per week, and if you add' $34 to that, you have $40 as the price of board per week up there, and no one will pretend to say that it would cost that much. While the cost of living is much dearer there than here, it is not dearer in proportion to the increased allowance we give these officials. The hon. minister says he is at liberty to cut down this item. But suppose he
notified one of the employees that he intended cutting down his living allowance, and the employee went on doing his work to the end of the year and demanded his allowance for living expenses as now voted, I am inclined to think that the Auditor General would say that he was entitled to it. I do not think we could prevent it.
That would be right.

That being the case, we ought to revise it. At the time this was struck I was going to mention that there were perquisites coming to these officers from many sources. I have no doubt that, with the salary, a liberal living allowance, and all these perquisites, we made their remuneration very high. And, as the cost of living comes down, we ought to reduce the allowance. But we are making no effort in that direction, so far as I know.
I would like to ask the minister from whom the- recommendation was received on which the allowances for expenses were based ? Who recommended to council to make these allowances ?

The position we took*last year, when this was fixed, was that the cost of living in the Yukon was about three times the cost of living in eastern Canada. I did not follow closely the figures given by my hon. friend from Ontario (Mr. Ross), but I should think the cost would be quite three times what it is in the east. In any event, that is the basis on which we proceeded.

I am glad the hon. minister has given that explanation, because it enables me to draw his attention and the attention of the government to a matter we discussed here last year. It seems to me there is a little government clique in the Yukon, and whatever they recommend or propose or desire they are able to have carried through. I drew the government's attention last year to the fact that men are working in the Yukon

not labourers or anything of that kind-at salaries of $100 and $150 a month, without any allowance, I refer to the telegraph operators. It will be found by the Auditor General's Report that these officers are paid only $150 a month. These gentlemen are not in the clique I mentioned, and, not being in this little particular family circle, they are not allowed this $1,800 to $5,000 a year for living expenses. They are men of intelligence, education and ability, and, besides, they have a craft at which one cannot become expert with less than from three to five years' training. I would ask the Minister of Justice if he thinks this is fair treatment for one body of men as compared with that meted out to the sheriff, the Crown prosecutor and others ?

I should not like to be asked to express an opinion

on what my colleagues may do; I have as J much as I can take care of to answer the questions with regard to my own department. But I do not think it fair to assume that this rate of living has been fixed at the suggestion of those who are benefited by it. X may say that when the rate was to be struck last year, I considered what was being paid out then, and I thought it ought to be reduced very considerably. I consulted those who, I thought, ought to be in a position to help me, including officials whose experience in that country would be likely to be useful in enabling me to judge what it would cost to maintain a man in that region. After considering the whole matter, X came to a conclusion that I thought fair. It may be that I looked at it from the generous side-I will not say that I did not; it may be that it is my nature to do so. I think I dealt fairly with these people. I may have transgressed somewhat, but I am willing to be criticised and to consider any facts relating to the matter that may be brought to my knowledge. When the supplementary estimates are before us, this matter will come up again. In the meantime I can discuss the question with those who are m a position to know, and, in that way judge as to the correctness of the conclusions we have reached.

I regret that the Minister of Labour (Hon. Sir AVilliam Mulock) was not here to hear the statement of my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) with regard to telegraph operators. These are * skilled workmen, and, in view of the fact that they must devote a number of years to their training before they can become expert in their craft, it is only reasonable that this should be allowed for in fixing their remuneration. And, if a subordinate official receives from $1,200 to if 1,800 per year for living allowance, surely the claims of the telegraph operators are deserving of consideration. The Minister of Labour or the fair wage officer ought to look into the matter.
Do I understand that this $5,000 of living allowance to the judges is not a matter of contract with the judges, but is within the discretion of the Department of Justice V

The position we took was that, under the statute, we would fix $5,000 a year as salary, and, with respect to the living allowance we would make that a matter of vote to be passed upon each year by parliament, so that each year we might reduce the allowance if we felt that the reduction of living expenses would justify it. That- is not a matter of contract at all, but it is a provision made by parliament for the maintenance of these gentlemen during the ensuing fiscal year. At any time, I take it, we could come here and say :	We will abolish the

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
living allowance altogether, or we could simply omit the item from the estimates. Or we could say :	In view of the altered
conditions in the Yukon, instead of proposing to parliament to give $5,000, we will propose to give only $3,000 or $2,500. Of course, there is a statute to fix the salary.
But once the amount is passed in the estimates and fixed for the year by parliament, the judge is entitled to it as a matter of right ?

With regard to the amount for a judge, I would say that it would be difficult to interfere with it. But with respect to an official who is not in a position to be able to say that his position is permanent, I think we can say to him :	Parliament has voted $1,800 for
your living allowance, but I consider that excessive. I would be within my right to notify an official that, in addition to his salary, instead of $1,800 living allowance, he would be allowed $1,000 or $1,200. If this were done, it would be for him to decide whether he would remain in the employ of the government or not.
But, so far as the judge was concerned, does the minister think it would be a matter of question whether their allowance was within his discretion ?
Clearly.

It seems to me that it is at variance with the principle of the independence of our judges to give the government control, practically over their salaries -for that is what it comes to. Most certainly, under these circumstances they cannot be as independent of the government of the day as-well, as the rest of the judges of the country are.
The judge is appointed by statute, and his remuneration is fixed by statute. In addition, he receives this amount, but that has nothing to do with his position.

Nothing to do with his position, but very much to do with his remuneration. As I said before, it seems to me that this is calculated to interfere very seriously with the independence of the bench, which is recognized as part and parcel of our very constitution. There are no other judges, so far as I am aware, whose salaries can be at all interfered with by the government of the day.

I think my hon. friend has suggested a broad question in bringing this matter up. But it does not go any further than we have been in the habit of going when we appoint judges, for instance, to act as commissioners and vote them remunerations in addition to their salaries. All these questions are on the same line. When parliament under-i takes to give additional remuneration to I a judge for additional services, we get on

the fringe of the independence of judges, as my hon. friend has pointed out. I remember some years ago reading an interesting article on the subject as to whether, when a judge had been appointed for the purpose of giving the whole of his time to the country, it was not unconstitutional for us to take him from the service, to the-performance of which he was appointed, under the statute, and employ him for some other purpose, or to give him any other remuneration whatever for that additional work. However, that is one of the broad questions that I think I would not like to discuss now without giving it careful consideration.

I think we might direct our attention for a moment to what has been said by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). The Minister of Justice pointed out that he has no direct control over this matter of the telegraph operators, but he tells us that his sympathies are in the line of generosity. I think we ought to enlist his sympathies on behalf of this class of persons. It is unfortunate that the Minister of Labour is not here. It would be satisfactory if we could get that hon. gentleman down to some practical action in relieving these parties who require In many instances the assistance of the Minister of Labour in order to get fair remuneration. We make a mistake in think-tbat because a man holds a pen, or fills some other jjosition that requires no particular amount of intelligence, he should get a large salary, whereas a man in a mechanical occupation which requires a good deal of skill, where he requires to be constantly on the alert, should be paid much on the line of an ordinary labourer.
Less than a Servant girl.

Yes, because according to what the Minister of Justice has said, a servant girl gets $75 and her board up in the Yukon. There seems to me to be a great disparity between the pay of these two classes of individuals. I think the scale of wages should be revised up in the line of assisting the telegraph operators, and revised down as regards these officials whose living expenses we have been discussing.

When I total up the items for the administration of justice in the Yukon, I find they aggregate $123,800. That sum is spent in a country not as big as one of our ordinary counties. It seems extravagant, and ought to be reduced.

By way of illustration, let me remark to the hon. gentleman that for the maintenance of prisoners in the North-west Territories we pay to the mounted police sixty cents per head per diem. But when you come to the Yukon the charge is $2 per head per diem. So you get some indication of the reason
why the administration of justice is so costly in the Yukon Territory. These figures show the difference in the cost of living between the two countries.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I understood the Minister of Justice to say that the living allowance for the sheriff had been fixed. What was it ?
One thousand eight hundred dollars.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will he explain why he paid $2,437.23 from September to June ?
That was for last year finishing in the month of June. The $1,800 was fixed during last session.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Could not the hon. gentleman have found a gentleman in the Yukon country suitable to be appointed police magistrate, without coming east and getting a man to whom he had to pay $461 to get him in there.
I don't think you could find a better man than Mr. Taylor.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The name is all right. He must be some party who wanted a government office pretty bad, and the government thought the best way to get rid of him was to send him out to the Yukon.

By chapter 36 of last year's statutes, we 'provided that the police magistrate may be paid, in addition to his salary, such living allowance as may be fixed by the Governor General in Council. Are all these fixed by Order in Council ?
Yes, and voted in the estimates.
I do not understand how six of the judges were paid $3,000 living allowance according to the Auditor General's Report last year. Now we are to increase it to $5,000.

My hon. friend will remember what occurred last year when these items were voted. We had a very interesting discussion with respect to the payments to Mr. Justice Dugas. At the time I contended strenuously that he had been paid nothing except what he had received by way of living allowance from the Department of Justice. A reference to the Auditor General's Report established the fact that he had been allowed by the Public Works Department certain perquisites in respect to a residence and other matters of that sort. Then the question arose whether it was proper for the Public Works Department to make this allowance. I explained a moment ago that it had been necessary for us to take a suit against Mr. Justice Dugas to recover back the money

value of the perquisites he received from the Public Works Department, as a test question to ascertain whether he was entitled to receive these perquisites. Then we determined that the salary should he fixed at $5,000, and that the living allowance should be $5,000 each year-not $10,000 together, but in addition to the permanent salary of $5,000, we might give him from year to year a living allowance of $5,000 so as to be able at any time to reduce, that allowance without interfering with the independence of the judges.

I see in the Auditor General's Report, at M-54, that the Auditor General says :
An Order in Council passed May 31 last, increases the sheriff's salary from $2,000 to $3,000 per annum, his living allowance from $1,200 to $1,800 ; and in addition allows him to retain one half'of-the fees after paying remuneration and expenses of his deputy or deputies and other expenses.
Then a little further down :
During the summer of 1900, Sheriff Eilbeck was paid $2,751.37 by the Department of the Interior for fourteen days services as auctioneer at the sale of mining claims in the Yukon.
Now, I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Justice and also that of the right hon. leader of the government to these items. We all know the generosity of the Minister of Justice because his nationality would not permit him to he otherwise, we know the generosity of the right hon. Prime Minister himself. We all admit that and we are pleased with it. I would like to draw the attention of the hon. gentleman to the great disparity that exists between one class of the employees of the government and another. The right hon. leader of the government, I have no doubt, puts In the exact farthing that it costs to maintain the mounted police. Under the department over which the hon. Minister of Justice presides it costs $2 a day to keep a convict. They do not feed these men as a rule on delicacies; at least, they are not supposed to. If it costs $2 a day to keep one of these ordinary convicts what about the poor man who gets $100 a month, pays out $60 for board and has $40 left ? In view of the fact that a member of that particular family is involved in the question, $2,751 for fourteen days work does not seem to be out of place. This government will allow It to pass unquestioned. I would like to draw the attention of these generous members of the cabinet to the position of the mounted police to see if they will not do something for these men who, I believe, are under paid.
I am sorry to say that we have been guilty of being too economical. We will try and not do it again.
Is there no answer to make to the statement that the sheriff was paid this large sum as an auctioneer In

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: addition to the salary he received for his ordinary work ?

I have nothing to say about that. It is a question as to whether or not the Department of the Interior ought to have paid the sheriff any fee for the service he rendered in connection with the sale of mining claims. He never received it from my department and I am not responsible for the payment.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The hon. minister said : We will fix the salary of the sheriff at $3,000 and give him a living allowance, hut he said nothing about retaining his fees. The Auditor General makes the statement of the receipts and disbursements of fees by the sheriff. The disbursements were as follows :-
North-west Mounted Police and others
for serving papers	$	406 00
J. M. Eilbeck, as deputy sheriff		750 00
Retained by sheriff as his share of fees. 819 53 Deposited to credit of Receiver Gen-e-ral	 819 53
Total	$2,795 06
Now, some correspondence took place with the hon. gentleman's department in which the hon. minister's deputy, Mr. New-eombe, says :
The government i-s authorized to pay him a salary of $3,000 In addition to such fees of office as may be allowed by the Governor in Council.

I thought I had made myself clear about that. Last year there was a change in the position of the sheriff. We made provision that the sheriff, instead of receiving, as he had been in the habit of receiving, a share of the fees in addition to his salary, should be paid a fixed salary of $4,000 and $1,S00 living allowance. That was to take the place of tlie fees he had received heretofore and to avoid tlie difficulty which the Auditor General had pointed out. That arrangement took effect late in the year 1901 or in the early part of 1902.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Did you also relieve the sheriff of the privilege of being employed by other departments and being paid $2,700 for his services as an auctioneer, while neglecting his duty as sheriff, working fourteen days and drawing $2,700 for it 1
The Department of Interior made that payment.

I observe that a question arose as to the collection of the fines, the correspondence in regard to which will be found in the Auditor General's Report at page M-59. The correspondence is in an unfinished condition as a reference is made to the Hon. Mr. Ross who was then the commissioner of the Yukon Territory, and it is said that the matter will be dealt with upon his return.
Are those the fines paid to the magistrates ?
I think so.

These have been paid over. The fact is that a magistrate there was of the opinion that he was entitled as part of his perquisites to receive these fines. I agreed with the position taken by the Auditor General and as a result the magistrate's cheque did not go out until he had paid these fines in.
I think it is a very extraordinary view of the situation for a magistrate to take that he would be entitled to these fines.

He argued that he was entitled to receive a portion of the fines. I never had any doubt about the matter and it was speedily disposed of when it was brought to the attention of the deputy minister and myself.
I understood the hon. minister to say that he had stopped officers receiving perquisites or salary from any other source.
I did not say ' salary from any other source.' You have the services performed as auctioneer, for instance. I could not control that.

Does the hon. minister think that the government should allow a practice like that to go on, if a sheriff gets $4,000 a year and which is supposed to pay him for all his time ? For fourteen days work auctioning off mining claims we paid him at the rate of $195 a day in addition to his salary ? Is that not an abuse, particularly when we consider that in addition to paying $4,000 a year salary we are giving him $1,800 for a living allowance ? That is $5,800 a year that he receives by way of salary and in addition for fourteen days work he gets $2,751. Does the government think this is good management or that it is not unreasonable extravagance and mismanagement of the funds of the country ? It seems to me that it is. If the sheriff is paid for every hour of his time surely he is not entitled to charge the country with a large sum of money in addition to his salary.

I do not quite agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule). The sheriff has statutory duties to perform. His duties are fixed and circumscribed by the statute. He is obliged to perform these duties and he is not obliged to perform any other. If he is called upon to perform the duties of an auctioneer, then, be can reasonably be dealt with as if he were a stranger. He is not under any obligation to sell these mining lands or to perform these duties ? If he does perform them is it not possible tbat he may be dealt with as any other stranger would be ? It is not part 108
of his duties to sell them. If it were a stranger that was called upon to perform these duties would the stranger be entitled to receive this money ? What is the difference between them, and why should he not be employed as an auctioneer, not with respect to the Department of Justice but with respect to the Department of the Interior which has no control over him and no command over his services ? That is the answer as it occurred to me, but I would like at the same time to make it clear that I am not undertaking to be responsible for what anybody else may have done. I find that my road is as hard a one as I want to travel to explain my own short-comings.

As the result of a very long inquiry in 1891, we found that many officials were receiving pay from different sources, and they set up the same justification for that as the minister now presents to the House. They said that having discharged their duty to their own department, they could sell their spare time to other departments without any injustice to the service or to the country. We found that civil servants were obtaining money from different departments while they were paid what was considered an ample salary for the services they rendered to a particular department. That was declared to be an abuse, and it was stopped. The law was amended so that if a civil servant were paid anything in addition to his salary under the Civil Service Act, it should appear in the estimates each year, and parliament if satisfied that such extra payment was justified, could then vote it after deliberation. Here we have the same abuse cropping up again, and we have the Minister of Justice giving the same justification for it as was given by the civil servants at that time.
I did not justify it.

The Minister of Justice is not responsible from a departmental point of view, because this is not in his department, but the responsibility of one minister is not confined to the minister himself. It seems extraordinary to pay $2,751 for fourteen day's work to any man, but when you find that that amount is paid to a sheriff who is in receipt of an annual salary, it does require an explanation from some member of the government who is familiar with the circumstances. We should know who was discharging the duties of the sheriff during these fourteen days when he earned a sum equal to about two-thirds of his annual salary of $4,000. It may be that the sheriff is not bound to perform these services for the Department of the Interior, but if he does he should perform them for a reasonable amount. We are entitled to an explanation from the Department of Justice as to whether the sheriff was discharging the duties of his office during these



fourteen days, because I suppose if the sheriff could earn $198 a day by conducting auction sales, he must have given his whole time to that particular work. Why, the remuneration which he received from the Department of the Interior was at the rate of $70,000 a year. I can hardly believe that possible ; surely this amount must include disbursements or something of that kind.
Are there no disbursements ?

I do not know. I cannot find out. I am not surprised that the Minister of Justice cannot tell us, but some member of the government should be able to explain what seems to be an extraordinary condition of affairs.
Is there any explanation given in the report ?

This is what the Auditor General's Report says :
During the summer of 1900, Sheriff Eilbeck was paid $2,751.37 by the Department of the Interior for fourteen days' service as auctioneer at the sale of mining claims in the Yukon.
That was paid to a salaried officer of this government; an officer who is receiving $4,000 a year as salary and $1,800 for living allowance. We ought to have some explanation of that transaction.

This item was paid in 1900, and therefore it would not come up in a discussion on the estimates of the Interior Department, but I am quite willing that this particular item should stand over, and I will get the best information I can. I recognize that something should be said about it.
That is perfectly fair.

Would the minister give us information also as to on what basis deputy clerks and assistant sheriffs and stenographers and so on, are paid a living allowance at the rate of $150 a month, while telegraphers in the employ of the government in the Yukon are receiving no allowance at all.

It was understood that this question of the living allowance would be resumed on the supplementary estimates, and I will then endeavour to deal with my own responsibility as to the question of the living allowances paid to the officials under my control.

The Minister of Justice has suggested that the cost of living is perhaps three times as much in the Yukon as it is in the east. The Yukon judges get exactly the same salary as that paid to judges in this part of Canada, and out of which the judges here are required to meet their own expenses. That certainly presents an anomaly. If the judges in the east

had a living allowance of $1,700 a year each, then according to the view of the Minister of Justice, they would only be in the position which the Yukon judges now occupy. It, therefore, seems to me that some further consideration of these living allowances is necessary. I also recognize what my hon. friend (Mr. Lavell) has said as to the undesirability, on general principles, of having what is virtually the salary of judges, fixed by Order in Council so far as one-half of it is concerned. I do not think that is a very good principle to adopt, or one that should be persevered in any longer than is absolutely necessary. I understand the reason why these living allowances were given in the first instance. It was suggested that if you fixed a salary measured by the cost of living in the Yukon, you might have that salary fixed for all time, and, therefore, it was better, until the conditions of living in the Yukon became normal, that you should pay a salary and a living allowance as well. The question is whether the cost of living is not now approaching what will be the normal level for some years to come. If this is the case, speaking for myself, I should be in favour of fixing the salary and abolishing the living allowance, not only for judges, but for all other officials in that country. However, I understand that the matter will come up again when the supplementary estimates are before the House.

The difficulty we found ourselves in was this, that if we fixed the salary of a judge at say $10,000, that would be fixed for all time. The conditions in the Yukon might at any time become normal, and we could not explain how it was that we paid so large a salary. There is also this to be considered. The residences of these judges may not be permanent. It may be considered advisable at some time to take a judge from the Yukon and bring him to the North-west Territories. In that event, with this large salary, his position would be anomalous, and not fair to the other judges. So, under all the circumstances, while I agree that the conditions are not normal, and should not be continued for a day longer than it is possible to prevent them, this is the best solution I have been able to arrive at, that we should keep parliamentary control over these living allowances, and be in a position to regulate them each session.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The hon. minister has asked that this item stand until he can get some information with regard to the large payment made to Sheriff Eilbeck by the Department of the Interior. Will he bring down information as to the time that money was paid by the Department of the Interior, the time Mr. Eilbeck received leave of. absence to leave the Yukon and come down to Ontario, and the date of the bye-election in West Durham, which was at the same time

as he was granted leave of absence, and may have had some connection with it. Perhaps there will be some explanation why he was paid this large sum of 52,700 for fourteen days' work in the fact that he camped down in the town of Bowmanville during that election.
And if there is no connection, what will my hon. friend undertake to do ?

I wish to call the minister's attention to a matter which I think requires immediate consideration. We have from the minister the fact that a lawsuit is pending against a gentleman who has acted very badly, a gentleman who was originally appointed to his position by the government, and we know that lawsuits are expensive. It is important, therefore, that the minister should carefully consider whether there is any reasonable ground for expecting that this lawsuit will be successful; because if it is not, it will only have this result, that it will be expensive to the government and that the only person who will reap a reward will be some friend of the government who may be employed in prosecuting it. My reason for directing the minister's attention to the matter is this : He tells us that a year or two ago the judges were receiving a living allowance of 53,000 a year from his department, and that they were also receiving from the Public Works Department certain perquisites which brought their full allowance up to |5,000, or perhaps more. Now, I wish the minister to take into consideration whether, in view of these facts, there is any reasonable prospect of success in this suit. We have one minister allowing 53,000 for living allowance, and another making certain allowances by way of rent, fuel, &c., towards the living expenses of the judge. How can we expect, under these circumstances, the allowances having been concurred in and probably originating with the ministry, that that same government bringing action can possibly succeed ? I do not think the attention of the Minister of Justice has been directed to that point, or I imagine that with his astuteness he would hardly expect to succeed. I believe the suit cannot be undertaken with the object of getting back this ill-gotten gain for the government, and, therefore, 1 have great confidence in submitting the matter to the Minister of Justice for consideration.

I may say to the hon. gentleman in all seriousness that I have carefully considered the question, and here is the way it appears to me : 108$
No man, whether a judge or an official of any other kind, is entitled to receive anything from the public exchequer, unless it has been authorized by statute. In this matter the Department of Justice was authorized to pay Judge Dugas a certain amount by way of salary, and a certain amount by way of living allowance. The Department of Public Works, when the judge went in there, gave him certain assistance in connection with his going in, provided him .with transportation, a house, fuel, light, and other perquisites. The question arises as to the authority of the Department of Public Works to do anything of the sort. It had no statutory authority to do it. The judge, on the other hand, says : These perquisites which I received, and the money value of which you ask me to refund, were paid to me under a contract which I entered into at the time with the government, as represented by the Minister of Public Works ; the Minister of Public. Works agreed to supply me with these requisites. The question comes back to the authority of the Minister of Public Works. The Auditor General came to the conclusion that the remedy was in his hands, and that all he had to do was to stop the monthly cheque payable to the judge, on the ground that he being indebted to the Crown and the Crown being indebted to him, he had the authority to stop the cheque. That appeared to me to be a rather high-handed proceeding, in view of the plea set up by the judge that if there were laches, the government were partly responsible for them. We have determined to try the suit with the judge and endeavour to get back these moneys, we urging that the Department of Public Works had no authority to make these advances, and the judge, on the other hand contending-I have not yet seen his defence-that the Department of Public Works, as a department of the government, made a contract with him, and that if he had not received that consideration he would not have gone in at all. There is the case, and I need not attempt to foreshadow the result. I have stated the facts and the law as I understand it, and my hon. friend must be content to let the decision remain with the judge of the Exchequer Court, always bearing in mind the proverbial uncertainty of the law.
Surely there is an anomaly which must have presented itself to the Minister of Justice, that the Minister of Public Works had the statutory authority or he could not have paid the money.
That is what I was trying to say.

With the checks we have provided against any expenditure, unless authorized by the legislature, and with the Auditor General, how could the minister possibly spend the money without the statutory authority of parliament.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Oh, there is a connection all right.	.
We still undertake to say that it is a pretty high sum to pay for fourteen days' work.
As this is an important case, might I ask who is acting for the Crown.

I am under the impression that we drew the information ourselves, but I must confess that I did not want to take the responsibility of pressing the suit myself, as we had been in the habit of doing, through the action of the Deputy Minister of Justice, but handed it over to Mr. Chrysler or Mr. McDougall, 1 do not remember which. The information however was draughted by the deputy minister, and there is no man more competent to do it.

I quite appreciate the force of what the hon. Minister of Justice has said. He puts an entirely new feature of the matter before the committee. I had no reason to apprehend that there was so great an irregularity as is disclosed by what the hon. minister has told us, but even should the suit result disastrously as to costs, if it is shown that the government may be estopped by the action of its ministers, that will be a useful piece of information for the country, and we will probably not be paying too high a price for it.

The DEPUTY SPEAKER took the Chair at Three o'clock.

The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick) moved that the House go into Committee of the Whole to-morrow to consider the following proposed resolution :
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Supreme and Exchequer Courts Act, the Exchequer Court Act, and the Act respecting the Judges of Provincial Courts, and to provide as follows :-
1. If any judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, or of the Exchequer Court of Canada, or of any Superior Court in Canada, resigns his office. His Majesty may, by letters patent, under the great seal, reciting such judge's age and period

of service, grant unto him an annuity equal to the salary of the office held by him at the_ time of his resignation ; to commence immediately after his resignation, and to continue thenceforth during his natural life, provided such judge has (a) attained the age of seventy-five years, and continued in office as judge of one or more of the said courts, or as such judge, and as stipendiary magistrate of the North-west Territories, for twenty years or upwards ; or (b) attained the age of seventy years and continued in office as judge of one or more of the said courts for twenty-five years or upwards ; or (c) continued in office as judge of one or more of the said courts for thirty years or upwards.
2. Every County Court judge who has attained the age of seventy-five years shall be compulsorily retired ; and His Majesty may, by letters patent, under the great seal, reciting such judge's age and period of service, grant unto him an annuity, if he has continued in office as such judge for twenty-five years or upwards, equal to the salary of the office held by him at the time of his retirement ; or if he has continued in office as such judge for a less period, equal to two-thirds of such salary ; the said annuity to commence immediately after his retirement, and to continue thenceforth during his natural life.

Before you leave the Chair, I would like to bring to the attention of the government a matter of some importance, and as to which I think there should be some announcement of policy by the government at the very earliest possible moment. In the speech from the Throne we find this passage :
The great influx of population into our Northwestern Territories and the very large additional areas of fertile lands which are being brought under cultivation, combine to further press upon us the need for increased transportation facilities for the forwarding of our grain and other products to the markets of the world, through Canadian channels. The whole question of transportation and terminal facilities continues to occupy much attention, and my government will immediately appoint a commission of experienced men to report on the subject.
That speech was delivered to parliament nearly eleven weeks ago, and up to the present time we have had no announcement of policy, and no commission lias yet been appointed. The utmost we have been able to obtain in the way of Information on this subject is from one of the ministers of the Crown, some four or five weeks ago, who announced in the city of Montreal that certain gentlemen were to compose this commission. But there was some question as to whether he announced that as a matter that had been determined upon, or merely as a sort of prophecy witli regard to the gentlemen who would probably occupy places

Unless the Grand Trunk Pacific build their line through to some maritime province port we believe the export business will continue to go through an American port as in the past.
Mr. Hays rightly says shippers can route freight as they please and if the Grand Trunk are interested in route via Portland, shippers can be easily influenced to route practically every ton of export freight that way.
We cannot believe that any arrangement can be made between Intercolonial and Grand Trunk which will prevent this.
We urge in the strongest terms that no government assistance be granted to any transcontinental railway that does not undertake to build their line through to some maritime province port.
I must confess, that, having regard to the conditions as they are in Canada at the present time in regard to the Grand Trunk Railway, I have not been able to reach a conclusion that such guarantees as have been spoken of in the press and in these resolutions, can be very easily enforced or carried out. I should be glad indeed to see the Grand Trunk Railway taking its part in the solution of Canadian transportation problems, and I hope it will be able to do so, but we have to consider conditions as they are and we know that the interests of the Grand Trunk Railway to a very considerable extent are, of course, centred in a winter port in the United States in which it has expended a very large amount of money in terminals and shipping facilities. The subject is one that I have not been able to consider carefully or attentively, and I am not professing to express an opinion upon it at the present moment, but, be that as it may, I think the House and the country are entitled to hear from the government an announcement in regard to this very important subject. Is the government in a position at the present time to say to the House and the country in what way it proposes to deal with this transportation problem ? Is it able to disclose to the House and the country any really comprehensive national policy by means of which it may be able to deal with this question of transportation in the west and in the east also ? We know that not on'y in the west of Canada, but in the east of Canada as well, it is of the utmost possible importance to the people, it is vital to the interests of the people that they should have means of transporting their products to the foreign market equally as cheap and equally as available as those which are enjoyed by their competitors to the south of us, and we know that it is otherwise impossible for our people in the east or in the west to compete on fair conditions with their chief competitors, the people of the United States of America.
Now, has the government any policy upon this matter which it is prepared to disclose to the people of this country, and if it has not any policy at the present time when may we expect that its policy shall be announced to the country ?

It is some eleven weeks since this session began. It is no new question. Transcontinental lines have been engaging the attention of the people of Canada for a year at least. During last session it was currently said that great pressure was placed upon the government for the purpose of inducing it to grant aid to a proposed transcontinental railway and the right hon. leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) made a statement in the House during the latter days of the session in which he announced, as far as I recollect his language, that the government would come to a conclusion in' regard to the matter at an early day, but that they were not able at that time to make any announcement to the House.
There are some interesting problems in connection with the transcontinental railway question at the present time. There are some interesting questions arising in connection with it. For example, has the government at the present time determined whether or not it will grant assistance to a transcontinental railway, and if it has decided to grant any such assistance is it prepared to state what form that assistance shall take ? I think this is a matter upon which it is right that the House and the country should be informed while this Bill, to which I have alluded, is under consideration by the railway committee.
In the next place, has the government any policy in regard to the construction of an additional line from Winnipeg north of Lake Superior so as to connect with the east ? This is a subject which is discussed very much in the public press at the present time, and it is one of tbe gravest possible importance to the country. Has the government come to any conclusion as to whether or not the congestion in the west can in any way be relieved by the construction of another line north of Lake Superior ? Is it a fact, as has been stated in the public press and as has been stated, I think, by public men in this country, that tbe present line which runs north of Lake Superior does not command one-fifth, or even one-tenth, of the traffic which it would be capable of handling, and if that be a fact does the government seriously think that the building of another line north of Lake Superior will in any way relieve the difficulties with which transportation between the east and west is confronted at the present time ? Whether or not the government lias any policy, or any ideas upon this subject I do not know, but it does seem clear, speaking with all deference, that this is a subject upon which the government should have made up its mind before this, and it is a subject upon which it should have been prepared to state to the House and to the country what it intends doing.
Has the government any policy in regard to the proposition of my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock), who seems to adopt the view that the best

solution of the difficulty is to build a line which can be used in common by all railways between Port Arthur and the east, or between Winnipeg and the east, and in that way assist in bringing the produce of the west to the east at such rates as will enable our people in the west to compete on fair terms with the people of the United States ?
And let me ask this, especially : What guarantees or safeguards does the government think necessary, or efficient for the purpose of seeing that traffic over any transcontinental railway to which assistance shall be afforded shall be carried from the east to the west of Canada through Canadian routes and shall leave Canada for the markets of Europe by Canadian ports ? What is the policy of the government with regard to that ? Does the government regard that as a sound policy, and if so, in what way does the government expect to meet the difficulty pointed out by the telegram from St. John which I have read to the House, and which, quoting the language of Mr. Hays, says : Traffic must be routed in accordance with the wishes of the shippers. I think we might even go further than the business men of St. John have gone. Suppose that the Grand Trunk Railway should construct its line to the maritime provinces; suppose that it made connection with a port in the maritime provinces, what guarantee can you have, what safeguard can you have that the traffic from our Canadian west shall go through Canadian routes and via Canadian seaports.
Lastly, but not the least by any means ; why is it that the government has so long delayed the proposal which they laid before the House and before the country at the opening of the session ; why is it that they have so long delayed the formation of this commission on transportation. If we are to have in Canada any broad comprehensive policy of transportation, it seems to me that the government must call to its assistance the very best experts with regards to such matters that this continent can produce. It is not any ordinary problem that confronts the government of this country at the present time with regard to transportation, and so we understand from the speech from the Throne :
The whole question of transportation and terminal facilities continues to occupy our attention and my government will immediately appoint a commission of experienced men to report on the subject.
If what we hear through the press, the organs of public opinion which are in very close touch with the government; if what we hear is true, the government proposes to deal with this question without obtaining the slightest assistance from the commission which is proposed to be formed; indeed it would appear that the government is likely to deal with the matter even before the commission has undertaken its work.
I would submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that on a question of this kind which touches the whole future history of the transportation question of this country, the government ought not to take any leap in the dark, it ought not to take any step at haphazard. If the government proposes to appoint a commission it should have appointed that commission long ago, and that commission should have been at work dealing with and studying the very problems of transportation which are now confronting the government. I submit that whether the government proposes to deal with the matter in that way or not, it is highly right and proper at this stage, when a very important measure is engaging the attention of a committee of this House, that the government should give to the country some indication of what its intentions are with regard to this matter, and should thus enable the House and the country to deal with the question of transportation between east and west in a more intelligent way than it otherwise could. I think therefore, Mr. Speaker, that under the circumstances, I am justified in asking the Prime Minister to take the House and the country into his confidence with regard to this matter, and to mftke that announcement of policy which it seems to me should have been made long ago in this session which has already occupied nearly three months ; and to state to us fully and frankly what we are to expect from the government in the shape of a policy on a question of so much importance to the most vital interests of the country.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

I have to express my regret that my bon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) did not give me any notice of his intention to bring before the House such an important question as this. I would have been able to give him more information than I feel warranted in doing at this moment had he given notice, but at all events, I shall endeavour, though it be on the spur of the moment, to give to lion, gentlemen all the information to which they are entitled on this question which is no doubt of very great moment. In my humble judgment, the transportation question under existing conditions, resolves itself into three different parts. First of all there is the question of water transportation, chiefly connected with the terminals.
