Then there is the transportation question for the new and rapidly growing settlements in the prairie sections ; and then there is the question of transportation from the prairie sections to the seaboard. With regard to the first, this is the question which we had chiefly in our minds when at the opening of parliament we declared that the transportation question was engaging our attention, and that we intended to appoint a commission to deal with the subject. We

have been carrying on works of great magnitude at all parts of our great water system, in order to develop it and to make the transportation of the products of the west, and of the products going from the east to the west cheaper to the producer and to the consumer. We have works on the great lakes ; we have works on the St. Lawrence ; we have works at Port Arthur and Fort William, and it is possible that we may require some more. We have works at the head of canal navigation at Port Colborne which are now under construction ; we have works in the city of Montreal which have been carried on both by the Harbour Commission there and by the government; we have works at Sorel and Three Rivers carried on by the government; we have works at Quebec and we have also extensive works in St. John, New Brunswick. Now. 1 think it may be said that all these works have been carried on, not under any general system, but chiefly from the local point of view of each particular place. We deem it of the greatest importance to have, if possible, all these different works carried on under a general comprehensive system. Before we ask for more money to be expended upon them, we think that it is advisable to have the report of a commission of the best experts that we have in the country in order that we may be able to lay before parliament at this session or next session a comprehensive plan, as to what should be done in these different localities or in other localities in order to meet the object in view. I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) that the commission has been organized, and not later than tomorrow its terms will be laid on the Table of the House. I may say now that the commission is composed of men of great experience whose names will X think command the confidence of the country. Sir William Van Horne is one, and Mr. John Bertram and Mr. Harold Kennedy of Quebec are the others. As to Sir William Van Horne it is useless for me to say anything. His experience, his great ability and talents will at once command the confidence of the country, and I believe it will be admitted that no better selection could have been made. I am sorry to say, however, that I am not yet sure if we can secure the services of Sir William Van Horne for this important work. He is engaged in so many other enterprises that it is doubtful whether he will be able to engage in the work of the commission. At all events we are using our best efforts to induce him if possible to take charge of this commission as we intended that he should do. Mr. John 'Bertram is one of the great merchants and ship-builders of the province of Ontario, and next to Sir William Van Horne I think that no better man could have been selected for the position. We have been informed that Mr. Harold Kennedy who is an experienced and extensive ship-owner in the city of Quebec cannot undertake the work of the Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
commission as we intended, and we propose to replace him by Mr. Fry of the city of Quebec, who is Lloyd's agent there, and who is a man of great experience in the shipping business. The commission will be laid on the Table of the House to-morrow, and my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) will be able to judge whether or not its terms are sufficient to meet his views, think myself that they will be found not only to be sufficient, but extremely practical, and that they will form the basis of what I trust will be a very valuable report.
There is another feature of the system of transportation to be considered. At the present time the west is filling very rapidly. Next year the valley of the Saskatchewan will be one of the greatest producing areas of the country. It is of immediate necessity therefore that another artery in the form of a railway should be built in order to afford the settlers not only an outlet for their products, but a means of bringing in what they require from the eastern provinces. Probably this week, certainly at an early day, it will be the duty of the government to lay on the Table of the House certain resolutions with regard to this railway. But apart from that, there is another scheme which has been engaging the attention of the House and the country at large. It is generally accepted, I believe, at the present time, that we must have another trunk line to connect the producing centres of the prairies with the tidal waters of the east. This is the point which my hon. friend had chiefly in view when he spoke a moment ago. I may say to my hon. friend at once that the government are not connected, though he implied that they were, with any scheme which has been proposed. We are considering the matter, but I am not prepared to say that we can at this moment lay on the Table the conclusions at which we have arrived; but we shall deem it our duty to do so before the session is over. If we are not prepared at the present moment to lay on the Table of the House the conclusions at which we have arrived, we cannot be accused of dilatoriness. The scheme is a new one. It has only recently been launched. My hon. friend says that I referred to another transcontinental railway scheme last session. My hon. friend is in error.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: I did not say with regard to this particular company ; I said with regard to transcontinental railways.

It was not with regard to transcontinental railways, but with regard to railways from the east to the new and rapidly settling districts of the Northwest. Our policy in that matter is prepared; and we shall be able to place it on the Table of the House probably this week, at any rate at an early day. The proposi-

tion to liare another transcontinental railway is a new idea, and it behooves the government not to launch too rapidly upon its consummation or to come too hastily to a conclusion with regard to it. X may say to my hon. friend that the government are not prepared to say that on that subject they have settled on this or that policy; but we are prepared to give at once to the House the salient ideas which we think should be kept in view in carrying out this new proposition. The first idea is that such a line must be exclusively on Canadian territory, from tidal water to tidal water, that is to say, eventually to connect the waters of the Pacific with the waters of the Atlantic; and that the first point at which it would reach tidal water at the east would be the city of Quebec in summer and Halifax or St. John, or both, in winter time. My hon. friend rather assumed that the government were committed to the scheme of the Grand Trunk. I may say that the government are not committed to the scheme of the Grand Trunk nor to any other scheme; but we say that if we are to have another transcontinental railway-and it may be that we should have to take steps in this direction during this very session-the salient idea which ought to guide our minds, and on which I believe we can command the support of the House, is that that road must be built exclusively on Canadian territory and afford the cheapest possible route to the east for the products of the west. My hon. friend asked what guarantee we had that the trade would not be diverted to American ports. I may say to my hon. friend that this is a subject which will be discussed with more propriety when we come before parliament with any proposition. At the present time perhaps it is premature to say how we can bind any company or any undertaking of that kind in such a way as to make it absolutely under any and every possible circumstance, that the trade should not be diverted from our own channels to American channels. Whenever we should lay any proposition before parliament on this subject, we shall do the best we can by legislation to ensure that object; but I have very little hope that any legislation which this parliament could place on the statute-book would ensure the result which my hon. friend and I have equally at heart, if we had to rely on legislation alone. It is always easy for lawyers, such as my hon. friend is, and as I was at one time

Jj. BORDEN (Halifax). I hope my hon. friend has not left the profession.
The PRIME MINISTER

to legislate on
such matters; but even railways have sometimes found it not easy to carry it out. But there is another way of guiding the railways so that every pound of traffic shall go through Canadian channels; it is to take
advantage of our geographical position, and to make sure that such a line would be the cheapest and the shortest between the Pacific ocean and the Atlantic ocean at the city of Quebec. A line of that character should run from the city of Quebec north of the mountains and on west to the prairies. With such a line we should have solved the problem, because we should have provided the shortest route from the Pacific ocean and the prairies of the west to the tidal waters of the Atlantic ocean. I am not prepared to say, however, how that line is to be built. Three propositions have been made to us, and between them we should have to choose. It has been suggested to us that the government should own and operate a railway itself, just as we do the Intercolonial railway. It has been suggested also that the government shouud build a railway and not operate it, but lease it or give it to any lines which would take charge of it. It has also been suggested to us that we should subsidize and give assistance to any of the companies now seeking aid. There are three companies seeking aid-the Trans-Canada, the Canadian Northern, and the Grand Trunk. I may say to the House that the government have not made up their minds to any one of these schemes-whether they will be prepared to aid this one or that one, or any one at all. The question is under consideration, and requires a good deal of consideration before any conclusion is come to. The field is open to all. I may say this much, however, to dispel some anxiety which exists in the minds of a good many people, that if the government make up their mind to give assistance to some company, it cannot be in the form of a land subsidy. The subsidy must be given in some other form. More than this I do not know that I can say at present. But I may say, before sitting down, that no conclusion will be come to before we shall have an ample opportunity of discussing the matter with those who do the government the honour of giving it their support.

It seems to me that the weakness of the government's position is this, that an intimation was given to the House in the speech from the Throne at the opening of the session that a commission would be appointed immediately. After we have been here ten weeks, we have the announcement that a commission has been appointed or is about to be appointed. But, if I am not mistaken, the government intimated in the beginning of the session that this commission would be appointed in time to make inquiry and report to the House before the session closed. But certainly if the commission be only appointed to-day, it will be utterly impossible for it to report to the House before prorogation. The right hon. gentleman tells us that the commission will be appointed immediately. What does he mean by imme-

diately ? Ten weeks have elapsed, and it has not yet been appointed.
The right hon. gentleman also told us that the transportation problem consisted of three important links :	First, water stretches and
harbours ; second, eastward to the seaboard; and third, an important space which must be built up by railway. I presume, then, no scheme can be the very best which will not embrace all those different portions and dove-tail them into each other so as to work in one harmonious whole. But no such scheme can be framed until the information which the commission is intended to gather is in the hands of the government.
Have the government proposed a policy on any portion of the scheme for a transcontinental line, on which, we are told in the press, week after week, the government intends giving us information ? But should a decision be arrived at without any definite knowledge on the part of the government, such decision cannot be in the best iuterests of the country. The government are face to face with a; choice between two things. They must either bring down an immature scheme this session or await the inquiry and report of the commission. There are three schemes mooted-Grand Trunk Railway scheme, the Canadian Northern, and the Trans-Canada Railway. The government have not given us any information as to which one of these it will take up or whether it will take up any of them or not. They are therefore misleading some of the companies or the companies are misleading the country. The Grand Trunk Railway have certainly given the people to understand that their scheme has been practically adopted by the government. The president of that company wired home to his directors that the Grand Trunk Railway scheme will undoubtedly be carried out without any additional burden being imposed on the company. If that means anything, it means that the government are prepared to give the Grand Trunk Railway ample assistance to carry out their project. Is that correct or not ? Has the president of the Grand Trunk Railway misled his own directors, or are the government misleading the company, or are both the Grand; Trunk Railway and the government misleading the country ? It is important that the House should have information on this question at an early day, because if brought down at a late day, it cannot be maturely considered and the worst results are likely to be the outcome. The government should come to a decision and inform the House without delay. If they wait for the railway resolutions, which are usually passed through the House at the dying stages of the session, that information will be received too late to be of any practical utility. If the government have any policy on this very important question, they should give that policy to the House and country at the earliest possible day. The House ought to be in a position to deal with

any such policy intelligently, but if the government should spring such a policy on this country when it is too late to give it full and careful consideration, they will be doing considerably less than they ought to do.

I am very much interested, Mr. Speaker, iu the discussion of this important question. I agree with the right hon. the leader of the government that it is one of the utmost importance. It is the most important that has engaged the attention of this House for a number of years. This question divides itself, as my right hon. friend has said, into three sections :	The prairie, the lake and
river, and the section connecting with the maritime provinces. I wish this House to remember that all grain exported from the North-west will seek the shortest route to Lake Superior, because it can be carried down thence to the place where it can be consumed, either in American or European markets, cheaper by water than it possibly can by rail. All railways that are carrying western products to the east try to secure the shortest possible route to the head of Lake Superior. The Canadian Northern Railway has done it, the Canadian Pacific Railway are doing it, and any railway which carries the surplus products of the Northwest and Manitoba will get to that point as quickly as possible. We have in the Canadian Pacific Railway, which has a route fromi Winnipeg to Lake Superior, a line of route as good as it is possible to get from the western prairies to Lake Superior-a line with low gradients and built at an immense cost to our people. Coming eastward, the grades are about twenty-six and a half feet per mile, and going westward fifty-two feet per mile. It has an even roadbed, well constructed and capable of carrying three times as much as is carried from the west to the seaboard. We have besides another route, the Canadian Northern, which goes partially through American territory, connecting now with Port Arthur. It is not perhaps quite finished or in a proper state for carrying products, but I think it will be shortly. Then that part of our transportation policy will be accomplished, namely, to get all the routes we possibly can, with the easiest gradients to the head of Lake Superior. There will be no grain of any account carried on any road constructed to Quebec or Montreal, or St. Johns, or Halifax, because such a road would compete with other lines which connect with the waterways and reach the Atlantic. Any grain that is carried down that route, and over the Intercolonial Railway will be carried at a loss to the country-the people will get no return in any respect. We carry grain from Quebec to St. John and from Quebec to Halifax at an expense to the country, and it will be| the same in carrying it from Winnipeg to Quebec, if it is carried to compete with grain going by the Canadian Northern or the Canadian Pacific

Railway, and other routes through the North-western States that reach Lake Superior. The very quickest all-rail route from the North-western to the seaboard would not at all compete with the route which goes in part by waterway.
How about the winter?

I dealt with.that in the remarks I made a couple of years ago. I showed the advantage the water route had over the all rail route. I showed that it amounted to from one cent to one and a half cents a bushel. I am not going over that again, but I assert it to be a fact that cannot be controverted that grain that reaches the head of Lake Superior and is carried eastward by the water route has the advantage over grain carried by any all rail route that it is possible to construct across the continent of America.
As to the traffic going westward, it may be necessary to build a road from Quebec to the north, not necessarily a competing line with those which we already have and which we have subsidized : the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific Railway. I would favour the route proposed by the right hon. Prime Minister, keeping it as near as possible to the height of land and running, perhaps, to the north of' Lake Winnipeg and the Saskatchewan valley. This would open a new country, and I hope to see the day when there will be cities to the north of Lake Winnipeg greater than Winnipeg and a traffic in that country greater than that now carried by the Canadian Pacific Railway to Port Arthur and Montreal. The right hon. gentleman says that he is bound to no route. In other words, he says that the government has put off the formulating of a plan of transportation policy until another session. He says that when the government have considered it, and decided upon a policy, they intend to bring that policy down to this House and ask that it be given the fullest con si diction. When the speech from the Throne was discussed in this House on the 13tli March last, I took the opportunity, when the right hon. gentleman was addressing the House on the question of transportation and saying that this question, including that of affording terminal facilities at our lake ports and seaports would be referred to a commission, to ask when that commission would be appointed, and the right hon. gentleman said that it would be appointed 'next week.' I asked the right hon. gentleman :	Then we shall have the
report of the commission, with its full consideration of the whole subject, so that we may intelligently discuss it, before any aid can be given toward the building of other routes, and the providing of facilities on our ports on the lakes and on the Atlantic ? And that commission has not been forthcoming yet, and its members not yet appointed.
The commission is appointed.

I believe the right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) says the commission has been appointed. But he has not yet received acceptance of appointment from the most important man on the commission, and the only one named that I know of as fit to sit on such a commission. I know Mr. Harold Kennedy. He is a very efficient man. But he has not accepted the appointment. I never heard Mr. Pry's name in connection with transportation. He may be a very excellent man and fit for the position. But the man whose name sticks out, the man whom we at once recognized as acquainted with the subject is Sir William Van Horne. If he accepts a position on the commission where his interests would not conflict with the interests of the Canadian Pacific Railway-for the Canadian Pacific Railway's interests come first in all he is bound to do-I would pay a great deal of attention to his report on the subject. But having been for so many of the best years of his life the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, his interest must lie in the furtherance of that enterprise.
Then, there are only two roads that can possibly receive assistance from the government. The Canadian Northern cannot, because, as I believe the right hon. Premier says, if assistance is given to any road it must be one running entirely through our own country, and the Canadian Northern passes in part through the United States. It could not get assistance unless it diverted its through line from the United States and built it altogether on Canadian territory. I strongly believe that any line that receives assistance from the government, no matter what development it may afford the country, must be one that goes through within our own borders. I agree with the right hon. gentleman in that. The lines then open are two. There is first, the Trans-Canada route. That is like a good many other roads-in the air. I do not know whether a mile of'it has been built. It is a road from Quebec I gather-for we get pamphlets about it every day-and is to run through to Manitoba and the North-west. I do not know who the promoters are or anything about it. But, if the Grand Trunk Railway propose to build a road into that section of country that is another matter. The Grand Trunk Railway has done a great deal towards the development of this country, and the stockholders of that concern have had but meagre return on the money they have invested. Anything the Canadian people can do in return for the great benefits that that company has yielded to this country ought to be done, other things being equal. If they propose to build a road which will open up a new territory in the North-west and make a connecting line with Quebec, I would rather see it assisted than

any other scheme I hear proposed, that is, if the government have determined on a policy of subsidies, and that is a policy which commends itself to the country- which X doubt very much, for I think there is a feeling in the country, voiced in a good many of the organs of public opinion that the day of subsidies is done, and that any railroad that proposes to build a line any where on our territory hereafter must build it as a commercial undertaking. The right hon. premier says that, they will receive no land grant. Well, that seems very likely, for I do not see where we have any land to give them in the North-west, unless we go some where in the neighbourhood of the Arctic ocean.
Or the Klondike.
Yes, or the Klondike, as my hon. friend suggests.
Who gave the lands away ?

I suppose it was the late government. And friends of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Johnston, Gape Breton) in Manitoba and the North-west were coming before the government every day insisting that the land of that country belonged to the people of that country, and urging that as the government would not give them sufficient money for the purpose of building railroads to develop that region, the lands should be given away for the purpose of building railroads. Who was it, for instance, who advertised in the newspaper press for offers to build the Canadian Pacific Railway for a sum of money per mile and nearly all the available lands in that country ? In those days the feeling, even amongst those who were resident in the North-west, was that the public lands should be given to enterprising companies and corporations for the purpose of building railroads into that country. It was in obedience to the wishes of the people that that was done, it was done at the dictation of the people in that section of the country.

I would ask the hon. gentleman how in that case the government could propose to retain the power to fix the price of those lands, to name a maximum price and keep in its own hands the control of the price of those lands for the protection of the public interest ?

I never heard of that, certainly that was not the proposition. The land was offered to any company competing for the building of the road, and the company was told :	If you won't do it for
this, how much more land do you want, how much more money do you want to build the road ? I say therefore that no attack can be made upon the late government by the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston), who asked who it was that parted with the land of the country. I say it was done at the request of the people themselves in that section of the country, it was done in order to afford facilities for them to communicate with the east and to get their grain to market. If that had not been done we would not now see that great country opened up as it is at present with railroads running in every direction. The development we see there now is due to the policy of the late government in granting both land and money for the purposes of railway building. However, enough upon that subject.
As I said before, we have a choice of deciding between two companies for the building of this road. My opinion is that if the government should decide to give syiy assistance for that purpose, the company which is entitled to the preference is the Grand Trunk Railway Company. That company has done a great deal to open up this country, they have spent a great deal of money, and have received very little return for it. It may be the fault of the management of the company, but the fact remains that for the vast sums of money which that company has invested and which have had the effect of developing this country more than any other railway except the Canadian Pacific Railway, it has received very little return in the way of profits. I think the policy of the government should be to have this road built as far north as possible, to pass as near as possible to the height of land in order to tap a region of country which has not been opened up at present.
Now with regard to the policy of the government with regard to waterways and terminals, I think they should have decided on a policy long ago, they should have known exactly what they wanted to do, they should have come to a decision whether to expend money on little harbours here and there throughout the country, or to devote it to the development of a broad Dominion policy. Let them build a harbour at Port Arthur which will accommodate ships drawing twenty feet of water, ships which will pass through the Sault Ste. Marie canal and come down through Lake Erie. As to the building of that harbour at Port Colborne, I do not see a great deal in favour of it, though the late Minister of Public Works, as well as many others, were in favour of building it to a depth of twenty feet, so that it would take in vessels which would lighter there and pass through the Welland canal. They could do the same thing at Buffalo, they could go to Buffalo andi tranship their cargoes into vessels that go through the Welland canal. I do not see what benefit there would be in that arrangement unless you intend to deepen the Welland canal to twenty feet. But there is no use deepening it to that depth, because in that case you would have to canalize the whole route of the St. Lawrence from Kingston to Montreal. The bed of the river is not deep enough, I and you could not raise the water by dams

on account of the over-flowing of the farms on each side of the river. You would therefore have to deepen the whole river from Kingston down to Montreal. The plan which I proposed some time ago, and which I think is best in the interests of the country, and the one which X think must be ultimately adopted, is to build from Lake Superior down to Montreal, via Lake Nipis-sing and the/ Ottawa river, a canal with a depth of twenty feet which will take vessels drawing that depth of water down to Montreal. Such a route would give us the command not only of the carrying trade of our own country in our own territory, but it would draw from American sources the whole of the trade of the American Northwest which at present goes down the Erie canal and finds its way to New York, Philadelphia and Baltimore.
As Mr. Hays stated to the committee the other day, water finds its own level, transportation finds its own level. When a vessel Is loaded with grain it will inevitably go by the cheapest route, notwithstanding any legislation that you may put upon the statute-book to divert it into any other route. The right hou. gentleman is right, no legislation will prevent trade going by the cheapest route to the point of consumption. The cheapest possible route for grain grown in Manitoba and the North-west, and in Michigan, Minnesota and the neighbouring States adjoining our territory, is through our country via the St. Lawrence to the ocean. I am fully convinced on that point. Let the St. Lawrence be made navigable by the means that were mentioned the other day by the ex-Minister of Public Works and by the present Minister of Public Works, that is, by lighting the whole route in such a manner that the river can be made safe by night .or by day. There is no reason! why that should not be done from Montreal to Quebec, the same as it is on the River St. Mary, with a line of piers bearing electric lights, so that by night or day a vessel could navigate those waters quite as safely as any part of the ocean. The St. Lawrence, I believe, can be made navigable from Montreal to Quebec, and just as safe as any other river on the face of the globe. There are no tides, there are no heavy storms, there are no ocean waves to take away the piers upon which you plant your lights and fix your booms. You might have a boom all through Lake St. Peter, and in fact all the way down to Quebec, lighted night and day, which would make the St. Lawrence as safe for navigation as any other river in the world. I hope that our natural advantages will be utilized to their fullest extent by the government, and that a system of works will be carried out by which the traffic of the country may be taken through a twenty foot channel from the Canadian shores of the great lakes down to the waters of the sea. It is a cheaper way of carrying grain. It is
the cheapest form of transportation. No railways that you can construct with the least possible gradients can ever compete in cheapness with that form of transportation. What grain does the Canadian Pacific Railway carry north of Lake Superior and down to Ontario and that section of the country ? It is carrying less than it does from Port Arthur down. It is just a moiety of what is raised in the western section of the country. The great bulk of it goes by way of Port Arthur, and it is being carried from there to the ocean. Part of it goes to Duluth and part is carried by the Canadian Northern to Port William, but the cheapest possible way to get it down to the point of consumption Is to get it to Lake Superior and have it carried down from there to the maritime provinces and from the maritime provinces to the point of consumption. That is all you can find out from any commission which you may appoint to make an inquiry. The question of transportation has been answered as far as railways are concerned. When you have ascertained the quickest possible way to reach water transportation, you have solved the problem. When you have reached that point, you must furnish means by which produce may be carried as cheaply through our waterways as it can be carried on the American side of the line. We have natural advantages. Make use of these natural advantages, and the carrying trade will be done in our country. I am sorry to say that the question is virtually put off until another session. If I understood the right hon. leader of the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) rightly, he said that the policy of the government when formulated would be brought down in the form of an Order in Council for the full consideration of the House. If the right hon. gentleman is going to consult this proposed comtiiission on transportation and' terminal facilities, it is not possible that this can be done this session, because, to get the report of the commission as to transportation and other facilities, it would require the remainder of the session and perhaps longer, and if the government are going to make a practical use of the advice that is to be given to the commission, it cannot possibly be done this session. I do not think there is any necessity for a commission. If there be any necessity, the only necessity for a commission is to determine which is our best waterway. The work of the commission should be confined to the question of terminals. There is no necessity for a commission as to railways. That commission might have been appointed before this session and the government might have formulated some policy, because now is the time to formulate a policy and to build the works that are necessary. The day of depression may come within a year or two, because this country cannot always be in the position which it is at present, and it should take advantage of the tide. A

few years is a great deal in tlie history of a countoy, as it is in the history of a manufacturing enterprise. We should take advantage of the opportunity at the present time to divert the traffic into this section of the country while the routes are being formed, because once you have traffic going in a certain direction it is almost impossible to turn It into another channel. Take advantage of the present tide in our favour. Canada is in a better position now than she will be for a number of years to come to adopt a definite transportation policy, because this is a state of affairs that cannot continue for a number of years. Take advantage of the present, formulate some policy which is destined to build up this country, take advantage of the opportunity which nature has afforded us, because we are now in the best possible position to secure for ourselves a place amongst the foremost peoples on the face of the globe.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. ISRAEL TARTE (Montreal, St. Mary's).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. leader of the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has made to-day three statements of importance. He has informed us, first, that the government has not yet come to any arrangement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and, second, that next week, or in a few days at any rate, the government will place on the Table of the House resolutions concerning help to another railway company. The right hon. gentleman has not told us what that company is. I apprehend it is the Canadian Northern Railway Company. The last statement he has made is, that the government have not succeeded as yet in convincing some gentlemen to whom they had applied to accept positions as commissioners on the board that was announced in the Speech from the Throne. Sir William Van Horne is too busy, Mr. Harold Kennedy has not the time, and two other gentlemen will replace them. However, the government have fully made up their minds, as the right hon. gentleman has told us, not to spend any more money on the waterways before the commission, which is not yet appointed, reports. If my right hon. friend would allow me, I will say that it will be sad news to the country to hear that. The right hon. gentleman and the government have led us to believe that the commission to be appointed will cover the whole ground, not only in regard to waterways, but the whole ground. Now, we are informed that the government have resolved, without waiting for any report, to grant help to a railway company in the North-west. Well, we are all glad, indeed, that there is a North-west, and we are all very ready to help the North-west, but at the same time we believe there are other parts of the country which deserve consideration, and they are those parts of the country in which the waterways are located. The North-west is very mucli interest-Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
ed in the development of our waterways ; if not more interested, at least as much interested as the older provinces are. The older provinces are deeply interested, the North-west is deeply interested also, and the whole country is interested. I fully share the view which is expressed by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) when he says it is not necessary to appoint a commission to know that certain works have to be done. We are all aware that our great national waterways have to be equipped. If we are to handle the trade we must equip our harbours, we must deepen, light and prepare our waterways. Now, there is a port which is called Montreal, and which is, I believe, known to this country. Montreal is quite a village, and I have no doubt is known throughout the land. Montreal is located at the head of ocean navigation and at the foot of the lakes. It is one of the great centres of exchange between the west and the east. That port has to be equipped and equipped now. We have started too late. There is no public man who knows what the transportation question is, and who knows our geographical position, who will not freely admit that we have not constructed in the port of Montreal in past years the works of importance that should have been constructed. We have started ; we have started by borrowing money, and borrowing money means dues on every pound of goods and every bushel of grain that goes through Canadian ports ; whereas, in my humble opinion, they should be as free from dues as it is possible to make them.
Hear, hear.

I believe that the government have done right in making the canals free this year, but that is only a small matter after all. The port of Montreal, the port of Quebec, the port of St. John and the port of Halifax should be free ports. What is the use of doing work by piecemeal as we are doing now. The result of the consideration I have been able to gi've to this important question-and it was not difficult to come to the conclusion- leads me to believe that to complete for the time being the improvements on the port of Montreal it will be necessary to spend at least $5,000,000 or $6,000,000 additional, and that is a small sum compared with the large amounts which are spent on the American ports. The harbour of Quebec has to be equipped also. The works carried on there in past years are scarcely of any value because they have been wrongly planned. The government is doing something there this year ; not as much as in my opinion they should do, but they are doing something. Three Rivers has to be equipped also ; St. John has to be equipped.
And Halifax.

Halifax is a natural harbour and it is fairly equipped. Halifax will be an important port for passenger traffic, but so far as the western freight is concerned, St. John will be the port. The people of St. John have taken great risks upon themselves. They have spent about $1,000,000 of their own money and as they have to pay interest on that it means that they have to exact dues. X say without hesitation that it is the duty of the government to take over that debt and to make that port free just as it is the duty of the government to make the port of Montreal a free port. The port of Quebec is practically free now because the Quebec Harbour Commissioners have borrowed money and they have been wise enough not to pay interest on it.
Some bon. MEMBERS. Oh.

I do not ask them to pay the interest ; far from it. They cannot pay interest ; the trade is not there and they cannot afford to do it. Now, Mr. Speaker, this is not a Montreal question ; it is a Dominion question. From one end of the country to the other we have the same interests at heart. Let us develop our waterways. Will the right hon. the Prime Minister permit me to ask him that we should not take as filial what he said a moment ago. There are works for which no commission is necessary. The equipment of the ports of Montreal, Quebec and St. John, and the completion of the deepening and widening of the river St. Lawrence are works for which there is no necessity for any commissioli. The raw material is there ; the work is under our eyes and let us do it. I do not object to giving a few additional millions for the development of the west.
How much have you spent on Montreal in the last twenty-five years ?

We have spent very little money on Montreal. Unfortunately we have not spent enough money there, and unfortunately too that money has been borrowed. The trade of the country has to pay interest on that borrowed money which is a bad thing, because every poun<1 of merchandise and every bushel of grain has to pay dues to meet that interest. These ports should be free unless of course we make up our minds to ship through American harbours. The whole question is between the St. Lawrence route which is our national route, and the American route. That is the question just as clear as the sun at noonday. There is no use recriminating now. We have been doing for the best in the past but we did not expect such a rapid development of our country and so we did not understand the position. This is not a party question. Both parties are responsible for what has been done in the past and now let bygones be bygones once for all, and let us look to the future. What are we
going to do. The right hon. gentleman has told us that the government have resolved to give a few millions additional to the Canadian Northern, because that is the meaning of what he said. Well, the Canadian Northern has been subsidized by us in the past. I repeat that this is not a party question, but as my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has said, the Canadian Northern goes through a hundred miles of American territory in Minnesota and it will be the easiest possible thing in the world to have a little tapping line to Mr. Hill's railways which will divert that trade of the Northwest through American channels. The best way and the only way to keep our own trade and to divert American trade through Canadian channels is to improve our waterways. If my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works would within the next fortnight give his personal attention to the reports that are available in his department, he will find that the plans d'ensemble for that portion of the work at Port Arthur and Fort William is a very easy matter. It is only a question of money, and not very much money at that, to make these two harbours safe and cheap harbours for some years to come. As every one knows, there are a certain number of harbours on the lakes and are terminals for the Grand Trunk Railway, the Canada Atlantic Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, but properly speaking the Canadian Pacific Railway has no terminal ports on the lakes for through traffic. Up to the present time Owen Sound has not been looked upon as a port for export trade because the grades are too steep, and so to-day the fact is that the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canada Atlantic Railway are the lines which have terminal facilities on the lakes for the transportation of grain. The Canada Atlantic Railway has done a great work in the past but it is not sufficiently equipped on the lakes because they have not sufficient plant to carry the traffic between American and Canadian ports. Mr. Hays agreed last year to settle in Montreal-to settle additionally in Montreal if I may say so. However, the most important thing to be done now is the equipment of the ports of Montreal and Quebec, but Montreal especially. In the port of Montreal to-day there are fifty large steamers and at least for forty of these there is no accommodation. I again say that the right hon. gentleman should not ask us to take the statement which he made to-day as final. The government should make up its mind before the session is much more advanced to strengthen and equip the port of Montreal, because it is essentially our national port. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has alluded to the canalization of the Ottawa river. Well, it would be a good tiling but it will take years to accomplish it. There is one thing that should not be lost sight of. The conditions to-day require that we should get along as quickly as it is possible to get along, and although the

canalization of the Ottawa and the French rivers is a good scheme, it will be a pretty slow process. Let us put the port of Montreal in the same position as the port of New York is in. Let us have some harbours on the lakes like Buffalo, to be reservoirs of freight. Midland is about 365 miles from Montreal, North Bay is about the same distance and Depot Harbour about the same distance. These three ports are the ports to which we must give our very best attention. There are other ports which are used today for the grain trade ; but these are the ports best located for the trade between the St. Lawrence and the west.

Will my hou. friend allow me to inform him that Mr. J. R. Booth a short time ago told me that he could have taken 5,000,000 bushels more grain to Montreal in the season than he did if we had proper harbour facilities there.

There is no doubt that if we had proper harbour facilities at Montreal, all the railways would take more trade than they do. Yet I cannot forget that when I began talking about improving the port of Montreal, there were business men who called me a little notary from St. Lin. But the little notary had travelled a good deal, while the business men who spoke in this way had not travelled with that subject in view, which proved that notaries and lawyers may be good for something. I fully agree with the lion. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals as to the importance of improving the navigation of the St. Lawrence river. Let us have it lighted in the best possible way. The American waterways from Duluth down are lighted in such a manner that it is possible to travel through them in the darkest nights and meet the largest ships without any danger. There are also good captains and seamen on these routes. Many of the accidents on the St. Lawrence route are due to the negligence and incapacity of the commanders of ships. The steamship companies have their duty, and the government have their duty in this matter. Let me ask the government not to direct their attention to one part of the country exclusively. In so doing, they would carry out an anti-national policy. If they do not improve the navigation at the outlets of the trade, vainly we shall develop the trade of the west, that trade will become Americanized, and we cannot help it. Let us develop the trade of the west, but for God's sake, let us develop the trade of the east as well if we want to be a nation. For that reason I would regret exceedingly if the government would not during the present session bring down to the House all the appropriations necessary to carry out the improvements required in our waterways, at the same time that they carry out the projects for the development of the west. For this parliament there is no west and no east, but there is a great country which is all Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this question as presented to the House, divides itself into three parts- the central, the west and the east. The great object before the country is to secure additional means of getting the products of the prairies of the west to the seaboard. The proposition is made that the Grand Trunk Pacific should be the only transcontinental route, and the one selected by the government and the people of Canada for assistance. I am prepared to endorse any proper scheme of assistance, that does not involve the country to too great an extent, to enable the Grand Trunk to reach the prairies of the west from North Bay ; but to suppose that the Grand Trunk Railway will abandon all their $40,000,000 or $50.000,000 worth of property between North Bay and Portland, and the $20,000,000 or $30,000,000 of improvements which they have made in Portland, and let all that property go to waste in order to have an allCanadian route to the seaboard, is, to put it mildly, perfect nonsense. The Grand Trunk are not going to abandon, and no sensible man would ask them to abandon, their great system from North Bay to Portland. We find in this country many people advocating the admission of the Great Northern of the United States and the Northern Pacific into our Canadian North-west : and the farmers there will not hesitate to tell you that it matters not to them whether their grain is delivered to the Canadian or the American seaboard, so long as they get a better price for it. What they want is the service, and if we can give to the farmers a better service by extending the Grand Trunk system to the prairies of the west, I am prepared to assist that scheme. But there is another aspect of the case. We are in danger of losing sight of a very important part of the Dominion of Canada. If you consult the reports of the officers of any of the departments who are familiar with the vast region north of the height of land to the north of Lake Superior-and these reports are undoubtedly as accurate as it is possible for any reports to he-you will find that there are vast areas of valuable farm lands in that region. Those of us who have travelled on the Canadian Pacific Railway north of Lake Superior cannot fail to have been struck with the barrenness of the region traversed by that railway. But, forty or fifty miles to the north of that line you strike a fertile belt like the country around Lake Temiscamin-gue, which is to-day being rapidly settled up. Then, why should we not build a line or half a dozen lines through that country if the needs of the country demand it ? My own notion is that the government should be prepared to guarantee the bonds of. or endorse, to a reasonable extent, any legitimate scheme for building one. two, three or more lines across the country from our Canadian seaports or the eastern parts of Canada to open up the great west. If

the people of Canada thirty or thirty-five years ago had had the same confidence in the country that they have to-day, that country would have been opened up long ago ; but unfortunately the people of Canada had then very little confidence in their own country. Those times have all changed, however, and we should not now go in for half-hearted measures. The hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Hag-gart) in dealing with the question what road should be assisted, has wiped the Trans-Canada out of existence altogether. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that that road is partly in existence now. The Lake St. John Railway really forms part of the Trans-Canada system, and the surveys are made from that railway westward.
Be that as it may, I am not an advocate of one route more than another, but will take the liberty of pointing out to the right hon. the first minister that when he says that the people of Canada owe an immense debt to the Grand Trunk Railway, he is not exactly speaking by the book. I am quite prepared to support the Grand Trunk Railway, but when an appeal for support is made on the basis of sympathy, X would point out that the people of my county are made to pay higher rates of freight to the Grand Trunk Railway than are charged on freight to Chicago. There is no use saying that the Grand Trunk Railway or the Canadian Northern Railway or any other railway company are actuated by patriotic motives, and that we should assist them because of these motives, and because forsooth they charge cheap rates. Why, Sir, there is not a railway company in existence which will not grind the last dollar it can out of its customers and look for more. The eastern portion of the transcontinental business, I regard as by all odds the most important. You cannot expect the Grand Trunk Railway to abandon their road from North Bay to the east. No amount of prohibition can force them to travel over certain routes any more than prohibition can force people to be temperate in the use of intoxicating liquors or cigarettes. Freight will travel along the routes that people ship it by, and if the Grand Trunk Railway wants to bring freight over its route to Portland, the Canadian government cannot stop it.
The PRIME MINISTER, Unless the company have a shorter route to the ocean.

If the government should make the company a present of another route to the seaport, no doubt the company would be glad to accept and use it. I submit that there is room at Lake Superior for at least three transcontinental roads, and these roads should be forced to take the Quebec and maritime provinces route. Then in summer these new railways would develop our ports of Montreal, Three Rivers, and certainly Quebec, and in the 109
winter they would develop St. John, Halifax, Louisburg and Canso and the other magnificent ports of the eastern sea board.
There is another aspect of the case which does not seem to strike the House at all. Any one who has visited the Pacific slope will know that the people out there are not so interested in the eastern as in the western route. The people of the Canadian North-west are awake to the value of the Pacific ocean trade, just as Mr. .T. ,T. Hill of the Great Northern realizes its importance.
They realize that all the grain grown in the North-west is not going to find a market over eastern routes, but that as soon as routes are constructed west, the products of the North-west will find markets in China and Japan as well as in our Pacific ports. The question of a transcontinental route involves the eastern as well as the western part. As regards the question of profit in carrying grain by rail, which was raised by my hon. friend from South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) let me point out that grain is now hauled from the foot of the Rocky Mountains in the United States to New York harbour by rail in competition with water.
What charge ?

The same by rail as by water. Owing to the reduction of grades, the improvement in rolling stock and road beds, &e., it is to-day possible-it is being done throughout the length and breadth of the United States-to haul grain by rail to the seaboard as cheaply as by water. When we are told it is impossible for the Canadian Pacific Railway to haul grain to the seaboard from Port Arthur and Fort William, I would point out that if the curves on the Canadian Pacific Railway north of Lake Superior were straightened out, that would mean a shortening of thirty-five miles in the northern section alone. The grades are heavy and there are many curves. Reduce your grades and curves, and you can haul grain at a profit. Two years ago, in conversation with Mr. McGuigan, whom I regard as in many respects the ablest railway man on this continent, he pointed out to a number of gentlemen that an engine on the Vanderbilt system was capable of hauling 2,000 tons to New York, the road was so perfect. But that same engine could only haul about 700 over the Grand Trunk Railway system. The same engine, which could haul" 2,000 tons over the American system, could only haul one-third that quantity to Canadian ports. I believe that the government should give liberal assistance to railway companies, but not in cash or land. We have been told that there is not much land available, but although a great deal has been given to railway companies, there are still millions of acres of excellent farm land in the Peace river valley, which will yet be filled with prosperous sturdy settlers, and where the



soil and climate will be found more productive and genial than in Manitoba to-day. I would suggest that the government should, either by guaranteeing the bonds or by loans repayable in a certain period, give legitimate assistance to two or three roads. This country is young, and our people, in the near future, will be able to pay. The government should give assistance to the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, if necessary, to improve their roads to the east of Port Arthur, so that these roads may be able to haul the grain to the east in winter, and I am satisfied that, in ten or fifteen years, the government would be amply recouped for its expenditure.

This debate, Mr. Speaker, which has been sprung on the House somewhat unexpectedly, certainly opens up a question of great importance. Views have been expressed which will be of great service indeed in instructing the public as to the extent and character of the problem which now confronts the government-the problem of affording an outlet to the great and rapidly settling regions of the North-west Territories for the productions of that country. The hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) in the course of his speech, made reference to matters which, though not exactly ancient history, yet occurred some time ago. I might crave the indulgence of the House while I refer for a few moments to what was said by that lion, gentleman as to the scheme at first propounded by the Mackenzie administration for the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the comparison made by him between that scheme and the one adopted in 1881, by the then government of Canada. The scheme of Mr. Mackenzie, broadly stated, contemplated the construction of a line from some point south of Lake Nipissing to the Pacific ocean. It provided that:
-the road, with its branches or sections, bridges, stations, engines, freight and passenger cars and rolling stock shall be constructed under the general superintendence of the Department of Public Works.
What Is the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) quoting from ?

I am quoting from chapter fourteen, thirty-seven Victoria, section seven. The Act went on to provide, in subsection three of section eight, that the company formed under this Act should receive aid to the extent of $10,000 per mile, and it went on to provide that aid should be provided on progress estimates. In subsection four of section eight the Act provided that the company should receive 20,000 acres of land per mile in separate blocks of 20,000 acres each, with a frontage of from three to six miles upon the railway, these blocks to be alternate blocks. Two-thirds of this land was to be sold-but I may as Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
well quote the language of the Act with regard to that
Two-thirds of the quantity of land so appropriated shall be sold by the government at such prices as may be from time to time agreed upon between the Governor in Council and the contractors, and the proceeds therefrom accounted for and paid half-yearly to the contractors free from any charge of administration or management. The remaining one-third to be conveyed to the contractors.
Here are the broad features of the Act-810,000 per mile cash subsidy; the road to be built in all respects under the supervision of the government; the government to control-of course with the consent of the contractors-the sale of two-thirds of the land grant; the land grant to be given in alternate blocks of 20,000 acres-which was superior to the practice subsequently adopted of making the land grants in alternate sections of 640 acres, for then the company would be required to make the improvements necessary to make the land valuable, while under the subsequent arrangement, the company would only have to leave the homesteaders and purchasers of other portions of the township to develop the township, the company reaping the benefit. Now the scheme ultimately adopted in 1881 involved a grant of $25,000,000 in cash, 25,000,000 acres of selected lands in the fertile belt of the North-west-the land grant under the Mackenzie scheme was to stretch along the entire line-and, in addition, the government built sections of the road at a cost of $32,000,000 which it handed over to the company, and it also subsequently loaned to the company $20,000,000 and took back land to pay $10,000,COO at $1.50 per acre. Thus the company received cash and other resources sufficient to build the main line; they received 706 miles of the most difficult portion of the line completed, and they received $20,000,000, only one-lialf of which they required to pay. They also received privileges and exemptions of the most important character-freedom from taxation for all time to come upon their main line and equipment; freedom from taxation on their lands for twenty years-(and it seems that twenty years under their interpretation of the law is almost an indefinite period)-and a monopoly of the transportation of the North-west by a prohibition against the making of connections between that country and lines to the south of the American border, in fact, a prohibition of the construction of any railway further south than within fifteen miles of the American boundary; the free admission of material, a privilege under which they imported for many years after the construction of the line material for renewing bridges and various other purposes. Now, I think a fair comparison of conditions and character of the two schemes would result in the exoneration of the Mackenzie administration from the charge of having proposed a

scheme not in the country's interests as compared with the scheme actually adopted. I will say no more upon this point, but I felt that, out of regard for the memory of my old leader, the late Alexander Mackenzie, it was as well to place the facts before the House. I am sure that my hon. friend from South Lanark had no intention of placing Mr. Mackenzie in a more unfavourable light before this generation than the facts of the case would warrant.
What is the amount of cash bonus and what the extent of the land grant under the two schemes, leaving aside all the rest ?

If the hon. gentleman <Hon. Mr. Haggart) will give me the exact length of the line from Lake Nipissing to the Pacific coast, I can give him the land grant by multiplying the number of miles by 20,000 acres, and the amount of cash subsidy by multiplying by $10,000. I have not the exact length of the line, but it was about 2,600 miles, I imagine.
Was that the last proposition made by the Mackenzie government ?
I think it was. That was the offer placed upon the statute-book which the Mackenzie government
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) is not aware of any other ?

No, and I have not the time, at the moment, to examine the statutes and see. Now, in the position taken by the hon. member for South Lanark as to the futility of attempting to force trade against natural conditions, I fully concur. Of course, it is necessary, in our own interest, to have railway lines through from one of our own seaports on the Atlantic to one of our own seaports on the Pacific. That line, in my opinion, should run from Quebec, which is our natural seaport, in summer at all events-much superior in many ways to Montreal and certainly more accessible. I believe that our effort should have been to concentrate trade at Quebec and make that our great national seaport instead of dredging a channel through Lake St. Peter to bring sea-going vessels up to Montreal in spite of the obstacles that nature has imposed. A railway from Quebec to the Pacific is a scheme which commends itself to us and that should be carried into effect. The only questions to be considered are the questions now before the government-whether there shall be a cash subsidy, a land subsidy, or a guarantee of bonds, or whether government itself shall undertake the construction of that line. It has always seemed to me that we had in our North-west one of the most magnificent fields for embarking in the business of government ownership 109J
of railways and government transportation that has ever been open to a government. It has seemed to me that it would be a wise policy for the government to build that road from Quebec to Port Simpson, from ocean to ocean; that such a road would be an asset worth very much more than its cost, and that we should not have to consider its cost, because it would pay interest upon that cost and pay, in addition, large sums of money toward other expenses of government, and so give to the government control, to a large extent, of freight rates through that whole country.
There has been, however, and is now, a question as to whether this business could be undertaken by the government of Canada, whether it is not a line of business foreign to the genius of our government, one that our government is not capable of grappling with upon business conditions. It rfiust be admitted that if this road cannot be built honestly, if it cannot be built in conformity with sound business principles, and unless it can be run in the same way, placed in the hands of railway men who will run it upon railway principles and not allow it to be made a political engine for furnishing places for camp followers and so forth-unless these things can be avoided, it is useless to talk about the construction of the road by the government. The experiment would be a very hazardous one. I am free to confess that I have to some extent been forced to forego the strong bias that I had in favour of building a government road, and the bias I have now, believing it almost impossible to secure the condition that I mention regarding the construction and operation of that line. Be this as it may, however, the line is necessary, the line must be constructed, Canada demands it. The line should be pointed towards Quebec, with a winter outlet at Halifax or St. John, preferably, I think, at Halifax, so that the trade of the North-west could be accommodated, and an ocean port reached over our own railway lines, passing the entire distance across the continent upon our own territory. That should be done, we should be able to offer facilities, and the best conditions that can be attained, to the business of the west.
But after having done this we will find, as my hon. friend from South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) points out, that actual conditions will in all probability divert the greater portion of that trade to another route. That trade will seek the waters of the great chain of lakes; inevitably, during the season of navigation, that grain will be carried to Lake Superior, and improvements have been made in the construction of lake vessels and the deepening of channels between the head of Lake Superior and Buffalo, which enable forwarders to secure the shipment of wheat from Duluth or from Port Arthur to Buffalo at a ridiculously low rate as compared with rates prevalent a

few years ago. For a cent and a quarter or accent and a half per bushel, you can transport your wheat from Duluth or Port Arthur, and put it in an elevator at Buffalo.

That is only occasionally.
Mr. -CHARLTON. Well, you may count two cents as more than an average rate. Now when you reach Buffalo, there is a canal from that port to New York, which for years past has not been a factor in the transportation problem at all. It is a canal with seven feet of water, which served a good purpose years ago in regulating railway freights, but I doubt whether it has much influence in that direction at the present time. So when you reach Buffalo, if the competition is keen, if the American railway lines find it necessary, in order to secure the control of the business of carrying wheat from Buffalo to New York at a price which would leave them a bare profit, it can be done, I am told, on the New York Central Railway at fifty cents a ton, or one cent and six mills per bushel. So you have the possibility of carrying wheat from Port Arthur to New York for three cents a bushel, or at most four cents a bushel. Now there are conditions which render it, in my opinion, impossible at present to compete with that route. It is useless to think of hauling wheat from a point as far west as Port Arthur by an all-rail route to Quebec or to Halifax at prices such as those I quoted with regard to the American lines. Of course in the winter we should control, to a large extent, the transportation of that country. We should certainly, and under all conditions, control the transportation of all the products of the soil and of the forest north of the height of land, and between Lake Winnipeg and Quebec.
With regard to the appointment of a commission, some of my hon. friends have said that we have gone on and spent enormous sums of money in Canada on a system of waterways, and we find ourselves now in the position, after expending more than fifty million of dollars, of having a system of waterways and improvements of a character that are worthless. Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not quite agree with that statement. We have a canal from Lake Erie to Lake Ontario with fourteen feet of water, and locks of a large size, not large enough of course to accommodate the large vessels of the upper lakes. We have the St. Lawrence canals deepened to fourteen feet. Now this is the system which we have created. The American system is a system of canals, one from Buffalo to Albany on the Hudson river of seven feet of water, one from Whitehall, on Lake Champlain to the Hudson river with seven feet of water, canals which are so inconsiderable in their capacity, so ridiculously inadequate for the immense amount of business they would be called upon to perform, that our own system of waterways, I think, is a credit to us. I think for the
money expended, we have a system of waterways that have done us good service, and will do us good service still.
I do not believe that we are in a condition to-day, even if we decided to improve the Ottawa River Valley route, to decide what are the proper conditions upon which to proceed. For this reason I think the appointment of a commission to take this whole question under consideration is in the highest degree desirable, is not only desirable but is necessary. We are now confronting conditions that require careful consideration. We are called upon to inaugurate a policy and to proceed in a direction that has for its purpose the affording to the great North-west of transportation facilities. It is beyond all things necessary that we should make no false step, that we should proceed upon no false hypothesis or basis; and for that reason it !s a wise thing to appoint a commission, composed of men who are capable of examining this question and arriving at correct conclusions. We cannot do it here in an expert and scientific manner, we must rely upon the service of men of the character of those who are to be appointed upon this commission. Let us wait untill we have the decision of these men as to the proper course to pursue.
Now with regard to the Ottawa Valley canal, if we decide that we must have that canal constructed to afford competition with the railway companies and afford another outlet for the North-west, for myself-and I have given a good deal -of thought to the matter-1 would be at a loss to say) to-day whether I would favour the construction of a ship canal with twenty-one or twenty-two feet of water, or whether I would favour the construction of a barge caual for the transmission of grain to the mouth of the French river, thence carrying it in barges to Quebec, there to be elevated into vessels. I say I would not be able to decide at present which is the proper course to pursue. True, 1 would have before me the evidence takeu by the commission in the state of New York, I would have the outcome of this investigation; I would have the fact that after the consideration for several years of the question of a ship caual versus a barge canal, the authorities of the state of New York have arrived at the decision to construct a barge canal with a draft of twelve feet of water, with large locks, and -with barges of a capacity of 1,500 tons, these barges to be hauled in tows.
Can they build a through one to a depth of twenty feet ?

Yes, they are quite competent to build a through one. They have the alternative of building a ship canal from the Niagara river to Lake Ontario and of leaving Lake Ontario at Oswego and going by way of Albany or by taking the old Erie canal route. All these things have been considered and the state of New York, under the advice of competent men,

and especially of Major Symons, who has made a life-long study of this question, has decided that a barge canal has advantages over a ship canal. Among the reasons they assign for this conclusion is that when a vessel fitted for the navigation of 4he lakes, or of the ocean, enters a ship canal she retains the whole of her crew, she retains all of her outfit and goes plodding through that canal at the rate of three or four miles an hour, when her normal rate of speed upon the sea would be fifteen or sixteen miles an hour. This is a consideration which has very much weight in determining the cost of the transmission of grain, and it is a question as to whether that grain had not better be transhipped into barges and sent through the canal and transhipped again into vessels at New York. There is an advantage in transhipping it. Elevating the grain at Buffalo cools it and improves its condition. It is put into these barges and goes through the canal, handled again and exposed to the air when it goes into the hold of the vessel. It is claimed that it is absolutely cheaper to transport it in that way and that the condition of the grain under this method is very much better. Here is a question that would confront us if we were proceeding with due caution, in determining the nature of our premises at the outset; here is a question that we have to decide, a question that may most properly be referred to a commission of experts, to collate information and statistics that will enable us to decide among other questions that we want to decide not from a party standpoint, not for the purpose of making party capital, but on a sound economic baisis for the purpose of commencing the prosecution of a system of works upon proper principles that will be found to be the best under the circumstances. If, after having given to our seaports connections in the form of a railway to Quebec right through the country, and a railway from Quebec for winter communication with Halifax and St. John, we attempt in addition to affording facilities and the best facilities that can be given, roads with low grades and great capacity for hauling heavy loads-such as the loads that can be hauled over the New York Central and Lake Shore of 2,000 tons to a train-to force trade over these roads we will make a mistake, because we have to allow this trade to find a natural outlet. We cannot prevent the diverting of grain to American channels unless we do it in an artificial manner. We might do it by export duties and customhouse restrictions which would provoke the resentment of the North-west, and we must remember in addition to this, that the time is not far distant when the North-west will be the master of the situation. That country is filling up rapidly, that country will demand that it must have access to the best markets it can obtain. The wheat growers of the North-west will not be particular whether they sell to the Minneapolis millers, or the millers at Rat Portage, or the millers in Ontario, or the millers in the eastern states, or the millers in England. What they want is the best market. They want access to that market, they will demand it and they will be entitled to have it. We must simply make with care and make efficiently, provision for securing this trade in our own seaports under circumstances which are possible, having regard to our natural facilities and natural advantages. The hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) says that the question resolves itself into a mere question as to whether there shall be American trade or Canadian trade. Of course, there will be competition between American channels and Canadian channels which will have a salutary effect upon the business of the country that furnishes that trade, which perhaps will lower rates, which will keep down the rates of the Canadian Pacific Railway and of the Canadian Northern, and which will keep down the rates of the transCanadian line if it is ever built. In so far as the diverting of trade from the Canadian Northern, south of the Lake of the Woods to .the Jim Hill line is concerned, 1 have no fear of that. Let them divert the trade to the Jim Hill line if the farmers of the North-west are to be benefited, if their freight rates are to be reduced or if their facilities for reaching the markets are to be increased. The trade will reach its natural level and it will go by the best and quickest route notwithstanding any efforts we may make. The hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's demands that we should put the port of Montreal in the same position as that of New York. We cannot. It is impossible. New York is perhaps the finest harbour on the Atlantic coast. Montreal is away up the St. Lawrence, where you have to keep digging a channel through Lake St. Peter to maintain the thirty foot depth of water, when under natural conditions there is only a depth of fifteen feet.
That is one of the most beautiful rivers in the world.
Yes, it is a magnificent river and the outlet of a great chain of lakes, and down at the point where the river meets the sea, is found the proper national harbour, and it is the harbour of Quebec.
We have no objection to that.

Montreal has great advantages and displays great enterprise and the hon. member does well to stand up for his native city. I admire him for that, but it is impossible to make the port of Montreal the same as the port of New York, because nature has said you cannot. You have to spend large sums of money to secure an entrance to this harbour. The port is closed for several months in the year,

insurance rates are against it, many things are against it, and so it is impossible to place the port of Montreal on exactly the same footing as to natural advantages, because the natural advantages do not exist. For that reason I may say again, that I have always been In favour of attempting to make Quebec the seaport of the Dominion. I have always thought that it was the natural seaport. I believe we would find, if we went into the business of maintaining access to the port of Quebec as long as possible, that we would have a season of navigation six weeks longer in the year at the port of Quebec than at the port of Montreal, and I think that we have been acting on false premises and that we have been expending money injudiciously in overlooking the natural advantages of Quebec, in overlooking the fact that this is actually and positively a seaport at the head of deep water navigation where vessels of the size that navigate the high seas can come in without dredging or artificial aid.

Of course, we do not object to Quebec having as much done for it as it is possible to do, but how can the hon. gentleman explain that with its deep harbour and its natural advantages there are fifty large ships in Montreal to-day although the channel has not yet been completed, and this has been going on for fifty years past ? How is it ?
