I give the hon. gentleman and his fellow citizens of Montreal credit, and they do deserve great credit for showing greater enterprise than the citizens of Quebec. I give them credit for having had these natural difficulties overcome. 1 give them great credit for concentrating business in Montreal, and for securing the apropriation of money for overcoming the natural disadvantages, and for making Montreal a great port, but notwithstanding that, I hold that Quebec is the better port, that it is more accessible, that it will answer the purposes of the Dominion much better than the port of Montreal, and that we should at least give Quebec a fair show by the construction of this railway line from Quebec right through the interior, by the construction of wharfs and elevators at Quebec, and by-if we ever construct the Ottawa valley canal-having transhipment take place at Quebec. Thus, we will give the ancient capital and the historic city of Quebec the position which nature destined she would occupy in this Dominion.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend (Mr. Charlton) knows as well as I do that neither Montreal nor Quebec, nor any one port, can possibly in summer time handle the whole trade of this country. On the American side we have New York, Philadelphia, Boston. Portland. Let Quebec have all the trade we can give her ; let the biggest Mr. CHARLTON.
ships come to Quebec ; but surely my hon. friend does not mean to insinuate that the port of Montreal should be closed up.
Oh no.
Or that the St. Lawrence should not be improved as much as money can improve it. Both ports combined will not be able to handle all our trade in the future.

All right Mr. Speaker ; we will give Montreal all the show my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) asks for it, and we will concede that we want more ports than one, and we will hope that Montreal will maintain its position and continue to grow. But all these things do not detract from what X have said, that Quebec has natural advantages and is the point where our natural seaport is situated. We must give to each fair play, and in view of the vast development of the trade of this Dominion and especially of the Canadian North-west, as the hon. member (Hon. Mr. Tarte) says, one port or two ports, or three, or four ports are not going to handle that business and the business of the American west. There will be Quebec ; there will be Montreal
Three Rivers.

There will be Three Rivers perhaps ; there will be Halifax ; there will be St. John, and Portland' and Boston, and New York and Philadelphia, and Baltimore, and perhaps ultimately a great city may grow up at Newport News near Chesapeake Bay. All these will claim western trade, and we have to confront conditions here and not attempt to force trade in any direction, but to give to each place the benefit of its natural advantages, to develop its natural advantages as well as it may, and to secure for our own route and our own seaports all the trade of our Canadian North-west that can possibly be attracted. But we must not allow ourselves to suppose that we can divert the whole of the trade or that we can overcome the natural advantages X have referred to with regard to some of the American lines.
Noyv, Sir, this debate sprung up upon the presentation of certain matters by the leader of the opposition who called the government to task for its failure to announce its policy with regard to transportation routes ; for its failure to announce the names of the transportation commission ; for its failure to deal exhaustively and finally with all these great questions. Why, we could not deal with these questions at once. We must take time. If we acted precipitately and hastily we might make very grave mistakes. The transportation commission, even if named at an earlier date in this session would not have been in a position to make a report before giving it a proper and intelligent consideration which would guide this House in its action. We must give them some time. The govern-

meat have had to deal with many propositions. The government have had to look over a vast field ; a field where great conflicting interests are contending for the mastery ; a field where they had to decide whether they would themselves enter upon that field as a competitor for business and afford an outlet under their own supervision for the products of the great west. We must have a little patience ; we must unite altogether in seeking to arrive at a decision and formulating and perfecting schemes for overcoming these difficulties and meeting these .problems that confront us in the interest of the country without reference specially to this party or that.
Hear, hear.

Let us look at this thing from patriotic motives, for it Is the biggest question that ever lias confronted us. We feel to-day the thrill of a new life in our veins ; the electric thrill of a new energy that is flowing through all classes of our population. We are confronted by new questions. We realize that we have the resources of an empire ; we realize that that country which we bought, supposing it to be a howling wilderness for $1,500,000 in 1871 ; we realize that it is an empire. We realize that it is the granary of the world with room for forty or fifty million people, and we wrant to look at these things candidly, carefully, and like business men. Let the opposition spur on the government if it does not do its duty or comprehend the issues, but let the opposition give to the government fair consideration, and fair play, and let us work together for the good of Canada and its development.

Might I ask the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) a question. He spoke of the enormous sacrifices that the Grand Trunk Railway had made for the development of Canada, and X would like to ask him how much the Grand Trunk Railway has spent to improve their shipping terminal facilities on the St. I.awrence.
They have very fine terminal facilities in Montreal.
How much have they spent ?
They have as fine terminal facilities as any railroad in the country. I am not an advocate of the Grand Trunk Railway
You are speaking of their railway facilities, but my question was directed as to their shipping terminal.

I suppose no railroad makes a port a shipping terminal or improves the shipping facilities. What the railroad does is to bring its freight to where there is shipping facilities, and these facilities are afforded them in the shape of docks and wharfs and depth of harbour.
What about Portland ?
I do not know, I never was in Portland in my life.

Might I ask the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) a question ? When the hon. gentleman was speaking I was not quite clear where he intended the railway to which he referred, to run from west of Quebec, and whether he intended that it would be a private enterprise ; an enterprise encouraged by government aid, or a government built and controlled railway.

I do not profess to be in a position to lay down absolutely or accurately what the route of that road would be. I have a general idea that it should strike from Quebec pretty well north. As my hon. friend from Victoria (air. Hughes) said, it should go through the valley of the Notaway river and the aioose river, north of the height of land, and I would imagine that if it were a government road and was aiming for the Pacific Ocean, that it had better go north of Lake Winnipeg and skirt the Peace River Valley, having in view ultimately the construction of a branch from its main line to Fort Churchill for the purpose of utilizing, if it,is capable of being utilized, the navigation of the Hudson's Bay. If I was outlining it, it would be a pretty broad and comprehensive scheme of national character and national importance. With regard to the question as to the method of the construction of this road, I do not think I expressed any special preference. I did descant in a general way upon the advantages I supposed would result from the construction of a government railway, always supposing that we could get ourselves into a position to keep ourselves free from the ordinary debasing influence of politics, so as to have that road built upon business principles and managed upon business principles by competent railway men who would have no connection with politics, who would not be influenced by politics at all, and would not be hauling coal at a loss of three or four mills per ton, or doing any business on that line for the accommodation of localities and to meet the demands of politicians. All these things would have to be secured to us, or I would at once condemn that proposal and say it was not a good one.
Since we are discussing this matter in a friendly way, would the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This discussion is irregular. Hon. gentlemen cannot put questions from one side of the House to the other after they have made their speeches. An hon. gentleman can make a speech and include in it any subject he wishes, but this is not an interrogatory discussion.

I do not rise to put a question Sir, but to make a few remarks upon this very important matter. I cannot join with my hon. friend (Mr. Charlton) in congratulating the government on not announcing their policy to the House at this late date of the session. This question has so long occupied the attention of the country, that long before this, the government should have made a definite announcement to the country on its transportation policy. Not only during the present session but in the last year of the last parliament, this question was under discussion, and the very idea of this transportation commission was suggested to the government in 1899 by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). In a speech which I see in ' Hansard ' of 1899, the hon. gentleman suggested what I thought at that time and still think should have been the policy of the government. In a very exhaustive examination of the question, after going fully into all the intricacies of it, the hon. gentleman expressed himself thus.
For this reason I for one would be very glad to see the government hold its hand for a year, and in the meantime appoint a commission of engineers from the Department of Public Works and the Department of Railways and Canals to inquire, not only into the feasibility of the Ottawa, Lake Nipissing and Georgian Bay route, but also into the feasibility of the Toronto and Collingwood route. I am sure that no factious opposition will be offered by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, if they are satisfied that the government have selected the best route under all the circumstances ; and it is because I believe we have not yet the necessary information before us to justify us in endorsing the expenditure of $150,000 as an initial expenditure on the very vast work at Port Colborne that I have risen to make these remarks.
These remarks were made to the House as far back as August 2, 1S99, by my hon. friend from West Toronto. What have the government been doing ever since ? The question has been discussed in this House. I remember the late member for Quebec West, the Hon. Mr. Dobell, who was a great believer in the possibilities of the west and also of the east, and especially of our seaport towns, getting up year after year as a minister of the Crown and calling the attention of the House to this very question. It seems to me that having had the valuable suggestion of my bon. friend from West Toronto, it was the boundeu duty of the government-if it was necessary for them to appoint a commission, to obtain information which they could not supply themselves -to have done so, long before this. What have they been doing since that time 1
Marking time.

It seems to me they have been doing to a great extent what my hon. friend says-marking time. They have had no definite policy. We have spent large sums of money in improving harbours on the Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
lakes and improving the navigation on the St. Lawrence river ; but there has been no general plan, and to-day we are face to face with this position. In the North-west we have, or are going to have in a short time, a great many roads-the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian Northern, and probably the Trans-Canada and the Grand Trunk Pacific-all supplying the needs of that vast territory and bringing to the seaports of the east the crops which grow there. In the face of this state of tilings, is it not a patriotic duty laid on the shoulders of the government and also upon the members of this House to see, as far as possible, that we have every benefit we can get from the hauling of the grain from the North-west down through the eastern portion of the Dominion of Canada ? I am a strong believer in a policy which would force, as much as nature would permit, every bit of the grain produced in the western xirovinces to come down through Canadian territory and help to build up our seaboard towns on the Atlantic and on the St. Lawrence river. My right hon. friend who leads the House says the government are about to appoint this commission. They are not yet appointed. Hon. gentlemen do not seem even to be quite decided on the names of file gentlemen who will form this commission. We all regret, I have no doubt, that it is impossible for Sir William Van Horne, as we are informed to-day, to be the head of this commission, because there is no man so well qualified to be the president of this important body, which will, to a certain extent, decide on the future transportation policy of the government of Canada. The names of other gentlemen have been suggested. I have the pleasure of the acquaintance of Mr. Harold Kennedy, and if that gentleman had been able to accept the position, I am sure ail who know him would have been most pleased, and would have felt that the interests of Canada could not have been placed in better hands. As to Mr. Bertram, I know nothing. I am told that he is a ship-builder ; but whether lie has sufficient knowledge for the position, I am not at present well enough informed to be able to say. With regard to Mr. Fry, I may say to the right hon. gentleman that there are ten or twenty men in the city of Quebec who would be superior to liim in occupation to be a member of this commission in the place of Mr. Harold Kennedy. I have nothing to say against Mr. Fry ; he is an estimable citizen of Quebec, but nobody heard of him outside of his having been agent for Lloyds in Quebec for a number of years. It seems to me that if this commission is to be appointed, the government should first of all endeavour to obtain, irrespective of politics, the very best possible talent in the land, no matter what it would cost; as all hon. gentlemen agree that this is probably the most important question that has been brought to the notice of this

parliament. I may say that I for one do not believe in government by commission. I believe it is the duty of the government to handle these questions themselves. When this government came into existence in 189G It was heralded all through this continent and through the continent of Europe as the greatest conglomeration of business men that was ever called into being ; and it seems to me that such distinguished lights as those I see before me-as my right hou. friend who leads the government, the Minister of Railways and Canals, and my hon. and learned friend the Minister of Justice, who has studied this question-should have formed a commission to deal with this question, and obtain the information necessary to enable the government to come before the House with a definite policy. When I said a moment ago that I did not believe in government by commission, my right hon. friend smiled ; the sunny smile with which we are all so familiar beamed on his face. But my hon. friend from West Toronto in XS99 probably did not believe that the government was such a great conglomeration of business men, and he thought it was necessary to harm a commission to find out and report what policy the government should adopt.
My hon. friend has a better opinion of us now.

I have not. I am not yet converted; but it seems to me that, with the time they have had since my hon. friend from West Toronto gave them the cue in that speech which was so replete with information, and after all the discussions which have taken place in this House since that time, the government should themselves be in a position to state their policy to the House. I do not believe in government by commission. I really do not believe that it is constitutional for the government not to shoulder the responsibility of a great question like this, but to put it on the shoulders of men who are not responsible to this parliament. Here we are face to face with this great transportation problem, as to how we are to get the products of the wheat fields of the west down through Canadian territory and to Canadian ports. We have not decided that question yet. We are now going to appoint a commission; but before that commission will have time to report, the end of the session will have gone by, even should the session last until August or September. No doubt the commissioners will have to take their information in all parts of the country in order to become thoroughly acquainted with the transportation facilities, but in the meantime the traffic of the west which we desire to send through our Canadian ports will have taken another direction. Hon. gentlemen opposite, I am convinced, desire as strongly as we to see our own ports built up, but, judging by the experience of the past, if our western traffic
should become diverted to American ports, it will be exceedingly difficult to bring it back into Canadian channels and Canadian ports, either on the Atlantic or the St. Lawrence river. Some time ago we were told by a gentleman of undoubted authority in railway matters that our spouts were too small for our hopper. Well, now is the time, Mr. Speaker, when we should enlarge our ports on the St. Lawrence and Atlantic coast. Now is the time when we should make our spouts sufficiently large to receive and to distribute everything that comes from the west. Now is the time to provide means for bringing the enormous products of the west to our own ports. In my opinion, the ports of Montreal and Quebec and the other important ports on the St. Lawrence and on the Atlantic coast should be made free. The government boasts of an enormous surplus, amounting, they say, to $13,000,000. They boast of having had the largest surpluses this country has ever seen. Well, Mr. Speaker, this is the time to use this enormous amount of money in equipping Canadian ports on the St. Lawrence and the Atlantic ocean with all the facilities required to receive the enormous traffic of the North-west. I have every desire, and have always had, to do everything possible for the advancement of our North-west. The very earliest political speeches I ever made were in defence of the acquisition of the North-west. I was then convinced that the acquisition of that country would be of the greatest advantage to Canada as a whole. The Conservative government of that day was condemned by the Liberal party for their policy with regard to the North-west, but to-day the statesmanship of the Conservative party is fairly vindicated, and we have hon. gentlemen opposite compelled to admit that the prosperity of Canada depends in a great measure on the enormous wealth which flows frorni the North-west. We must not forget however that the people of the Northwest owe something to the eastern portion of this country. We find in some newspapers the opinion expressed that the people of our North-west do not care at all about the east, that all they want is to sell their grain, and they care not whether it is exported through Canada or the United States. I feel convinced that such statements do not reflect the real opinion of our western friends, and I have no doubt that they are prepared to back as much as possible the patriotic policy of sending Canadian grain through Canadian territory to Canadian ports. I am" not one of those who think that the improvements I have mentioned would cost too much. We can deepen our St. Lawrence, we can deepen the channels we now have sufficiently to allow us to ship the grain from Quebec or Montreal. Just see what the Americans have done to build their ports and waterways and other means of transportation from the west to the east. We have in this country a population every whit

as patriotic as tlie population of the United States. If we want to build up this country as the United States has been, we must not shirk our opportunities. We ought to be able to accomplish everything, which can be accomplished with the aid of money and patriotism.

House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, when you rose at six o'clock I was adverting to the acquisition of the North-west. I am certainly not one who would not grudge a cent of the money that Canada has paid very lavishly for the acquisition of the the North-west Territory. If it were to be done again, I would be glad to support any measure which would bring into the country this large territory which has proved to be of such advantage to Canada as a whole. But what I say is that Canada to-day must reap the benefit of the large expenditure which it made at that time. It is said that grain cannot be hauled at a profit-a profit either to the railways or to the farmers of the North-west-if it passes around the north shore of Lake Superior. But it is admitted on all hands, I take it, that grain can be brought down to Port Arthur or Fort William and there transferred to barges and brought down to our ports ou the St. Lawrence or transferred to other parts of our railway system and taken down to the port of Halifax or St. John. What, then, is our manifest duty ? It is to so improve our waterways as to give the cheapest and most direct route to Europe. It is said that this will cost a great deal of money. Well, what if it does 1 We have the money. As I said this afternoon we pride ourselves on having immense surpluses. It seems to me that in no better way can the surpluses and immense amounts of money the government is deriving from the country be put to use than by building up our seaports. What I advocate is a bold policy at this very moment. It seems to me it is the duty of the government and of this House to have a bold policy. When, many years ago, it was decided to build the Canadian Pacific Railway, people said that this was a bold policy and our lion, friends on the other side of the House said, many and many a time, that this railway would never pay, even for the grease for the wheels. Of course, since then, we have changed, and, to-day, we know that there is no greater factor in the prosperity of Canada than this very Canadian Pacific Railway. It was a bold policy which animated our predecessors on the Conservative side when they made an agreement with a syndicate to build the Canadian Pacific Railway. It was a bold policy when, in 1882, I believe, they loaned $20,000,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway. At that time, the agree-Mr. CASGRAIN.
meat was that the Canadian Pacific Railway was to be completed not later than 1891. But, Sir, in 1886, the Canadian Pacific Railway was built from end to end and the traffic came pouring into the eastern ports of Canada. To-day, we want a return for the sacrifices Canada made at that time, and the best return that can be made is to build up ports on the St. Lawrence and on the seaboard. My hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) seemed to advocate the claims of Quebec as against the claims of Montreal. There need be, and there is, no jealousy between these two ports; each port lias its advantages and each should receive from this country and from the government the liberal encouragement that it deserves. Of course, Montreal is situated nearer the heart-centre of the wheat growing Northwest. Situated, as it is, as the commercial centre of one of the principal provinces of the Dominion, of course, it will always be a great shipping port. I am not here to advocate the claims of Quebec as against the claims of Montreal or the claims of Montreal as against those of Quebec. But I say, as I said this afternoon, that what should be done, what should be the policy of the government, is to make the port of Montreal and the other principal ports iu Canada free ports. And not only that, but, if it is true that we can secure the traffic at least during the summer months through the St. Lawrence route, we should deepen the channel between Quebec and Montreal, we should so light it and buoy it that it shall be as easy to navigate the St. Lawrence by day or night as it is to navigate the ocean itself. Of course, in the natural course of events, the larger ships, the ships that are building to-day, ships of great tonnage, will probably not be able to go so far as Montreal. These will go to Quebec. And here is the fault I find with the government in this matter-they are certainly not doing their duty towards Quebec; they are certainly not doing towards Quebec what they should do in view of its natural position and in view of the faithful support that they themselves have received from Quebec and the district of Quebec. Consider what has happened. Sir, last year, when this question came up, my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) speaking then as Minister of Public Works, brought down a project by which it was said that at least a million dollars wmuld be spent to improve the harbour of Quebec. What is the condition of things in Quebec to-day ? How many berths are there for ocean going steamships ? How many elevators are there ? What accommodation have oceangoing steamships in Quebec ? I know very well that my hon. friends opposite may say, with some degree of certainty, that a mistake was made when large sums of money were spent in the port of Quebec. But we must take the facts as they are to-day. Conditions are not now as they used to be. We

certainly have the prospect in view that, if the port of Quebec were properly equipped we should be able to load large steamers there, and the fact is that every day almost, large steamers tvould go to Quebec to be loaded if proper accommodation were given.
I read in the papers the other day that there was one berth for a large steamer In Quebec, and that when a second large steamer came in, she had to stop out in the tide until the first steamer was unloaded. There is a state of things which the government certainly should have seen to before*lo-day. And, if this commission which they have promised is given, that is one of the first questions that should occupy its attention. The other day, again, I heard that the ' Mont-eagle ' came to Quebec to unload, but there was so little accommodation in the warehouses on the docks, they were so overloaded that they could not take any more goods into it. That is a state of things that it seems to me should prove to the government that they have not done their duty toward the city of Quebec. I remember very well when this plan of the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) was brought down to the House, ' Le Soleil,' the government organ in Quebec, had articles with great headlines on the subject. For instance, on the 20th July, 1002, it had an article with headlines which I have translated as follows :-
Hurrah for Quebec.
Construction of piers from Comner's Wharf to Beauport.
Work to he begun by the Department of Public Works.
And there followed an article which expatiated on the benefits that the city of Quebec would reap from these plans. Then, on the 8th of August, appeared an article with these headlines :-
Great news for Quebec.
Advertisement calling for tenders.
Cheques accepted.
-and the article said that these piers or wharfs were to be built from the St. Louise Basin as far as Beauport. Referring now to ' Hansard ' of the same day, what do I find ? I find this plan exposed to the House by the Minister of Public Works of that day, who said :
However, Quebec has practically no harbour equipment. There is only one berth for large ships in the whole harbour of Quebec. A ship loading or unloading there has either to anchor in the middle of the river, or to be loaded and unloaded with lighters. Now, we think the time has come when the port of Quebec will have to be equipped. I have here a plan of the improvement, which I invite hon. gentlemen to examine with me.
I remember the bon. gentleman unfolded the plan on the Table of the House.
It shows the famous Louise Basin, of which we heard so much years ago. W6 propose to
construct four berths for the largest ships. They will have 40 feet of water at high tide. Of course, we will build the cribs deeper than the existing walls of the old cribs, so as to give them greater solidity. These works that I intend to carry out gradually will cost about $1,000,000.
Sir, if I understand it aright, the policy of the government to-day is to build one berth in Quebec, not four berths as was then decided upon. It is decided now to spend $200,000 on the port of Quebec, and not $1,000,000 as was the policy of the government at that time. I say that that is not only unfair to Quebec but it is unfair to the country at large. And, if we are to carry out the policy which is based upon the saying that ' the spout should not be too small for the hopper,' we should see to it that, as soon as time will permit us to do it that the port of Quebec is so equipped that, when the grain comes down from the west, we in Quebec and Montreal may be prepared to receive it and ship it on board vessels which will take it to European ports. I cannot understand why the government has changed its plans upon this subject; I cannot understand why the government is not carrying out the policy which it propounded to this House last year; I cannot understand why this vast plan, which was heralded throughout the province of Quebec by the ' Le Soleil,' is not being carried out by the government this year.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister, speaking this afternoon, mentioned several lines of railway which were in contemplation. He spoke of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Trans-Canada. I was glad to hear my right hon. friend say that the policy of the government is to encourage some of these lines by subsidies, but that not only one of them had yet been decided upon definitely by the government. I must say I was a little surprised to hear some hon. gentlemen say that they knew nothing of the Trans-Canada, that the Trans-Canada' was a line that nobody knew anything about; they did not know where it started from, they did not know where it went, and they did not know the country through which it would pass. Now iu speaking of this line I may be anticipating somewhat, because to-morrow, if I am correctly informed, a deputation from Quebec is going to appear before the Committee on Railways and Canals, and that deputation will give the committee all the information which it can desire upon the Trans-Canada. But let me say just now that the Trans-Canada is a line which goes in an almost straight direction from Quebec, or north of Quebec, to Port Simpson on the Pacific ocean. This line, from the information which we have now, goes through an undeveloped country, but a country which is perfectly susceptible of producing as much wheat as the country which lies to the south of it.

It is a line far removed from the international boundary; and if at any time, which God forbid, a war were to break out between the United States and Canada, when other lines of railway would probably become an easy prey to an invading force, the Trans-Canada line would be far removed from any such attack, and therefore would afford a safe and easy means of transportation for troops going from one end of Canada to the other. Then again the telegraph lines along this railway would be equally far removed from the international boundary, and communication could be kept up by" them from one end of Canada to the other. There is another consideration I may mention, and that is that the Trans-Canada line will develop an important part of the province of Quebec. Now I fail to see from what I know, or from the informat-ion which has been given to us, that the Grand Truuk Pacific will have any such effect. If I understand the plan which has been imposed upon the Grand Trunk Pacific, that railway is going to pass through a part of the province of Quebec which will derive no benefit from it, and the province as a whole will derive no benefit from it. It is a line which, if my information is correct, will be almost impracticable. It is a line which is proposed merely to blind the eyes of the people of Quebec to the real situation. As to the Trans-Canada Company itself, I may say that it is composed of some of the best men in Quebec, and hon. members of this House who are acquainted with the incorporators know very well that they are energetic, that they are pushing, and that they will be able, if the government give them any support, to command as much capital in England as the Grand Trunk Pacific itself.
Now, Sir, let me briefly recapitulate the facts of the situation as they appear to me. First, the government has come down too late with this plan of appointing a commission to get information as to the best means of transportation through Canada; secondly, after all the discussions which have taken place in this House the government should be to-day sufficiently informed to be able to decide upon a policy and to propound it to this House; thirdly, government by commission is not in the true spirit of the constitution under which we live, and the government itself should take upon its own shoulders the responsibility of propounding tot the House and to the couutry a policy upon a question so important as the one we are now discussing.

It may seem out of place for a member representing a part of the_ country that is certainly the most deeply interested in the question of transportation, to take any part in this debate. The question of transportation has been up for discussion on a number of occasions ; but I must say, speaking for the

western part of the country it seems to me that what the House considers transportation is quite a different thing from what we consider transportation. Canada extends from the Atlantic -to the Pacific, a distance of 3,000 miles; I would suppose that national transportation meant the carriage of supplies from one ocean to the other, or over a part of that distance. But as this question has been debated in the House on the present and on previous occasions, transportation does not mean the carriage of produce or supplies, but merely their transference from rail to boat or from boat to rail at a lake or ocean port in the North-west are interested in the transportation question as Canadians, we are interested in the equipment of our ocean ports, we are interested in seeing Canadian traffic go through Canadian channels; we are interested in these things, I say, as Canadians, but not as North-westers. As North-westers, speaking locally and sectionally-we have no special interest in the equipment of these ports. But we do not look at the matter in that light, we look at it as Canadians desiring to build up Canada, desiring to see Canada developed in the east as well as in the west. Therefore we are prepared to vote money to build up ocean ports at Montreal and Quebec ; but we do not want it understood that the	building up of
these ports is for the special interest and development of	the North-west.
The great question of transportation is : How shall produce and supplies be transported most cheaply, to the benefit of the producer and the consumer ? It seems to me that we are wandering far from the real essence of the question when we think of the question of transportation as merely a question as to the port at which our supplies shall be transferred from the warehouse to the steamer. Would hon. members look at it in this way ? Our wealth is derived from our crop, and the question of transportation is important to us just in proportion as it affects the value of the crop. Give the crop a cheapening of transportation to the extent of a cent a bushel, and you add a cent a bushel to the trade of Canada. It makes no difference whether the crop goes out of the country by one port or another, you have added that amount to the trade of Canada by cheapening transportation. Is it more important to Canada that a crop of 100,000,000 bushels of grain shall be advanced in value one cent a bushel or that that amount of grain shall pass out of the country by a particular port ? If you can increase the vaule of your crop by cheapening your transportation, you are thereby benefiting the country by adding to the trade of the country, but if you are merely taking a course to, as it were, compel the trade of the country to go this way or that way, there is no special addition to the trade of the country and there is no benefit. Everything ac-

cording to its value. We want to see Canadian trade go through Canadian ports. We are willing to vote money to help to put these ports into proper shape, but let me tell nay hon. friends that the difference between the value in our export of grain that will accrue from the expenditure of perhaps some 80,000,000 at the port of Montreal will not possibly amount to more than one cent per bushel, taking the extreme view of the case. That amount of one cent per bushel could be added to the value of the crop of the west by a reduction in the rates over the railways very much more easily than it could by equipping the port of Montreal. If it is transportation we are to talk, let us talk transportation and the cheapening of transportation, and if we want to talk ports, we will talk ports and the improvement in the means of transfer. It was said here to-day by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) that the New York Central carries wheat from Buffalo to New York at, I think he said, something less than two cents a bushel.
I did not say that, but I said that they could do so.
Could the hon. gentleman tell us at about what price they .do carry it?
About three to three and a-half cents per bushel.

We will say four cents a bushel. The distance is about 400 miles. The distance from Buffalo to New York is approximately the same as the distance from Winnipeg to Thunder Bay, and we pay twelve cents a bushel to carry grain from Winnipeg to Thunder Bay, when that same grain, after it gets to Buffalo, is carried from Buffalo to New York for four cents a bushel. Do you want to talk transportation ? Do you want to cheapen transportation ? Then cut the rate on grain between Winnipeg and Port Arthur, and add the difference to the trade of this country instead of to the dividends of the railway company. The cheapening of transportation will come by the improvement and increase in our railway facilities, and by the better arrangements we may make from time to time as to the control of rates over these railways ; that is as to getting the advantage of the facilities which we provide.
Let me say that in my own estimation, and I believe in the estimation of the greater part of the western country, we do not look for the cheapening of transportation by the improvement of our present canal system or by the addition of another canal system. We have a canal system of which as an engineering work, I presume we may be very proud. But as a means of drawing the trade of North America through our country, it has been a dismal failure. Then, we do not look to the duplicating of the system to accomplish what it has failed in doing. The day of canals has gone by. Canada has
practically lost the money it has put into canals, and I am one to say that Canada has no more money to put into a canal scheme, the Georgian bay or otherwise. In regard to the equipment of ports, I believe, and we all believe, that our trade should go through our own ports, and that these ports should be equipped properly for the carrying of that trade, but there is a limit, or there should be a limit, to all things, and as one who is not amenable to the local vote, perhaps I have the opportunity of saying certain things that may not be convenient to hon. members representing localities in this part of the country. The qualifications of any place to be a national port depend upon the ease with which it can be made a national port, and I say that when it is declared that after the vast expenditures which have been made it will yet require $6,000,000 to equip the port of Montreal as the national port of Canada, it is evidence that Montreal is not properly the national port of Canada, that the day that Montreal could be so considered has gone by, and that we have to select a port nearer deep water than Montreal ; that is to say, Quebec. If we had only one means of reaching the ocean, and that one the port of Montreal, then we certainly would have to spend these millions of money, but we are not so confined. We have all the length of the St. Lawrence river, and I am credibly informed that from Three Rivers to Quebec these impediments to navigation which cause the great difficulty in reaching Montreal do not exist, that we are not tied to Montreal, but that we have from Three Rivers to Quebec as a means of accommodating the deep water ocean traffic without these vast expenditures which are necessary to bring it up to the port of Montreal.
Will my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) permit me to tell him that this is the worst part of the St. Lawrence.
Where ?
Between Quebec and Three Rivers. The Cap a la Roche is the most dangerous part of the St. Lawrence.
I will accept the correction, but I understand the large expenditures were made between Three Rivers and Montreal.
Oh no ; very far from it.

I accept the correction. I am not familiar with the circumstances, certainly not as familiar as is the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte). However, I repeat, that these expenditures are too vast for the good resulting ; and, that when we have a deep water ocean port at Quebec we cannot afford to spend so many millions of dollars to make Montreal that which nature did not intend her to be. This discussion, Mr. Speaker, has covered a great
848;

deal of ground ; lion, gentlemen who have spoken have gone pretty far afield, and I will take a similar liberty to a slight extent.
The question of a winter ocean port for the proposed Grand Trunk Railway line has been spoken of. I understand that our friends from the maritime provinces are making a stiff fight against the Grand Trunk Railway project, uriless there is connected with it a Canadian ocean port during the winter months. There is this difficulty about their position, if they will allow me to say so :	that they do not seem to
be decided as to which port is to be the Canadian winter port. To my mind there is only one port in the maritime provinces that is suitable as a Canadian winter port for freight traffic, and that is the port of St. John. If the maritime province people will unite in supporting the port of St. John I think I can promise them that many of our western friends will favour that port also. We want a winter ocean port in our own country, but we cannot have a perambulating ocean port.
Hear, hear.

Neither can we have an ocean port that is too distant from the centre of production. I would like to say to my friends from the maritime provinces, that it is St. John or nothing. If they will unite on St. John, I will be, for one, ready to give them a lift. I believe we can make St. John our winter ocean port, and if we cannot unite on St. John, then we cannot put ourselves in a position to deal with the Grand Trunk Railway company on the basis of having a Canadian winter ocean-port.
Did I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) to say that the government were going to spend $6,000,000 on the port of Montreal ?
No. I said it had been stated by the ex-minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that it would require $6,000,000.
If the hon. gentleman said the government were going to spend $6,000,000 on the port of Montreal, I would have wired it down there.
Hear, hear.
It is not such a large sum of money for such a purpose.

In regard to the projects of the Grand Trunk Railway Pacific and of the Canadian Northern Railway, let me ask what are really the transportation propositions that are before the House, and before the country. There is no doubt that the development of the west requires the construction of another trunk line of railroad by an independent company, if not by the government itself. The transcontinental trunk line of railway which we have now has answered a good purpose ; it has developed a part of the country, but it has Mr. OLIVER.
not developed the whole country. If we are to have the whole country developed, we must have other lines of railroad constructed. It strikes me that it is much better that these additional lines of railroad should be constructed by an independent company rather than that they should be constructed by that company which already has its transcontinental line. If we must have new lines we may as well have an independent company owning these lines, and have competition rather than have monopoly. Therefore, I say that we welcome the proposition of the Grand Trunk Railway and the proposition of the Canadian Northern Railway to open the western country by the construction of two railroads. There seems to be an idea that there is room for only one of those two roads. I am not prepared to say how it is from Winnipeg to Quebec, but I will say to the House that there is room and there is need for both the Canadian Northern Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway Pacific to develop the country from Manitoba west to the Rocky mountains through the fertile belt. There is need of a railroad at least every forty miles. I would say even every thirty miles in the fertile country. There is a country there every foot of which is fertile for a width of from 100 miles to 200 miles, all the way from the Manitoba boundary to the Rocky mountains. That country cannot be fully developed by one line of railroad. It must have two ; it must have more than two lines in order to be properly developed. Therefore, just as we need one line more than the Canadian Pacific Railway to develop the North-west, so we need more than one to develop that fertile belt. There is no danger of overcrowding in the fertile part of the North-west by two trunk lines of railroad. In the narrow strip of country between the international boundary and the lakes, a distance of 100 miles, there are five parallel lines of railroad and they were blocked with grain last fall. If 100 miles of fertile country in the province of Manitoba requires five parallel lines to do its work, surely the country further west equally fertile ; a strip from 100 to 200 and 300 miles wide will not be overcrowded with two lines of railroad.
Now, in regard to assistance to the building of a railroad through that country, I am sure that the people will hear with great satisfaction the announcement of the Prime Minister to-day that there will be no grant of land in aid of railroad construction in the North-west. There is the strongest feeling in the North-west against giving aid to railroads by grants of land. The country has been throttled by that system ; we do not want to_ repeat it. I was somewhat astonished to-'day to hear the ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Haggart) say that these land grants to railroads in the North-west had been made at the request

of the people of the North-west. That certainly was news to me, and I have been very well acquainted with the North-west for a number of years. I wonder if the people he alluded to were the half-breeds who in 1885 expressed their opinion in regard to the land administration of that country, by taking up arms in defence of what they thought to be their rights in regard to these lands-and the half-breeds were the principal people of 'the country at that time. Those deputations who came to the government here and asked that the lands of the North-west be given away to railroads-I certainly never heard of them starting. I do not know who they were, but we are bound to take the word of the hon. member in parliament. However that may be, I do not think they came from the North-west. Speaking, if I may, on behalf of the North-west, I will say that the people of that country have been so ill-satis-fled and are so ill-served by our present railroad that they would welcome-in fact they look upon it as the only full relief-the construction of a government railway as a means of settling the transportation question in that country ; a railroad built and owned and controlled, even if not operated by the government. I presume, however, that that view will not find favour in the House, and that we will be required to make a bargain with one or the other company to build the railroad in consideration of certain assistance to be given. On that point I want to say very definitely that it is the absolute understanding of the case by the people of the North-west that any aid granted to a railroad company towards the construction of its line in that country shall be compensated by a corresponding control of the rates upon that railroad. Our view is : no control, no bonus.
Hear, hear.

We would rather give a bonus and have control of rates than have the railroad built without a bonus and have no control of rates. The rates are everything. We can wait for the railroad for a year or two years, but if we have no control of rates, we are at the mercy of the railroad; the railroad is our master for all time, and we are its servants. Whatever bargain is made between the railroad company and this parliament or this government, our position is that for every dollar of assistance we give, either in guarantee or in money, we want a corresponding control of rates, which| control shall be actual and effective, and not visionary. We cannot afford, this country cannot afford, eastern Canada cannot afford, to load ourselves up with any more indebtedness for the construction of railroads, which railroads, after they are built, shall be run absolutely regardless of the interests of the people of Canada, either east or west. Do you people of eastern Canada know how you stand
in regard to this transportation question 1 Your market for your manufactures and for your wholesale dealings is in western Canada; it is there or it is not anywhere. Do you know that the manufacturing and wholesale centres of the United States are much nearer the Canadian North-west, than your manufacturing and wholesale centres are ? Do you know that the distance is much shorter from Minneapolis and St. Paul than it is from Toronto and Montreal ? Do you know that you have to get, not the same rates, but lower rates per mile on your supplies going from here to the North-west than United States dealers get on their supplies going from Minneapolis, St. Paul or Chicago ? But you say, we will put up the duty. You cannot put your -duty high enough, because just as you put up the duty the railroad puts its rates up to include the duty. You do not get the benefit of the duty; the duty is figured into the railroad rate every time, and do not make any mistake about it. Let my hon. friends look at the transportation question from this point of view; and when they are dealing with a railroad corporation to-morrow or on any other day, let them make up their minds that it is not the man growing grain in the North-west who needs control of the rates on his wheat going out, so much, as you need it on your merchandise going in. You need it more than he does, because if he does not send his wheat by the Canadian road, he cam send it by an American road; but you cannot send your merchandise in by any but the Canadian road. Make no mistake about it; eastern Canada is vitally interested in this question of the control of rates over any railroad that may be built between eastern and western Canada. There is no east or west in this matter. You want to trade with us, we want to trade with you, and it is for you as much as it is for us to see that our interests are protected according to the amount of money we pay or according to the amount of security we give.

Mr. Speaker, the present discussion arose this afternoon through two questions which the hon. leader of the opposition asked of the government. One question referred to the commission which the government had promised to appoint, and the other referred to the much-talked-of transcontinental railroad project. I do not propose to discuss in a general way the transportation question, which has been so much discussed this afternoon and this evening; but I will just confine myself in a few words to the two questions which the hon. leader of the opposition asked. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) raised a very important question this afternoon in stating what it cost to transfer grain from the head of the great lakes to the seaboard. He claimed that the cheapest route from Duluth and Port Arthur was by way of Buffalo and New; York, and he made out a pretty good

34SS
case in favour of that route. But it seemed to me that he was a little inconsistent when he came to deal with this transcontinental question foil a line from Quebec westward, because, having demonstrated that the cheapest route was by way of Buffalo and New York, he proceeded to show the House that if the government could be trusted to manage honestly a government railroad, the government should build that road. As he had already argued that that road could not carry grain as cheaply as it could be carried in other directions, his reason for advocating the government undertaking the road was evidently because he felt that no private enterprise would do so. Then with reference to the commission, we were told by the Prime Minister that this commission was for the purpose of looking into the question of water routes and Canadian ports-Montreal, Sorel, Three Rivers, Quebec, St. John, and so forth. We were told that the commission was not to look into the question of railroad transportation. It seems to me this is a mistake. It seems to me that this commission, which was to have been appointed a week or two after the opening of parliament, should have power to look into the great transportation question in the broadest possible manner. If what the hon. member for North Norfolk has told us is a fact, that grain can never be carried as cheaply around the north of Lake Superior, through a country in which it is difficult to operate railroads, and if we have in view sentimental and patriotic motives in building up Canadian ports, what this commission should be in a position to tell us, after they have solved the problem to their satisfaction, is, how much more it will cost to carry the grain from the North-west by this northern route through Canada. For my part, I am prepared to support the sentimental Canadian idea, but I want to know when I come to vote what the extra cost is going to be. When we have the information we will be in a position to decide whether we ought to put our hands in our pockets and pay the amount required or not. We are informed however that it is very doubtful whether the gentleman mentioned as president will act. Possibly Sir William Yan Horne may refuse to act. He may plead that he himself does not require the advice or counsel of the other gentlemen whom the government have suggested to advise with him on this commission. Or he may say that he is quite competent to advise the government forthwith. Or for any other reason he may decline to act. If Sir William Van Horne should refuse the appointment, I would suggest that the government should avail itself of his great experience and invite him to come to Ottawa and discuss that matter with them. Whether discussion should take days or weeks, it will be time well spent, and the government will have received valuable advice and suggestions from one thoroughly competent to speak on Mr. KEMP.
the subject and thoroughly versed in all its details.
Another matter with which the government have been dealing, and with which the government have been exceedingly dilatory is the Canadian Northern Railway. We are told by the right hon. the First Minister that a measure dealing with what we understand to be this road would be laid on the Table in a week or so. We must presume that the right hon. gentleman intended to convey the impression that a money subsidy would be granted this company. But why have the government not dealt with this matter before ? Population has been flowing into the North-west far beyond our facilities for receiving and distributing it. There can be no possible excuse for the delay of the government. Last session they were not prepared to face this question, and they are in an equally helpless condition today. They knew last year that the tide of immigration was setting in, that greater facilities were needed to handle this immigration, still they had not the courage to deal with the question, and the Canadian Northern Railway people were asked to wait until this session. And here we are, beyond the middle of the session, and yet this measure is not before us. It is high time the government took some action. It is high time that we had a pronouncement and a definite policy submitted on this great transcontinental railway question in general. But leaving the question of the commission and the question of the Canadian Northern Railway and its subsidy, we come to another great question, we come to another proposition to build a transcontinental railway from a Canadian port on the Atlantic to a Canadian port on the Pacific. This is a matter which has been talked of for a year or more, and on which supporters of the government have been for a long time urging the government to take action. The granting of a charter to the Grand Trunk Pacific is now before the railway commission. Surely in a great national enterprise such as this, it is the duty of the government to announce its policy before the charter is granted. Members of the railway committee are called upon to discuss this charter, in complete ignorance of the policy of the government. We all realize that no railway will be built from one side of this continent to the other, through a country certain parts of which cannot furnish much freight or passenger traffic for many years to come, unless that railway receives a certain amount of subsidy or aid of some kind from the government. But when in the committee we seek to have the government declare its policy on the subsidy question, we are told that as the question of granting aid to the company is not before the committee, but solely that question of granting it a charter, we are debarred from discussing the subsidy ques-

tion at all, and thus we are all at sixes and sevens and nothing is done. In contrast with this, an lion, member has pointed to another transcontinental charter which went through the railway committee at the rate of about a thousand miles a minute. It was said it was put through in three minutes and the line was 3,000 miles long. But supposing we should grant the Grand Trunk Pacific a charter embracing all the privileges contained in the charter before the committee what may happen. That charter gives them the right to go in for coal and iron mining and a host of other things concerning the propriety, of which I am not raising any question, but am simply pointing out what broad privileges and important concessions the company are asking. But supposing, I say, this charter should ultimately be granted and that the government then should decide to build a railway themselves from the Atlantic to the Pacific or that another corporation should come along and offer better terms, the question of vested rights would then stand in the way. We would be told that the Grand Trunk Pacific had gone to a great deal of expense and had acquired certain vested rights.
I insist, Mr. Speaker, further that we should have a declaration from the government as to whether it is the policy of the government to build a road from the city of Quebec or from a port in the maritime provinces to Winnipeg, or whether it intends to subsidize a company for that purpose, or what is its policy ? One hon. member referred this afternoon to the obligations this country is under to the Grand Trunk Railway. Well, we all recognize that the Grand Trunk Railway was the pioneer railway of the country and has done a great deal for Canada, but if the shareholders of that company did not reap the benefit they might have expected, I am not aware that the Canadian people are in any way responsible. Can it be charged to the Canadian people that they did anything or interfered in anyway in the management of the railway, which rendered it impossible for the company to pay such dividends as the shareholders expected. This question of a transcontinental road must be dealt with from a business and not, in this respect, from a sentimental standpoint.
Mr. Speaker, had the government the ability as well as the desire to deal with this transportation question, they would have no need to appoint a commission. Why delegate the powers of the government to a commission ? Why ask Sir William Van Horne or anybody else to submit to the country their views on this matter. It is the government who are responsible, and we should have had from the government long ago their policy. This business of shifting the responsibility on to a commission is not in accord with our ideas of responsible constitutional government.
What we desire to know from the government is the following :	Is it the intention of the government at this session of parliament to grant aid either with money or land, or by the guarantee of bonds, principal or interest, or in any other way, to another transcontinental railway ? If so, has the government decided upon a route the terminals of which at the seaboard will be in Canada ? Does the government intend, if aid is granted, to make it a condition that the freight traffic originating on such railway and its branches and destined to the seaboard shall be shipped all the year round through Canadian seaports ? Does the government intend to prepare plans and formulate conditions relating to the building, or to the equipping, or to the operation of such railway ? If so, is it the intention to submit the same to the public for tender, with a view of ascertaining the most advantageous terms that may be secured from various parties, syndicates or corporations for the building of, or.for the equipping of, or for the operation of such railway ?
Now, as I said before, we are all at-sixes-and-sevens with regard to the government's railway policy. We are more than half through the session, and we are supposed, during the remaining weeks of the session to develop a great transcontinental railway scheme, to arrange for the granting of bonuses and so on, in a manner that will meet the views of the country. The right hon. the ITime Minister is reported, in a despatch to the Toronto ' Globe ' which is printed with very heavy headlines, as stating that, so far as he is concerned, he would favour guaranteeing the bonds Cor the railway. What bonds ? What route ? What terminals T What conditions ? The amount which the government are to guarantee is not stated. These are the headlines on the despatch which is dated, Ottawa, May 20th :
Bona interest guarantee for Grand Trunk Pacific.
Government policy not decided, but the Premier personally seems disposed to advise an interest guarantee-no land.
Now, Sir, is this as far as the government has got on this great question ? I say we should have some more definite answer from the government with regard to this question which involves one of the greatest projects that has come before this country since the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway. We have had very little satisfaction, and I am very much disappointed with the attitude of the government at this date with regard to this matter.

The interest that has been displayed in this debate and that has been aroused on all questions of transportation, I think, should convince the government that the transportation problem is the most important that they have to deal with. Of course, when I



speak of interest displayed, 1 mean displayed by the House, not by the government-they have not shown much interest in the matter. This question has been before the House ever since I first had the honour of a seat in this chamber. It lias been talked of most earnestly, and, undoubtedly the speakers, and I think all lion, members on botli sides, are in earnest on the subject. This question of how we are to get the products of the North-west to the market, that market being for the most part in Great Britain, is the most important question before the people of Canada to-day. It behoves us, then, to look at this question in the broadest possible way and to grapple with it-not to refer and to defer it from day to day and from year to year. Personally I have expressed my views in this House before on the question of railway subsidies, I have not altered my opinion. I believe that it is vicious, absolutely and entirely, to grant railway bonuses. I would appeal to the lesson taught us by the experience of the United States. I think I am right in saying that for twenty-five years, neither by states nor by the central government, have the American people given any aid to railways ; and I can appeal to my friends from the west, and I think they will not contradict me when I say that there is no lack of railway building in the western states. If the government sees fit to grant aid to railways or to grant aid to public works, that aid should be granted in the general interest of the country and not in the interest of any one section. I contend, however, that the government, in the proposal which we feel is practically before the House, to grant aid to another transcontinental line, is going the wrong way ; as some lion, gentleman has said, it is putting the cart before the horse. By building another railway they will still more cougest our ports, will still more overwhelm our means of export and so will force, to a greater extent than now, export by way of foreign ports. I say that the first thing the government should do in this great question is to carefully look into the matter and make up their minds-if this government have minds that they can make up on any great question, which I very much doubt
On subsidies.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. A. PRINGLE (Cornwall and Stormont).
speechtext:
This discussion has taken a very wide range, and I will only occupy the attention of the House for a moment. In the speech from the Throne, which was delivered on the 13th day of March, we had tills statement:
The great influx of population into our Northwestern Territories and the very large addi-110}
tional areas of fertile lands which are being brought under cultivation combined to further press upon us the need for increasing transportation facilities for the forwarding of our grain and other products to the markets of the world through Canadian channels. The whole question of transportation and terminal facilities continues to occupy much attention, and my government will immediately appoint a commission of experienced men to report on the subject.
We have now reached the 26th day of May, and the right hon. the Prime Minister tells us that the commission has not yet been appointed, although we were promised in the speech from the Throne that it would be appointed immediately. We are also told that the government have no settled policy in regard to this transcontinental line. Now, Sir, that is entirely at variance with the utterances of Sir Charles Rivers Wilson, at a meeting held in London on the 16th day of April. He then told his shareholders that this whole matter had been discussed with Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the Prime Minister of this country, that Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his colleagues had that matter under their consideration, and that there was very little doubt but that substantial assistance would be given to that transcontinental line. He said :
The Bill has been introduced, and the form and extent of the government assistance are under discussion with Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his colleagues.
Now, Sir, if, on the 16th day of April, the Bill had been introduced, and the form of the assistance was under discussion by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his colleagues, is it not time that we should hear something as to the policy of the government on this great question ? We are dealing with the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill in the Railway Committee, and we are told from time to time by members of the Liberal party in that committee that we should discuss that Bill as if there was to be no subsidy, as if there was to be no assistance from the government. Why, Sir, it would be idle to discuss that Bill on any such idea as that. Sir Charles Rivers Wilson told his people at that meeting in London distinctly that they would not have gone into this great scheme which might involve them in heavy loss unless they were to receive substantial assistance from the government. I am not quoting his exact language, although I have it here. So I say it would be idle for us as members of this House to discuss that Bill on any other basis than that the Grand Trunk Pacific are going to get substantial assistance from this government.
Now, I think before we go further in discussing this important Bill in the Railway Committee, we should know something of the policy of the government on this question. Nobody recognizes more than I do that the time is approaching when a greater Canada than we now know of will exist

west of Winnipeg. We all recognize that the North-west Territories are filling up at a tremendous rate. We all recognize that there may be a necessity for another transcontinental line, or at least a necessity for improved transportation from that country. But, Sir, when a Bill of the magnitude and importance of the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill conies before this House, or comes before the Railway Committee, we certainly should have from some member of the government a statement as to the policy of the government in regard to that Bill. We have had no statement from the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) who sits in the committee day in and day out. This is probably one of the most important questions that has come before this parliament for many years, and it is a question of such great importance that the government evidently have not been able to grapple with it and to tell us what their policy is. The hon. member for Alberta (Mr Oliver) has made reference to the cities of Chicago, St. Paul, and other cities, as being the most convenient cities for the people of the North-west Territories to deal with. I would like to say to the hon. member that this is bringing up the old cry that was raised by the western farmers of the United States against that great national policy which was inaugurated in that country in the form of protection. It is the old cry that they had no manufacturing industries in the west and that the policy which was then advocated was only a policy which would benefit the eastern portion o( the United States. I would like to call his attention to the fact that to-day in the state of Nebraska there are 5.414 manufacturing establishments with $71,982,127 of capital, and an annual production of over $143,000,000 ; in Iowa there are over 14.000 establishments; in Missouri over 18,000; in Minnesota over 11,000; in Kansas over 7,000; and in South Dakota, 1,639 establishments. Nearly all of these western states have developed large manufacturing establishments and the day is coming in this country when Winnipeg will develop just as large industries as Chicago has developed. It is poor policy for our friends from the western country to take any narrow or provincial view of this matter. These hon. gentlemen have to take a national view of questions of this sort, because, what is in the interests of the nation certainly should be in the intei-ests of all the different provinces. The government having promised us that this matter would be dealt with immediately we are entitled to know now before this Bill goes any further in the Railway Committee what the policy of the government is going to be in rgerad to this transcontinental line. But, Sir, it is the old policy of delay, the policy of leaving things alone. ' We saw from the utterances of the hon. member from Montreal. St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) how these people acted in regard to

the great question of the tariff. Let me just refer to a few words of the speech of the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary s, in regard to the course they pursued in 18Ji. Now, I do not want to go into the question of the tariff, because that question does not form part of this debate, but only to refer to the speech of that hon. gentleman to show the course that these hon. gentlemen pursued. The hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's, said :
Of course, if the past utterances of some of mv hon. friends of the Liberal party had been carried out. the tariff which is in existence today would not be where it is. W<s would have simply wrecked and destroyed this country. It was out of the question for any government in 1897 to try to carry out the utterances which some public men had delivered in the past.
Canada owes a great deal to the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's, in preventing these hon. gentlemen from carrying out their anti-election pledges which would have destroyed the tariff of this country, and which, to use his own words, would have wrecked and destroyed this Dominion of Canada.
Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask the attention of the hon. gentleman who is in charge of the House tonight-
Wrho is it ?
The hon. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson), or the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick).
The Minister of Customs to-night.

On the 19tli of May I asked the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) if he would find it convenient to lay the evidence taken in the inquiry in respect to the cause of the accident at Windsor Junction on the Table of the House. The hon. minister said that he had not intended to do so, but that if I desired, it would be laid on the Table. I did certainly desire to see the evidence and the finding of the commissioner, and on the following day-the 20th of May-I again drew the attention of the right lion. Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who was in his seat, to the matter.
What accident was it ?

The accident at Windsor Junction, involving the loss of four lives. The government were so impressed with the importance of having an investigation that a special commissioner was appointed to inquire into the cause of the accident. I asked the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals if he would lay the evidence and the finding of the commissioner on the Table of

Minister of Railways and Canals had made on the previous day. The right hon. gentleman was good enough to say that he would take note of the inquiry. I wish to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Customs to the fact that this finding and the evidence have not yet been laid on the Table of the House. I do not desire to take up the time of the House or of the Minister of Railways and Canals in discussing this matter the next time the House goes into Committee of Supply, but I think the hon. minister is in duty bound to implement his pledge by laying this information, which he promised to bring down, on the Table of the House.

speechtext: I would like to make an inquiry of the members of the government. For some years it lias been said that the government intended to appoint a Canadian trade commissioner with an office in London, England. I would like to inquire whether the government have the matter under consideration and whether they are prepared to make any statement in regard to it ?

I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) is giving consideration to that question. A gentleman was appointed not long ago to fill a similar position in Birmingham.
