speakername: The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS (Hon. Wm. Paterson).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I would like to make a few remarks in connection with the subject of discussion which has gone on for the most part of the afternoon and evening. It seems to me that the position which the House finds itself at present, not only in its work here but in its work in another place, seems to indicate that it has not been put in possession of as much information on the subject which every one in the IIousp
seems to think is of very great importance as it must have been. We are constantly hearing that the transportation problem is the great problem before this country, but when we come to discuss this matter we find that apart from the information which individual members can gather, there is nobody of ascertained knowledge on this subject to enable us to determine, what ought be done for the solution of this problem. Judging from the remarks made by our friends from the North-west, this is the great question to them beyond all comparison, but it is a question in which we are all interested and in which the west is not peculiarly concerned. We certainly are interested in the outcome of any action that will be taken by the government as a government in constructing a railroad itself, or, in aiding as it may see fit any companies that are now or may hereafter be disposed to add to the existing railway facilities. Generally speaking we are all agreed that it is highly important that all the products of Canada so far as possible shall be turned in such direction as to be exported from this country through a Canadian port. In view of the light that has been thrown upon the subject to-day, it is impossible to come to any other conclusion than that arrived at by Sir William Van Horne in his celebrated expression ' that the hopper is too large for the spout.' Sir William Van Horne seems to be the gentleman whom the government is exceedingly anxious to secure as chairman of the Transportation Commission, and Sir William Van Horne has already given all the answer to the question that the commission would possibly give if it sat for months. His Idea is that the urgent tiling in connection with the transportation problem is to develop the facilities for exporting via the port of Montreal.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Enlarge the spout.

Yes, enlarge the spout. As I understand it, there is an elevator capacity of about 4,000,000 bushels of grain at the port of Montreal, and at the joint ports of Port Arthur and Port William there is now or shortly will be an elevator capacity of 11,000,000 bushels, so that a spout representing
4,000,000 bushels is expected to relieve this hopper of 11,000,000 bushels. It seems certain that what is urgently required now is that some action should be taken inutile direction indicated by the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) namely, that for the immediate relief of the situation you do not need the construction of any further railroad in the west at present, but that you urgently need the enlargement of our facilities for export from Montreal.
And on the lakes.

Yes. I think I saw it stated a few days ago that the Canadian Pacific Railway elevator at Montreal had no legs for discharging barges, so that it presumedly is not in a position to'liandle any traffic com-

ing through our expensive canal system. If that be so, it is remarkable that after Canada has spent over $60,000,000 upon the St. Lawrence canals, there are no facilities at Montreal to discharge the barges which this $00,000,000 of expenditure has enabled to reach the port of Montreal.
We use floating! elevators.

Yes, they have some floating elevators in Montreal, but on the whole it is perfectly clear that Montreal is not properly equipped at all. You will iind a proof of that in the report of the Montreal Board of Trade which says that in 1902, Montreal handled 15,000,000 bushels of wheat; iu 1901,
12.000.	000 bushels; in 1900, 9,000,000 bushels; and in 1899, 10,000,000 bushels of wheat. Our crops in the North-west have developed to something in the neighbourhood of 100,000,000 bushels last year, and yet we iind that the exports of wheat from the port of Montreal actually declined from 1899 to 1900 by 1,000,000 bushels; only increased the next year by 2,000,000, and in the next year by
3.000.	000 bushels. This refers to wheat alone. The whole trade of Montreal shows that while they exported of grain generally
31.000.	000 bushels in 1899, last year they only exported 19.000,000 bushels or a little more than half the grain that was handled at that port in 1S99. What is the use of all the expenditure made by Canada upon our canal system if the fact remains that the receipts at Montreal from that canal system are practically stationary, or, in view of the enormous increase of grain offering for export, the proportion being handled through the port of Montreal instead of increasing, is, in proportion to the great output of the North-west actually diminishing. In face of these facts, to build another line of railroad in the North-west in order to increase the exports of grain through Canadian ports is going entirely to the wrong place. We are undertaking by that to do something which instead of relieving the present situation will simply aggravate it. The remark was made in the Railway Committee the other day, by a gentleman who spoke for the Grand Trunk Railway, that he could till the port of Montreal to congestion; that lie could till the port of Quebec to congestion-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman cannot refer to what took place in a committee until it has been reported to the House.
Mr. BELT,. I did not know that I referred to the committee. I thought I had said; in another place.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman mentioned the committee.

The fact is that one of the Canadian railroads which is now carrying to tile port of Montreal, could last year have sent 5,000,000 bushels more to that port if Montreal had facilities for handling that

amount of grain. In view of these statements which are undoubtedly correct, if we are going to develop the export trade of Canada so that our grain products can go out of this country through a national port, then the first thing for us to do is to equip that port in such a fashion that it can do the business. I understand that at present the debt represented by the Montreal harbour works is somewhere in the vicinity of $5,000,000. Although I presume the City of Montreal bears a portion of the burden, yet I believe they are not paying or have not paid the interest.
lion. Mr. TARTE. Every cent of interest lias been paid in Montreal.
I did not think so.
Oh, yes, they are not one cent behind in Montreal. Quebec does not pay the interest.

I believe that is so. There is an indebtedness of $5,000,000, in the port of Montreal. It is well enough that the city should bear its proportion, but if that port be of national importance as every speaker here assures us, then it is entirely worth the while of the government of Canada to supplement the efforts of the city of Montreal and to equip that port in such a manner that it shall become a great national port. We find that in the ports of the great nations of Europe, they do not hesitate to make very much larger expenditures. If I aui not mistaken, the equipment of the port of Hamburg, lias cost something in the neighbourhood of $75,000,000, and it was undertaken by the country of which that port is the outlet, and is looked upon, I have no doubt, as a good investment. It has been held to-night that it would be impossible to make Montreal the national port -that the very fact that we have spent so much money on it, and that it has not developed to a greater extent than it has. shows that it has not the advantages that it should have to become the national port of Canada.
Mr. BICIvERDIKE. Would the hon. gentleman say how much money the government has spent on the port of Montreal ?

I understand that the government has not spent anything, but it has advanced moneys to the harbour commissioners, which are looked on as their liabilities. It is held by some that because of what has been done for Montreal by the harbour commissioners without having effected more than it has, therefore the matter is settled, and we have proof that Montreal is really not a national port, and that it is impossible to make it such. This is not my argument ; I am merely repeating what has been stated in the course of this discussion. But when you compare the situation of Montreal with that of the other ports. I do not think you will find any reason for coming to the conclusion. The port

of Glasgow, the greatest port in north Britain, is situated 20 or 21 miles from what was originally the port of West Scotland. The trade instead of stopping at Greenock, tin? old port at the mouth of the river, has been by the expenditure of money carried 20 or 21 miles up the Clyde, and Glasgow, which has not the natural advantages of Montreal, has been developed into the great port of Scotland. In the same way you will find that the great port on the Thames is not at the mouth of the river, but at London, a long distance from the mouth, where the trade is carried only as the result of a large expenditure of money and of the enterprise of the merchants and business people of that city. It seems to me that you can lay it down as a proposition which is almost invariably true, that business will ascend a navigable stream as far as it possibly can ; and the natural feature which fixes the city of Montreal where it is, is the Lachine rapids, which make it impossible for trade to go further up the river. I feel convinced that Montreal is the natural port: and while some of the great ocean carriers drawing from 30 to 40 feet of water may stop at Quebec, nothing can take the trade away from Montreal except the construction of a' great railroad through the northern country, which could bring the trade as cheaply to the port of Quebec as it could be brought to the port of Montreal. If that project should be carried out, then Quebec would probably compete with Montreal ; but apart from that, I have no doubt that what has been the history of the country in the past will continue to be its history in the future. Quebec was not behind Montreal in the beginning ; but in the course of time business following its natural channels has made a selection of Montreal, so that Montreal has developed to be the greatest city of Canada, while Quebec lias remained where it lias been for a long time. An lion, member speaking to-night has expressed the view that if the railroad under contemplation is to be constructed in a manner to meet the wishes of the people of the maritime provinces, it is absolutely essential that they should agree in selecting a port. It does not seem to me that that is more incumbent on the people of the maritime provinces that it is incumbent on the people of the province of Quebec to make a choice between Quebec and Montreal. These ports may grow up side by side, and we hope to see tile ports of Halifax and St. .John developed side by side to a certain extent. St. John has advantages in the matter of distance, not very important, but so far sufficient to decide that all the heavy traffic carried to maritime province ports should go to St. John. But, I do not feel at all compelled to assent to the proposition that you must limit a country or any district of a country to one port. What we do find is that business, in seeking its outlet through this country is, to such an extent as to make its operations very plain, following
the line of least resistance. In the case of the maritime provinces, the fact that St. John is taking the export business rather than Halifax is simply because of the advantage of a few miles. If the port of St. John be the choice of the current traffic, because of the difference of a very limited number of miles indeed in comparison with transcontinental distances, then it seems that in dealing with this question of transcontinental transportation, we should have in view the shortest possible distance that can be obtained from the grain-growing districts of the west to some port on the Atlantic seaboard ; and apparently it is necessary to go as far north as possible, where the parallels are shortest, to obtain that shortened distance which is the determining factor in these matters. The greatest differences of opinion have been expressed in this House on important elements of this question. We had one lion, gentleman contend that the North-west country required not one new transcontinental line, but possibly two. We had the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals on the other hand say that the Canadian Pacific Railway could handle three times the trade it has now. The most diverse and contradictory opinions are expressed, and there is an absolute want of knowledge that must be had before this question can be satisfactorily dealt with. In reference to such a very important question all the information that can possibly be got should be obtained and laid on the Table of the House, and it seems to me that the mode in which the government proposes to get the information is not a very satisfactory or . efficient one. They propose to appoint a commission, and, judging from the names of the gentlemen mentioned in the House to-day, I do not believe their findings would carry a great deal of weight in the House or in the country. The only man who can be looked upon as the master of the subject, we are told, will not accept the position, and the other men whose names have been mentioned are not men of very great weignt.
The other gentlemen suggested are not, as far as I can understand, men whose opinions would carry a great deal of weight. I cannot see any great necessity for a commission to investigate this matter. There cannot be any great difficulty in arriving at certain facts. The government could very easily make the inquiries necessary, obtain the statistics required, and put the House in possession of all the facts necessary to determine what course should be followed. If grain can be carried, as was shown to-day by my hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) from Duluth to New York at three cents to four cents per bushel, there is no reason why it should not be carried at a lower rate from Duluth or any other lake port through our canal system down to Montreal. Otherwise all the findings of the commission which investigated this question of the

I'elative cost of carriage by water and by rail, in the interests of the United States, are at fault. We have every reason to believe that we have in our lakes and canal system, a channel through which freight can be carried at cheaper rates to the seaboard than it can be by any other route in any part of the continent. If this be not the case, there can be no confidence at all in the opinion generally held as to the comparative cost of moving freight by rail and water. This opinion is confirmed by this fact that, as far as possible, freight seeks the water route. From the prairies it comes to the nearest lakeport, then it follows the water route until it arrives at Buffalo, where it reaches the end of lake navigation for large freight carriers. It only takes the railway when compelled to do so by accident or by necessity. We have in Canada a canal system of fourteen feet navigation, and we have the findings of the American commission recommending' that the Brie canal be deepened to fourteen feet. That commission decided against making waterways of greater depth and against using large vessels or ocean carriers in canal navigation. The cost of carrying these large and expensive vessels at the low rate of speed compulsory in passing through a canal system rendered the smaller boats much more economical. Well, Mr. Speaker, we are to-day in the possession of just such a system ns this American commission says is what the United States require. Yet we find the traffic of the port of Montreal is worse than stationary; we find that in three years it declined from 30,000,000 bushels of grain to 20,000,000. Why then go to great expense in building other railways ? Why do not the government use their intelligence to find out the fatal flaw which prevents the port of Montreal from realizing the advantages which, according to this American commission, would be realized by the port of New York if that port were equipped with a fourteen foot canal such as serves Montreal to-day. Montreal is in possession of the very canal system which the American commission say New York requires in order it may get back the trade which lias been diverted from it. Yet Montreal, which ought to be the great exporting point on the North American continent during the summer months, is practically, so far as the grain trade is concerned, not only stationery but a long way behind the position it occupied in 1899, and this, in spite of the fact that the grain exports of this country have doubled or trebled in the course of those three years. In view of these facts, which cannot be controverted, the idea of asking the people of Canada to submit to an expenditure or liability in the shape of endorsing or guaranteeing bonds for the purpose of building another railway to compete with those already existing-not to bring business to Montreal because there is no use of bringing business where it cannot be handled, but to Ontario, whence it must be diverted to the port of Portland, is absurd. It would mean asking the people of Canada to throw away their money on a piece of work which could not do this country a particle of good. If it is necessary to increase the facilities for moving freight from the western end of Lake Superior and the lakeports on the Georgian bay to Montreal, I am satisfied that it could be effected in a much cheaper way than by building a new and independent line. No one has yet pretended to show that any such line is required; no one has set up the contention that the Canadian Pacific Kailway is overburdened with traffic on that portion of its system extending from the western end of Lake Superior to Montreal or to any points in Ontario. There is no necessity for increasing the facilities for hauling freight by rail from Port Arthur to any Ontario point because no freight or very little comes in that direction at all. Our object is to gather into elevators on the lake front the grain of the west and they send it by steamers to Buffalo. Midland, Port Colborne, or some other point on the Georgian bay. There is nothing at all to show any necessity for increasing the capacity of the railway for carrying freight over that particular distance, and yet a great part of the expenditure this country would be called upon to make, if it were to subsidize or in any way assist the new transcontinental railway, would be applied to increasing the facilities over that portion of country, which, so far as we have reason to know, requires no further facilities. But if it were necessary to increase the railway capacity between the extreme west of Ontario and the Ontario Peninsula, then it seems to me that that might be done at a very much less cost than by building a new and independent railway, which would not only be very expensive, but would impair, to a certain extent, the efficiency of the railway system already in existence. It is a fundamental principle that we should not set up competition which would injure existing rights.
We know that it is a principle that we shall not parallel an existing line and induce a competition which will impair the efficiency of both the old road and the new. A work that would, to my mind, give increased haulage to that section-if it were required, which I maintain it is not-would be to assist the Canadian Pacific Railway to double track its system over that part. Generally speaking, while I think it is not hard to show that another transcontinental railway is not wanted and cannot be justified at present to the people of Canada who are to be asked to pay for it, I think that a large amount of influence ought to be exerted upon the government of Canada to make a positive declaration of their intentions in this regard. In the Railway Committee, which is to meet to discuss the questions which are before the House and the govern-

ment, as was very well pointed out by the hon. member for Cornwall and Stormont (Mr. Pringle), the knowledge of the course the government is prepared to take In regard to this matter is an essential feature. If you are asked whether you will grant a charter to another line of railway, that in itself is not a difficult matter to decide- you treat it as you would treat any other question, and consider whether it would be a disadvantage or an advantage to set up a competing line, or to open a line through new territory. But the really important question must be and ought to be settled before any reasonable result can be reached by the committee, and this involves a clear declaration on the part of the country as to whether or not they propose to give assistance by a money grant or extensive guarantee to the construction of any such public work. It is not enough-it is not enough by any means-for one gentleman or another to rise in this House and assert that the transportation problem is a great problem. That may be quite true. But the more important that problem becomes the more important it is that we should approach it intelligently, and that we should know every detail in connection with it ; that we should not blindly or ignorantly put our hand to the work of effecting what we think would be an amendment or improvement, where, perhaps, instead of effecting that amendment or improvement, we may be aggravating the situation and at the same time adding enormously to the burdens of the people of Canada.	.

It is not my intention to take up much of the time of the House, but I cannot let the motion pass without saying a few words. I was very much surprised by the remarks made by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) this afternoon in reply to the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax). I was particularly surprised to hear the right hon. gentleman say it was unfair that he had not received notice of the subject brought up by the leader of the opposition. It has been stated by the Liberal press and by many of the Liberal members of this House that this government is a government of business men, who understand the affairs of the country. I have also understood from many hon. gentlemen on the other side that the question of transportation was one of the most important questions before the House. It was surprising to me, therefore, that the Prime Minister should feel that he was taken unaware when he was asked to lay before the House and the country his policy on the question of transportation. As usual, the hon. gentleman from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), who is the apologist for this government on every occasion, cropped up, and delivered one of his usual interesting speeches. It was also very interesting to me, and, I think, to every member of this House, to hear him speak of the patriotism we should show on this question of transportation and how we should forget our party feelings and work to develop a transportation policy which would be for the benefit of the country at large. It seems to me the hon. gentleman has not always been the patriot that he asks us this afternoon to think he is. When we think of him preaching throughout this country commercial union and unrestricted reciprocity, I do not think we can regard him as acting patriotically towards this country. And, for eighteen long years, according to the confession he made to the House last year, that hon. gentleman preached the policy of free trade, although in 1876 and 1877 he had urged his leader to support a policy of protection as being more in the interest of the country. It appears to me quite plain that, before' the Railway Committee meets tomorrow to take up the question of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, the government should take us into their confidence and tell us what assistance they intend to give to that company. We have not had the policy of the government laid before us, and have no means of judging what that assistance may be. But we do know that Sir Charles Rivers Wilson has stated to the directors and shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway that it shall not cost the shareholders a cent, that with the assistance that is to be given by the government, and other means, they will be able to build the entire road from the Atlantic to the Pacific. If that is the case, I think it is fair that the Railway Committee should not pass a charter to that company. The business of the country would not be delayed if the government should take us into their confidence in this subject. I also think this House should adjourn now. We have had this transportation question discussed all this afternoon and evening, and only a few of the ministers have been present. The Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) has not been in his seat this afternoon, nor has the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland). These are the men who should tell us what the policy of the government is on this subject.

speechtext: On the first of May the warden of the Kingston penitentiary issued a circular which I presume was distributed to all the members of the House, stating the price at which the twine would be sold to the farmers this year and it quoted pure manilla 050 feet to the pound at 111 ceids. A price list was sent out last year to the farmers and only a small portion of the twine was sold to farmers, but before the season was nearly over the balance of the twine was sold to one individual, and sold to him at about half the price the farmers were charged for it.

My hon. friend will remember that a resolution was passed by the House some years ago which restricted the sale of twine exclusively to farmers. Notices were sent out and farmers were asked to take the twine, but at the end of the fiscal year more than two thirds of the twine was on hand. What was done was done in conformity with the instructions of the House. There was nothing left for us to do then but to offer it for sale by auction, and Mr. Henderson Black, of St. John, bought the twine.
At what price was it sold by auction.

At four and four-fifths cents, and five and one-tenth cents. When this matter was under discussion last year before the "Committee on Agriculture, the committee came to the conclusion that a mistake had been made and they cancelled the former resolution of the House, and reported in favour of the matter being dealt with by the Department of Justice.

What I complain of is that the price at which the twine was offered to the farmers was quite as high as they could buy it at almost any retail store in the country, and in the opinion of many it was more than the twine actually cost. Had it been sold to the farmers at anything like the price that it was sold for to this individual at auction, it would have been snapped up so quickly by them that there would have been none left before the season was half over. The farmers did not get an opportunity of buying it at a reduced price, but some favoured individual bought the balance at about one-third the price that the farmers could buy it. If the twine had to be sold at a reduction, surely the farmers ought to have had an opportunity to share in the advantage as well as some speculator.

My hon. friend is not fair in making that statement.
The House, not the Department of Justice, decided in 1901 that the twine must be sold exclusively to the farmers of this country. Not only did they do that, but they fixed the price at which it should be sold to the farmers, that price being the cost of the raw material plus the actual cost of manufacture. So that the Department of Justice had no responsibility whatever in fixing the I>rice, we having simply conformed to the resolution adopted by the House. We found, however, that the farmers did not want it. and my hon. friend says that we then sold it to favoured individuals. After the expiration of the time during which it could be marketed, we advertised for tenders, and it was sold to the gentleman who made the highest bid for it; and if my hon. friend will ask the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) who knows Mr. Henderson Black, of St. John, he will tell him that that gentleman would not be likely to be much favoured by the present government if there was any politics in it.
At what time was the twine sold ?
Immediately after the first of July. That was the date fixed by the resolution.

I can tell the hon. gentleman one thing, that if the farmers of Canada had known that the binder twine was for sale at any such price, it would have been taken very readily and very rapidly by them. But the price at which the twine was calculated was about the same as the price at which you could buy the product of any other factory in any hardware in the country.

But my hon. friend knows that the responsibility was not with us. He knows that we were acting in conformity with the resolution passed by the House. After the resolution had been in operation for a year, however, it was considered that we had made a mistake. I take my share of the responsibility for it, because the resolution was carried by a unanimous vote; but after it was in operation one year, it was found to be so unjust in its operation, that it was decided to withdraw the resolution and leave the Department of Justice to fix the price.
Will the minister give us the calculation showing how the price was fixed ?

We estimated the cost of manufacture based on the actual cost during the seasons of 1898-99, and 1899-1900. We took the number of pounds manufactured and added the cost of oil, bags, &c,; repairs and renewals; that convict labour; allow five per cent for depreciation of plant and three per cent for interest on the outlay; then add the actual 1 cost of the raw material, and I may say

that in the purchase of the raw material we enjoyed certain advantages, taking advantage of the lowest price, and of course having the cash to pay for the material. These are the items taken into account in fixing the price.
Do the number of pounds of raw materia] represent the number of pounds of binder twine you turn out ?

The inspector tells me that by the Auditor General's Report it would appear that there were 137,000 pounds of raw material manufactured. That would produce about the same number of pounds of binder twine-1 speak subject to correction, because I do not know very much about this business-because the oil supplements what is lost in the way of waste.
Do I understand the minister to state that the binder twine was sold last year on the terms of the resolution passed by the House ?
Yes, up to the first of July, 1902.
That was altered by the resolution adopted by the committee.

The resolution of the committee was passed on May 9th, 1902, but I read the resolution as being applicable to the next season'^ out-Piit. It would not apply to that season's output, because we had issued circulars all over the country offering the twine to the farmers at a price which we had fixed in accordance with the resolution of the House. The resolution passed by the committee on August is applicable to the output of this year, but not to that of last year.

I thought the complaint of the hon. minister to the committee was that the resolution called on the department to sell the twine on hand on the first of July by tender ; and when that matter was up for consideration in the comrqittee last year the committee passed a resolution setting aside that portion of the resolution of the House calling for tenders and the department were not called on to offer the twine for sale by public tender after July the first. That was my understanding of the matter when it was up in the committee.

I think that was about what was done. Here are the words of the resolution reported by the select Committee on Agriculture :
The committee having heard and considered the evidence of the officers in charge of the manufacture and sale of binder twine at Kingston penitentiary, recommend that binder twine industry thereat be continued, and the product sold directly to the farmers of Canada; and that the responsibility of fixing the date up to which such sale should be made to the farmers be left with the Department of Justice.

All the twine made last year was sold direct to the farmers, and that system has proved a success ?
Yes.

Here is a circular which was issued May the first, fixing the prices for the current year. It seems to me very strange tpat a second lot of circulars should be issued so soon saying the binder twine 650 feet to the pound was all sold. Surely all this twine was not sold direct to the farmers ?

There was only manufactured in all last year SO.-000 pounds of twine 650 feet to the pound, of which we had less than a ton on hand at the beginning of the season. That was snapped up by the farmers immediately. There are 200,000 pounds still remaining of twine 600 feet.
Who was the lucky man got that ?
The man who came first.
Do you know his name ?
I will get it.

There ought to be some dis-I eussion as to whether this system ought to

continue. I have no desire to unduly criticise the department for no doubt they are doing their best. I am personally a little interested because it was I who brought up the resolution turn years ago instructing the department to sell the twine direct to the farmers. That portion of the resolution calling for sale by tender on July the first, I am not responsible for, as I had nothing to do with it. Last year the committee struck out that portion of the resolution. With that portion set aside, the system of selling to the farmers at cost or about the cost has been successful ?
Yes, this year also. We cannot make the twine fast enough.

I think it rather strange that in this circular issued May the first:, and the other circular issued May twenty-second, we are told that all the best twine is sold. It looks as if one or two put in an application and bought it at a fixed price. I think that the department should continue the manufacture of this twine in larger quantities and sell it direct to the farmers. The department are quite right when they say that they should not be bound down to offer a commodity by public tender, because I am sure that when the farmers understand that they can purchase their binder twine direct from the institution every year, they will purchase their full quantity of twine from the government. This being a business government, the department will, no doubt, be able to do what is right, and see that all this twine is sold direct to the farmers. And in such case, we should not find such large items ns these $18,000 sold to an individual, another $11,000 sold to another individual, neither being farmers.
That was a good while ago.

It was some time ago. I accept that explanation. There should not be any disposition on the part of the government to abolish the manufacture of binding twine in that Kingston penitentiary, but rather to increase it, and put as much binder twine into the market as possible in order, in some measure, to keep down the prices.

This is an industry in which necessarily a great number of people are interested. It is one of which I can personally know but very little, but which I am anxious to see successful. 1 think it would be very useful if the Committee on Agriculture would fix a day for the purpose of discussing this question of binder twine. I would be on hand and have my officials present, and we would have the benefit of the experience of those in the House who are conversant with, the business.

If the government will take my advice they will sell the whole1
machinery or send it to the junk shop and save money.
Send $40,000 of machinery to the junk shop ?

I would do it immediately. Here we have a resolution at one time ordering the government to do a certain thing and at another session the House lays down another rule. The idea of parliament making rules for the sale of binding twine-
There is a statute governing that in the United States.

I would not care to follow that precedent. I believe that this was begun for political purposes-to try to make the farmers believe that the government was going to help them by reducing binder twine. And so it has been carried on. I think the wise thing to do is to let the farmers or the manufacturers produce the binder twine. A number of farmers have gone into this business, and I think there are seven or eight binder twine factories in Canada to-day. Why should the government, assuming the expense and doing little else, go into competition with them ? We are told that about 800 farmers have bought our binder twine. What is that number compared with all the farmers in Canada. I think the quicker we get rid of this as a business speculation the better. It will always be coming up in this same way ; no matter what party is in power, fault will always be found as to the method of carrying on the business. It is not a business for a government to go into, and I do not think that the results have proved beneficial either to the farmers or to the government.
What other lines of merchandise are the government interested in coming under the management of the Department of Justice ?
I am happy to say I have only binder twine-besides the quarrying of stone at St. Vincent de Paul and making brick in British Columbia.

I should think it would not be a very serious task for one of the minister's qualification to become an authority on one line of business. Since the question was brought up in the House, he tells us lie has paid great attention to the subject, and it seems to me he ought to have it down fine by this time.
My hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) overates my ability. I humbly confess it.

I am greatly surprised by the attitude of the hon. member for Guys-borough (Mr. Fraser). However, I do not know that I ought to be surprised. Last year, I called the attention of the committee

to the fact-a more than ordinarily gratifying one-that one minister of the Crown was prepared to take the representatives of the people into his confidence.
Who is that ?

The Minister of Justice. That lion, gentleman said he would be glad to have the advice of the opposition in his endeavour to make his industry more successful than it had been in the past. I think that is the proper way to approach such questions as this. I do not know whether that accounts for the warmth, the excitement, I may say, of the hon. member for Guysborough. I was afraid for a moment that we were going to have another of those family quarrels with which we have been so familiar in the past. I think however, that the Minister of Justice prevented this coming to a crisis. Now, 1 hope this industry will be continued. The hon. member for Guysborough asks us what arc seven or eight hundred farmers. I do not know that they are a large number compared with the entire population of the Dominion, or with the number of farmers of the Dominion. They are not a very large number in proportion to the amount of wealth that is invested in the farms of this country. But, if we can assist seven or eight hundred farmers, and if we can extend this industry in the way suggested by the hon. member for Peel-and particularly if the hon. minister continues to receive the able assistance of the opposition-this will be one of the most successful branches of the public service.

The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) desires this manufacture of binder twine under the government to be done away with. That hon. gentleman is more interested in fishermen than in farming. But the whole number of those engaged in farming is far greater than the number engaged in fishing. I am sure he would raise very serious objections if any hon. member of this House proposed doing away with something that was in the interest of the fishermen, and I think we have equal ground for objecting to his observations. He said, in the first place, that this factory was started for political purposes. Whatever purpose it was started for, it had one beneficial result and that was keeping down the cost of binder twine to the farmer. That is a fact that cannot be successfully contradicted. From the time that the factory in Kingston penitentiary began to turn out and sell binder twine, until the present government came into office, the farmers got their binder twine at lower prices than they ever got it for in Canada before or since. And why was this ? Because the government that then controlled the factory provided that the person purchasing the binder twine should sell it to the farmers at not more than 10 per cent profit. So, if any farmer found

that he was obliged to pay a higher figure for binder twine elsewhere he could apply to the Kingston penitentiary and purchase it at this low price, viz., 10 per cent above that for which it was sold wholesale. During the time that this factory was under the management of the predecessors of hon. gentlemen opposite who now control it, what were the farmers paying for binder twine ? They were paying from five and a half cents to seven and a half cents per liound. But when this government took control of it and began to sell it to speculators under their system-a very improper system as we contend-the manufacturers throughout the country were able to reach an understanding as to what they should sell it at. The same speculators bought up Die output of the Kingston penitentiary, and of the Central prison of Toronto, and controlling the output of these factories, they appear to have reached an agreement with other manufacturers of twine that all would sell at the same figure no matter where it was manufactured. Therefore, the farmer was obliged to pay a very much higher price than before. And, from that time to the present, binder twine has remained at a high figure. We say that binder twine has been at a high figure, because the output of the Kingston penitentiary has been improperly handled by the government. Why,, who got the output of the binder twine from that factory ? Mr. H. N. Bate, of Ottawa, the Hobbs Hardware Company, of London, and Mr. Connor, of St. John. When tenders were asked for the purchase of this twine, there appears to have been an understanding between them, so it did not matter who got the binder twine, they all shared in the profits.
Played Hobbs with the whole business.

The result of it was that the government paid Hobbs with the whole industry, and the farmers suffered in consequence. We remember very well when tenders were asked for and were put in by H. N. Bate, of Ottawa, and by the Hobbs Hardware Company, of London, and one by Connors as well. The contract was given to a firm in London, and when they were called upon to put up their forfeit the reply was that the Connors Company would put it up here in Ottawa-showing conclusively that they were in collusion.
The same parties who had conti'ol of the output at the Central Prison controlled the output at Kingston as well and then they sold it as they saw fit. The farmers were obliged to pay from nine and a half to twelve and a half cents a pound for their Wilder twine, whereas the year before the highest price paid was about seven and a half cents a pound for the best twine. Now we claim that increased price was a consequence of the improper way in which it was sold by the government.
What about the cost of the raw material ?

The cost for three years was very much the same, averaging about four and a half cents a pound. It has been shown over and over again by the Auditor General's Report that during the three years when binder twine was' sold at the very highest price to the farmer, the cost of the raw material was practically about the same as when the twine was sold at the lowest price. That shows plainly that the difference was not due to the increased cost of the raw material, because the twine was sold at a price out of all proportion to the raw material. Now we are told to-night that no matter who sold It, it got into the hands of Mr. Connor. One time it got into the hands of Connor under one name, and another time it got into his hands under another name. It seems that the same practice has been going on from year to year. At the commencement of this season, on the 1st of May, a circular was issued, at a time when no farmer requires binder twine, for his crop ; but in a few days the quality which was made 650 feet to the pound was all bought up. The regulation was that this was to be sold to the farmers only. Have we any information it was sold to the farmers ?
Yes, if my word is worth anything. You have all the information you want.
I understood the Minister of Justice to say he was not aware to whom it was sold.
Yes, and I am going to have it investigated. I undertake to give the quantities sold, to whom sold, and the price paid by each party.
I understood it was all picked up by one party.
No, never.

If it was sold to a number of individuals, then can we not get the number of those who purchased it, with the quantities purchased ? We are entitled to know whether it was sold to the farmers, because the resolution required that it should be sold to the farmers only. But if it was sold to the speculators, it is not carrying out the spirit or the letter of the resolution.

I desire to say now, as I have said on previous occasions, that this is not a business that the government should go into at all. The statement made by the hon. member shows that it has not been a success.
Since the present government took hold of it.

It has never been a success. We had trouble after trouble, and judgment after judgment against purchasers 111
of the twine when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power.
Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that it was not managed on business principles ?

According to the evidence given against the late government and statements made by hon. gentlemen opposite that things are not just right now, I would say decidedly that it was not managed on business principles. I believe the business is done now as well as any government can do it. But my point is that it is not in the interest of the country that any government should engage ill that kind of work.

I do not think this is a time for recrimination, nor for a discussion as to the way in which this was managed. If I wanted to go back to ancient history I might tell the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule) that when we took charge of the business in 1896 there was $50,000 odd of the price of the output of 1894 that had not been paid. Now, I do not want to go into these details, they are unnecessary, and it would not be wise for me to do so if I want to get my estimates through. But this industry has been managed since 1896, perhaps not successfully, but at all events, so far as my knowledge has gone, honestly, and every pound of twine sold from that day to this has been sold on tender, after public tenders were called for, and the output has been given to the man who offered to pay the highest price for it. As I said a moment ago, Mr. John Connor has been connected with this industry since its inception; that is my firm belief, perhaps if I were asked to prove it I might be at a loss to do so. In 1894 and 1895 he was undoubtedly connected with it, and I believe since that time he has continued in connection with every tender that has been put in. I thought under the circumstances it would be wise to make a change with respect to the management of the industry where his brother was in control in Kingston. I do not say there was anything wrong between them, any common understanding between the brothers, because I have no knowledge of anything wrong; still I did not think that the gentleman who was getting the output of the industry should have charge of the industry. A change has been made in that respect, and since 1901 the twine has been sold to the farmers direct. The result was that in 1901 we had a large amount on hand at the end of the year which we sold by public tender, and since 1902, it is now being sold to the farmers. As far as last year is concerned, the hon. gentleman will find in the Auditor General's Report the names of the farmers to whom the twine was sold, the prices paid and the amount sold to each man. So far as this year is concerned, all that has been sold up to the present time I will account for, I will give the names of the persons to



whom it was sold, the prices paid, and the amount sold to each. Now, with respect to the industry itself, if it is to be regarded as a regulator of the price of twine, I suppose to some extent it has effected that purpose. The amount of binder twine, if I am correctly informed, used in Canada, is 10,000 tons, of which 2,250 tons are manufactured in Canada. At Kingston the extreme limit of our capacity is only 500 tons. So to some extent it seems to me this may be considered a regulator of the price of binder twine. But with respect to the other feature of the business, let us bear in mind that we must find some occupation for the inmates of the penitentiary. Bet me say what we have accomplished by the means of this industry. We have charged against this output which we have put on the market by convict labour, $6,598 for one year. We give them a useful occupation and we realize that amount of money. We charge, in addition to the $6,598, the salaries of the officials connected with the industry. Then, in addition to that, we have the plant which is there. We charge for depreciation of the plant, five per cent, and we charge for interest on capital invested in that industry, three per cent. I do not know if there is any industry connected with the government that shows anything like the same result. Take the Printing Bureau here. I had recently occasion to look into that in connection with the prices they charged. They make no charge for plant depreciation, building, or the like.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And they run in debt.
I do not know whether they do or not.
Have you the amount of the salaries there ?

Formerly there was a superintendent, Mr. Connor, to whom we paid $1,500 and an assistant superintendent to whom we paid $900. Now the superintendent and the assistant superintendent have disappeared and we have appointed one man named Dickenson as superintendent of cordage at $1,000 to do the work of them both. The $2,400 in salaries formerly paid to Messrs. Connor and Price are saved, and we now have a man at $1,000 a year as superintendent.
Mr.l CLARKE. Would the hon. minister give us again the total amount of the twine estimated to be used in Canada and the total amount manufactured in Canada ?

It is almost impossible to get a correct estimate, but I have had an inquiry made by the inspector, and according to the returns I find that the total amount used in the country was about 10,000 tons, and the total amount manufactured in Canada by the industries here 2,250 tons last year. The limit of our capacity is 500 tons, but as a matter of fact, we have not exceeded 400 tons.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: The fact is then that nearly three-fourths of the twine is made on the other side of the line 1
What is the object of selling binder twine at a lower price than the farmer can buy it for from a retail merchant ?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Kemp) is a business man and he will appreciate the reason which I am about to give. We pay for our raw material, manilla 8-42 cents per pound, which is a better price than the' ordinary manufacturer has been able to get it at because we happened to pick it up at a time when the market was favourable; New Zealand 6 90 cents per pound, and Mexican sisal 5-50 cents per pound. If you add together the items making up the cost of manufacturing including oil, bags and paper, repairs, renewals, convict labour, salaries, freight, depreciation in plant and interest you will find that it adds 1-813 cents to the cost. As a result of that we manufactured 16,000 pounds running 650 feet, 120,000 pounds of 600 feet, and 86,000 pounds of 500 feet and 4,000 pounds of 500 feet. Taking the cost of pure manilla at 8-42 cents a pound, and adding the cost of production amounting to 1-82 cents per pound it gives us 10-24 cents per pound as the cost.
When you speak of pure manilla you mean that there is not more than one-third of pure manilla in it.
I am discussing the question of cost.
The question of cost will depend on what you put into the binder twine. When you speak of pure manilla you must understand that the twine does not contain pure manilla.

The hon. member is a doctor and of course an expert. I am a lawyer and I am not an expert. The inspector tells me that pure manilla means pure manilla. Take the cost of pure manilla at 8-42 cents per pound and the cost of manufacture at 1-82 cents per pound, that gives us the cost at 10-24 ceuts per pound and we put it on the market at 10f cents a pound and in ton lots or to clubs of farmers at one-quarter of a cent less than that price.

I can tell the hon. Minister of Justice that there is not a pound of pure manilla twine made in Canada today. The fact was brought out in the report of the committee which looked into the question that pure manilla twine was not all made out of manilla but that it was a mixture.
Of course I defer to the better knowledge of my hon. friend, but I have to rely on the reports of the two inspectors who are both here and who both re-aflirm that pure manilla is pure manilla twine.

I do not know that it is necessary to discuss tlie question as to whether pure manilla means pure manilla or not. The Brantford Company which I believe for years has made as good twine as you will find anywhere in Ontario, or perhaps anywhere in Canada, I was positively informed by one of the directors, who, at the present time, has a seat in this House, make their best twine out of 60 per cent manilla and 40 per cent sisal. My own impression is that any twine that contains 60 per cent manilla and the balance of sisal is equally as good and is much better than twine that is made absolutely of manilla. In fact I do not think that the farmers care about twine made entirely of manilla fibre. That may be the reason why the Kingston twine is not as popular in the country as it ought to be. Go through western Ontario and you will find that the twine made at Kingston is not popular with the farmers. They will buy other twine in preference to the Kingston twine, and it may be for the reason that they put in more manilla than should be put in. The difference in cost is not so very material. I find by reference to the Auditor General's Report of last year that whilst manilla hemp cost 6 cents per pound, sisal cost 51 cents per pound, only a fraction of a cent difference. It may be that I am not sufficiently familiar with the mode of calculating to arrive at just what a pound of twine ought to cost, but I followed the hon. Minister of Justice very closely, and *1 confess that I am entirely unable to reach the high figure of 111 cents as the cost of a pound of twine.
I said 10-24 cents.

Well take the lower price of 10-24 cents. A pound of twine does not consist all of manilla or all of manilla and sisal. We know that there is about one-fifth part of what is called cordage oil, a coarse oil that goes into the manufacture of twine. My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) here says one-sixth, but there is not very much difference between one-fifth and one-sixth. I have always understood it to be one-fifth. Now, taking one-fifth as oil, 60 per cent of the balance as manilla and the remainder sisal, I make out the cost of a pound of twine in this way :	The actual cost of the material would be the one-half of six cents which is the cost per pound of the raw material.
Where does my hon. friend find the six cents ?
In the Auditor General's Report for 1902, page 27-M.
I am figuring on the price paid to-day.

I am not aware that there has been any great disturbance in the market from which we buy this raw ma-' 111J
terial, and I have not access to any better guide than the Auditor General's Report. I will give the minister the calculation I have made. The manilla fibre in a pound of twine would cost three cents ; the sisal would cost two cents and the cordage oil one cent which would make six cents. Adding the cost of manufacture and the other incidentals the minister has referred to, we will say two cents, it would make the cost of a pound of twine eight cents which falls very far short of the ten and a quarter cents which is the price fixed. On this basis we would get it down to something like the cost that twine was manufactured at some years ago. I fail to see that the farmers are receiving justice at the hands of the minister, and I am afraid that in selling it at ten and one quarter cents he is demanding a large profit from the farmers. The late hon. David Mills when Minister of Justice stated that the cost of manufacture was three quarters of one cent per pound, and even allowing for the other things which the present Minister of Justice adds, it would seem that the price charged to the farmers is unreasonable when we consider that according to the Auditor General's Report he pays six cents for manilla, five and three-eights cents for sisal and nine cents a gallon for cordage oil. Eight cents a pound is a reasonable price to sell this twine to the farmers if it is intended that no profit should be made by the government. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser), who has now left the House, endeavoured to introduce the political element into this discussion. He said that the manufacture of twine was started in the prison for political reasons. I will give the hon. gentleman the credit for making one correct statement to-night. It was started by his friends in the central prison in Toronto no doubt to gain political advantages. That was however, years prior to the plant being installed in Kingston by the late Conservative government, They simply followed suit, and in order to offset what their political opponents were doing in Toronto. I shall not enter upon the larger question as to whether it is advisable to continue this industry in the Kingston penitentiary. The minister has told us that it is necessary to keep the prisoners employed, and they might as well be employed in making twine as anything else, but I do say that so long as twine is manufactured in Kingston it ought to be manufactured not for the purpose of making a profit but for the purpose of using it as a lever to maintain a fair level of price. As was said by the member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke) three-fourths of the twine used in Canada to-day is imported from the United States. These large American trusts combine together, and I am sorry to say they have combined with some of the smail Canadian factories to raise the price unduly to the farmer. Twine is not worth ten cents or eleven cents a pound, much less fifteen or sixteen cents, and I have no

doubt that the farmers will be called upon to pay by retail fifteen cents a pound for this American twine this year. The Kingston penitentiary is only able to turn out out about one-fortieth part of the total consumption, but still that is a factor and it may be used as a lever to protect the farmers against the exorbitant charges made by importers and by the large manufacturers in the United States who practically control this industry in Canada. I hope the day is not far distant when the government will see its way clear to encourage this industry in more ways than one. There was a time when we had a respectable duty on twine and when the greater part of the twine used in Canada was made in this country. Under the protective system the competition among Canadian factories maintained a fair level of price, but an agitation was started in favour of removing the duty and it was gradually reduced from 25 per cent to 121 per cent and finally it was removed altogether. The lower you made the duty the higher you made the price of twine, just the same as in the case of coal oil and barb wire. That has been our experience all along. The Americans keep up a good stiff duty against us of two cents a pound, and if we had an industry in this country manufacturing twine it would have to pay that duty going into the United States while they send their twine in here free. I believe there is to lie a small duty now of about three-eighths of a cent per pound. I maintain, Mr. Chairman that we should continue this industry at Kingston and increase the output as much as possible. I would not advise the government to make any profit out of it, but use it for the purpose of breaking down the price of the American twine that comes into this country. I would not sell the Kingston twine in large quantities to any one man, but would scatter it throughout the country as much as possible amongst farmers or small dealers, and use it in every way possible to operate against the attempts on the part of importers or American manufacturers of twine to unduly enhance the price against our farmers. Even if we should lose thousands of dollars I would not allow any one man to get possession of 200 tons of it so that he can fix the price to suit bimself and charge the farmer what he likes. I hope that will be the policy that the government will pursue. For my part I would rather lose money by it than give up the industry altogether. I believe there is a benefit accruing from it, and so far as I am concerned I would not advocate the making of any profit out of the industry.

I notice in the calculation which the hon. Minister of Justice has given us, that the price per pound for the raw material, taking the thre different kinds together, that manilla at $8.42, the New-Zealand at $6.90, and the Mexican sisal at Mr. HENDERSON.
$5.50, you get the average price per pound of the three kinds. Then $1.81 will cover the cost of the manufacture, which makes the average cost of the three kinds eight and three-quarter cents per pound. But at the prices you quote in your circular the average price would come to ten and two-third cents.
We are not dealing with averages.
Is it not fair to take the three different prices, and put them together and find the average price ?
Certainly not.

If you take 100 pounds of each kind.
The ailNISTER OF JUSTICE. What object has the hon. gentleman in view ?
air. SPROULE. The object is to ascertain the actual cost.
No, the hon. gentleman is trying to make a case.

If you take 100 pounds of each, you get what is the actual price.
The ailNISTER OF JUSTICE. Not at all.
air. SPROULE. Well, I do not know by wbat species of calculation the hon. gentleman can come to any other conclusion. You can only make 300 pounds of twine out of 300 pounds of raw material, except for the additional weight of the crude oil, which is about one-third or one-fourth of a cent a pound. But if you take the three qualities together, 100 pounds of each, you only make out of them 300 pounds. You sell these 300 pounds at the prices stated in this circular-manilla at eleven and a half cents, the other at ten and three-quarter cents, and the Kingston special at nine and a half cents a pound. You sell 100 pounds of each. You add the cost of the three together, you add the cost of manufacturing which the minister has given, and that represents the whole cost, does it not ?

I am afraid my arithmetic is out. I am lost, so far as the calculation of my hon. friend is concerned. You take a ball of manilla hemp containing 600 feet for which I paid $8.42 per 100 pounds. To that you must add ten per cent for waste, which is replaced by ten per cent of oil. When I make up my calculation as to what this has cost, for the purpose of ascertaining the price at which it should be sold, I take the cost of the raw material and the cost of the oil, but I have nothing to do with the average cost of New Zealand or Mexican sisal, which does not enter into the calculation at all.

What difference does that make if you take 100 pounds of each,

add them together, and divide by three. You have only so many pounds of twine, which costs you so much money. 100 pounds of one kind costs $8.42, 100 pounds of another $0.90, and 100 pounds of the third, $5.50. Add these together and divide by three, and you have the average price of the three. Then X take the average price at which the binder twine is sold, which is ten and two-thirds cents per pound, while according to the minister's calculations, the average cost was eight and three-quarter cents per pound.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) I think we have carried this debate far enough. The subject has been stretched too long. The question is, shall we go on manufacturing binder twine at the Kingston penitentiary ? I think the sense of the House is that we should, and that the farmers of the country should get the benefit of it. My idea is that we should take means to increase the output at Kingston penitentiary, not only for the benefit of the farmers, but for the sake of the men in the penitentiary. At a certain time some of them may come out to earn their own living, and they may be trained to some useful employment. The Minister of Justice is glad to receive advice from the opposition as well as from the supporters of the government in this respect, and if my advice would be worth anything, it would be that he should see that the best and most improved machinery be used in the Kingston penitentiary, and that the facilities be enlarged so that the output would be larger and the farmers would have the benefit. I do not think the price is too high, otherwise the farmers would not buy the twine from the penitentiary in preference to buying it from other manufacturers of the article. But I agree that it could be sold at such a price that there should be no large profit made, but that the farmers should get the whole benefit.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I fully agree with what my hon. friend has just said, if the farmers were getting the benefit; but since this government have undertaken the handling of binder twine, the farmer has been the man who has been fleeced, and the jobber has got the benefit. If my hon. friend will look at the Auditor General's Report at page M-47, he will find the sales given, as follows Beaver, 180 pounds at eight and one-third cents and 5,125 pounds at eight and one-half cents to the farmers; and 366,793 pounds, the balance of that quality, to Mr. John Connor, or Mr. Henderson Black, who represents him, at five and one-tenth cents.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) I am dealing with the future, not the past.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
This is the way it was dealt with up to the first of July, 1902. Why should this government sell the twine to this man John Connor for less than the cost of the raw material ? We have maple leaf, sold 17,325 pounds at ten cents. Was that
sold to the farmers ? John Connor got 220,000 pounds mixed manilla at five and a tenth cents, and the government are paying eight cents per pound for the pure manilla. The New Zealand was all sold at six and a half cents per pound, but none of it was sold to the farmers. The next sale is 60,000 pounds at four and five-eighths cents, and at the same time the farmer paid nine and a quarter cents for what he got. John Connor was a lucky man. Henderson Black was only another name for John Connor. $12,000 worth was sold directly to John Connor, and $32,000 worth "sold to Henderson Black. There was $45,000 worth sold at four and five-eighths cents in job lots, and then the department turned about and bought raw material for the next year's manufacture. There was evidently some job in every one of these dealings. First it was Hobbs Hardware Company, and then H. N. Bate, and afterward John Connor.

My hon. friend forgets that he is speaking to the committee and imagines that he is speaking to some meeting in a back constituency, otherwise he would appreciate the fact that a parliament in 1900 directed the sale of binder twine to be made to the farmers up to the first of July, after which date it was to he sold by public tender. Up to the 1st of July, 1901, it was sold direct to the farmers, and then the balance on hand was sold by public tender by parliament's direction. If my hon. friend see a job in that, I will go before a committee any time he choses.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is in the position of a trustee, and if he called for tenders and accepted a tender for the manufactured article at a less price than he could buy the raw material at, how can he justify that ?
The time for selling was gone by and it would depreciate 50 per cent if kept over a year.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not in business, or he would know that it would keep two or three years without depreciating.

We should know what this binder twine costs and whether it has been sold to the farmers at less than the cost or more. The complaint is that while the government have convict labour, they sell at the same price as in the retail stores.
There is not a manufacturer in the country who sells that at the same price as we do. I have letters from manufacturers complaining about our prices.

I can tell the hon. minister that it was sold, last year at the stores at the same prices.

We are talking of present prices.

What I complain of that it was not sold to the farmers at the cost price plus one cent a pound, which is what the resolution required. The hon. gentleman should bring his experts from the Kingston penitentiary before the Agricultural Committee.
I agree.
The information given to-night differs from that given a few years ago, and we wish to ascertain whether the firms are getting binder twine in accordance with the resolution.

I see that in the calculation which the Minister of Justice has made that the profit on the manilla is 1-26 per hundred or 10 per cent, in the medium twine the profit is 2-04 or 23 per cent. And in the cheaper twine 2-19, or a profit of 30 per cent.
I cannot have given the figures correctly.
The cost of pure manilla is given at 8'50, 1-82, 8-72, and 10-24 per pound. The cheapest was sold at 94 cents.

The cheapest is sisal, sold at 9J cents with a profit of 2 30 cents. Perhaps I should explain. With respect to the manilla the cost of the raw material is 8'42 cents, to which add 182 cents of manufacture, and you have a total of 10-24 cents. That is pure manilla running 050 feet, and sold at 111 cents. Then you have pure manilla-the same material-but running only 000 feet, at 10f cents. Then there is what we call Kingston special, which is made from New Zealand material. That costs 0'90 cents for raw material or adding 1-92 cents for manufacture, a total of 8-72 cents. That is sold for 94 cents. The sisal was purchased last fall at 5-50 cents per pound ; the price to-day is 8 cents per pound. Pure sisal, which cost 5-50 cents a pound for raw material and 1-82 cents for manufacture, a total of 7-32 cents, is sold at 91 cents. I ought to say, perhaps that if my hon. friend (Mr. Clare) would compare these prices with the prices ruling in Chicago on the same date, the 31st of March, he will find that for pure manilla of 650 feet, the Chicago price is 13 cents against 11J cents, which is our price.
MrJ CLARE. What I want to get at is this-why does the hon. minister add 10 per cent to the best twine and about 30 per cent to the cheapest twine ? Why make the farmer pay, more in proportion for the one than for the other ?

The lower grade made from pure sisal is a cheaper article and we have only about 4,000 pounds altogether. As it is a low grade and as we have but a small quantity, the in-Mr. .SPROULE.
spector thought that altogether the raw material is now worth 8 cents per pound, we might fairly put the price at the figure mentioned. It is much cheaper than any one else sells it. If my hon. friend would allow me, when I come back to my estimates, I will bring letters from manufacturers from all over the country complaining of the prices at which we sell binder twine.
Selling Canadian or American binder twine ?
Selling Canadian twine. The price in Chicago fixes the price elsewhere.
Was it not arranged last year that the government should add one cent per pound to the cost of. the binder-twine ?

I think it was left entirely to my discretion to decide. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clare) will remember that a resolution was at one time passed that fixed everything, but last year the Committee on Agriculture discussed the matter and decided that this should be left with me to exercise my own discretion.

I would like to ask the minister a question or two. I listened with great' interest to his statement. Like any other minister, the Minister of Justice must not be expected to carry all the details for whicli we ask in his head, but must necessarily depend largely on what his officers tell him. I wish to call the attention of the hon. minister to two or three matters which are in direct conflict with what he has said. He will remember that a very thorough investigation was made before the Public Accounts Committee two years ago, and that the evidence there went to show that, including all the services the hon. gentleman has enumerated, the cost of manufacturing the twine was one cent per pound. It is an important thing if, from changed conditions, or from the facts not being correctly stated then, or not being correctly stated now, the cost of manufacture is counted as being nearly double what it was counted at before. There was another statement made, a very important one, bearing on the selling of the twine-and, perhaps I may be permitted to digress here for a single moment. I think some question came up between the superintendent at Kingston and the Department of Justice as to whether the twine should be sold at the expiration of a certain time, it not having been sold to the farmers. The Minister of Justice gave it as his opinion that it was necessary, and so the twine was sold. That point I do not intend further to discuss. But' the point to which I wish to call attention, I think the minister will agree, is a very important one. The evidence taken before the Public Accounts, Committee disclosed the fact-correct or incorrect, I am not able to say-that twine did not deteriorate by being held over one

year. But we have from the hon. gentleman's own department two statements in direct opposition to each other, and I would like to ask the minister if he is able to account for that. The witnesses were under oath and were closely examined, and yet there was a clear contradiction. These matters as to the cost of manufacture and as to the affect upon the binder twine of keeping it over one year are important questions. I do not wish to prolong this discussion, but I think the minister will see that these points should be answered.

As to the question of deterioration, the inspector tells me that the result of keeping the binder twine in their warehouse is that the oil is apt to run out and the twine therefore may not work so satisfactorily as new twine would, and the farmer would not buy twine which had. been kept in the warehouse from one season to another, or, if he did, would not pay so much for it as for new twine. The proportion of deterioration is a matter of opinion. I had not consulted the inspector when I said that I believed that it would deteriorate 50 per cent, and I do not wish the officials to be held responsible for a statement that I made on my own responsibility. As to the cost of manufacture, I confess that I do not recollect the evidence given before the committee two years ago, I cannot carry the evidence so long in my memory. I will give the basis on which I proceed, and I think it is a fair one. First, I take the actual cost of raw material that goes into the manufacture of binder twine. Then I add the cost of labour at the same price as free labour.
If the hon. gentleman will permit me-

I will explain that as the inspectors puts it to me. They charge thirty cents per day for convict labour, and, as we feed and clothe and house these people, they count the total expense the same as free labour. Then I add the salaries of the officials connected with the industry, also the advei'tising and the freight on material. Then I add 5 per cent for depreciation of the plant-which I think is a very low allowance-and 3 per cent for interest. That is the basis of my calculation. And, as I say, it seems to me, to be a fair one. The result is a total of T81 cents and a fraction per pound-practically two cents in round figures.

The hon. gentleman has made what appears to be a fair statement. But I am amazed at the statement that was made on a former occasion when all these services were said to be taken into consideration. Now, could the hon. gentleman tell us offhand how much is charged to labour, how much for deterioration, how much for interest, and so on ?

These items are used to fix the price of the output of the present year, and we had to take the items of the expenditure for the past year to ascertain the true amount. We manufactured in 1898-99 and in 1899-1900, 1,726,320 pounds of fibre, for oil, bags and paper we paid $5,436.40 ; for repairs and renewals, $1,109.85 ; for convict labour, $6,598.35 ; salaries, advertising, freight, &c., $11,910.39; depreciation, five per cent, $4,000; interest three per cent for two years, $2,400. That makes itemized over each pound, 1 "813.

With regard to this bugaboo of depreciation, my experience is this : For three years in succession we kept twine over every year on my farm. I asked the men whether they found the twine to run all right and to give satisfaction, and they said it worked equally well with that which was bought fresh every year. Of course, we can imagine that it might dry a little.

Could the minister give us the cost per diem of the prisoners in the various penitentiaries ?

Manitoba penitentiary, $50,100.
I would ask the Minister of Justice if there is an understanding that some item will be reserved on which we may have a further discussion on penitentiaries ?
I will hold over any item my hon. friend may wish. I suggested a moment ago that we could resume this discussion in the Agricultural Committee.
That committee is rather overburdened now with work, and I doubt if we will be able to resume it there this session.
The minister has sent me over his report, but I do not find any place where the cost is given of the keep of the prisoners in the various penitentiaries.
